AN EXPERIENCE OF GRACE

St. Augustine's doctorate rests primarily on four things: an experience, a philosophy, a theology, and an ecclesiastical tradition of grace. Firstly, he, like few others, has a rich experience, fructified with the failure of a culture, of a religious or soteriological philosophy, the most admirable of antiquity. K. Adam has described his theology as a theology of experience: ist seine Theologie Erlebnistheologie2. This does not mean that for the holy Doctor a doctrine is a subjective projection, or a simple fact of consciousness, or a vital moment of an immanent process of the spirit, but rather a wonderful adaptation of a truth or a revealed fact to a very rich experience. The previous expression offers particular interest when talking about the theology of grace, which has a kind of experimental proof in the conversion of Saint Augustine. Thus, Father Chenu writes very well: "Saint Augustine has renewed in himself, let's put it this way, the religious experience and Christological realism of Saint Paul. Like Saint Paul, Saint Augustine carries in his soul and in his flesh the characteristics of the Christian: the feeling of sin and the misery of man without God. In the centuries of the history of Christianity there is no individual experience that has had so much repercussion, so much echo in the expression of Christian thought, as the painful experience of the son of Monica. Under the tension of his impotence, he has found, he has forged the expressive formulas of the mystery of the decadence of man at the same time as the omnipotence of grace. It is not only the dogma of the transcendence and the absolute gratuitousness of grace, which is already contained in the symbol of faith, but the very spirit of Christianity, the divine life in sinful man, which is universally fixed through this unique case. For both the Apostle and the Doctor of Grace, conversion was an intimately felt gift from God, like a sudden liberation due to a generous and brave hand. Conversion elevated the existence of both to a new beginning and a death of the past. Not that everything past remained dead and buried or that a total resurrection animated the new existence. Just as sin leaves many human essences intact, so also the newness of the Christian life, or resurrection by grace, respects and consecrates multiple aspects of the being. In the Augustinian experience, captured in its antecedents and consequences, three things stand out: the palpation of one's own misery, the feeling of psychological emptiness, of the weakness of the spirit to rise by itself to a higher life; Augustine traveled and knew well that royal egestatis, that country of misery and hunger that is the self abandoned to its own resources, disconnected from commerce with its Creator, or what he calls vita fluitans in obscuritate sua, life made a tremendous and painful enigma, a burden and sheaf of anxieties and dissatisfactions. In itself, the love of the creature is indigent and miserable and prone to slavery: Egenus et indigus amor. ita düigit ut rebus quas düigit subiiciatur *. A poor and indigent love loves so much that it remains imprisoned in what it loves. Slavery, that is, prison, is the irremediable destiny of love from creature to creature when it is not guided by the love of the Creator. In the epistle addressed to the pagans of Madaura he considers the triple aspect of divinity: as a universal principle from which everything we see proceeds, and as a Word, with which the greatness of divine majesty is spoken and expressed to Himself (quo se ipsa summitas maiestatis narrat et praedicat), and as holiness or ineffable and undivided communication of the originating principle and the Word that proceeds from Him: Est quaedam sanctitas omnium quae sancta fiunt sanctificatrix32. That union with which the Word returns to its beginning expresses the movement and essence of all holiness, as well as its universal source. Saint Augustine takes pleasure in this Trinitarian perspective when contemplating the divine being and its manifestations. His is a deeply personalist theology, because it moves in the sphere of the most august mystery of Christianity. "But the divine being is essentially communicative and fontal. Its richness and plenitude tends to double expansion: one internal, which gives rise to the mystery of the Trinity; another external, which is manifested in the works of creation and sanctification. There is no degree of being that does not come from the divine source. Creatures are drops of dew emanating from divine goodness and beauty. Hence the dialectic of spiritual elevations, so common in Saint Augustine: Si rorem sic amatis, fontern ipsum quomodo amabitis? Xi Everything that exists, everything that is light, everything that is good comes from the first Cause, from the first light, from the sovereign good. condidisti, tu non deseris qui creasti 15. The good being that the Saint speaks of is the good use of free will, which must be counted among the great goods that a creature can possess. There are large, medium and minimum goods. Among the means is free will, because we can misuse it; but it is of such a category that without it you cannot live well either. Its good use is virtue, which is counted among the great goods that no one misuses. And since all goods, as has been said, the great, the medium and the lowest, come from God, it follows that the same origin has the good use of the free will, that is, virtue, which belongs to the first category 17. Formally, this increase of being for good is a similarity with its principle or image. Saint Augustine describes the formation of the spirit as a process of illumination and assimilation to the Word, which is its exemplar. Like this, the human spirit is the image of God, which passes from a formless life to a formed life. Living is not the same as living well, that is, wisely and happily. It comes out of its formlessness and acquires its perfection when it is converted to the light of the Word, which is the immutable wisdom and source of its intellectuality, which does not stop speaking with hidden language to its created image so that it converts to that which is its origin, since otherwise it cannot reach its form and perfection 1S. This process of formation of the spiritual being is a dark zone of relationships between the creature and the Creator where the supernatural action of the first cause is easily inserted to attract the spirit itself. That is why the Word has a transcendental significance in the religious thought of Saint Augustine. As the image of the Father, it is his definition, his epiphany, his torch and his glory. It is also the organ of the deification of the free creature, associated with a mysterious personal communion, in which created holiness consists. If the proper and personal nature of the Word is to be the image and likeness of the Father, it is therefore the eternal and subsistent form of all similarities. It has no trace of dissimilarity with its principle. THEOLOGY OF GRACE

But, above all, Saint Augustine is the theologian of grace, that is, the scrutinizer and interpreter of divine thoughts in order to the plan of human deification. Since his conversion he always worked for a deep understanding of the oracles of the Lord and divine operations in favor of the human race. P. de Lagarde counted in his works some 42,816 biblical quotations, which give us an approximate idea of the assimilation of the holy books achieved by Saint Augustine. He always wanted to found truths on the certainty of divine faith and the sure judgments of the Church, its depositary. Thus it became an instrument of development and doctrinal progress particularly in the matter we are dealing with. Redemption constitutes a supernatural process of incorporation of men into Christ. The incarnation and deification are two moments of this salvific process, which Saint Paul defines as a mystery and, therefore, as an object of revelation in both Testaments. Only with the torch of the divine word can we approach him. That is, in the inspired books we are instructed about the origin, obscuration and renewal of the image of God, imprinted on man. THE TRADITION OF THE DOCTRINE OF GRACE

One of the objections that the Pelagians presented to the doctrine of Saint Augustine was its novelty. Et nos conantur arguere quod wliquid novum dicamus. They insist on accusing me that I am an innovator in the Church 71. The accusation was unfounded, because the Doctor of Grace organized a teaching contained in the Catholic tradition without separating himself from the rule of faith, or norm of the authority of the Church, from the antiqua et indubitatu regula fidei, to which he alludes in the polemic against his enemies 72. The Pelagians were truly the friends of novelties, because "when has there not been prayer in the Church for the infidels so that they believe? When did relatives not pray for the conversion of their relatives and relatives to the faith, if they were not faithful? Who has not ever prayed for continuation and perseverance in the faith? Nor who has rebuked the priest for having invoked the Lord to grant the gift of faith to those who do not have it? Just as the Church was already found at birth with these prayers, so it was born and grew and grows with this faith, professing it? that the grace of God is not granted according to the merits of those who receive it" 7S. This living tradition, incorporated into the Church, was one of the firm supports of the Bishop of Hippo, and that is why he could boldly tell them: "Let them know that I defend the true Catholic faith, founded in antiquity": Sctant a nobis rectam et antiquitus fundatam catholicam fidem defendí™. And he returned to them the insulting epithet of innovators, describing their naturalism as novitas, error novus, novitius, novitia deformitas, perversitas novitia, pestis novitia, novitia pestilentia, dogma novum, novellum, etc. He triumphantly embraces the faith of the Church when he says, for example, regarding original sin, the scandal of the new heretics: "This the Church always maintained, this it professed, this it received from the faith of its elders, this it keeps without giving up until the end": Hoc Ecclesia semper habuit, " Serm. 294, 20: PL 38, 1348.

With frequent recourse to Catholic tradition, Saint Augustine has rendered a notable service to the introduction of theology, because, as Hofmann says, "he has incorporated the teaching of the Fathers in dogmatic proofs to the place that it still retains today; like the first, he knew its high significance, as well as its limits." 82. Liturgical arguments also had demonstrative value for him against the Pelagians. Regarding the prayers that he himself made for the conversion of some of his friends affiliated with Manichaeism S 3, he writes in his Retractations: "Praying in this way, he already believed that not only those converted to God receive the help of grace so that they progress and perfect themselves, but also conversion God belongs to the same grace, since He prayed for those who were far removed from Him so that they would convert to Him "Yes. 6.

The first runs from his conversion to the publication of the book On Various Questions, addressed to Simplician, bishop of Milan (386-397). It is distinguished by an optimistic conception of the nature of man. On his own initiative he can embrace the faith, laying the foundations of the new life: Quod ergo credimus nostrum est: quod autern bonum operamur illius est, qm credentübus dat Spiritum Sanetum 85. "I had not yet delved into the gratuitous and supernatural value of faith, considering it as a fruit of man's natural efforts and investigations": Nostrum est enim credere et velle. Although in good faith, he then professed the error that he later had to combat among the Semi-Pelagians 86. In the aforementioned book to Simplician he formulates his new doctrine on the gratuitousness and supernaturality of faith even in its beginning, so that the initiative to believe is the work of divine mercy and not of human will, although this has its own part in the consent to faith. Pelagius considered the possibility of nature as a fertile root that, through the work of human will, can flourish in virtues or become covered with thorns of vices. For Saint Augustine, the root is a divine gift, charity. "Where, if we consider what he (Pelagius) said, he put an identical root in the good and the bad, contrary to the doctrine of the Gospel and the apostles. For the Lord does not say that the good tree can produce bad fruit, nor that the bad tree produces good fruit. And the Apostle, by calling greed the root of all evil, implies that charity must be considered the root of all good. Therefore if two trees, one good and the other bad, mean two men, one good and the other bad, which one? will be the good but the one who has good will, that is, a good root? And what will be the bad one if not the one of the bad will, that is, the one of the bad root? Because the fruits of these trees and roots are the sayings, the actions, the thoughts, and the good ones come from the good will, and the bad ones, from the bad one. And man produces good fruits when he receives the grace of God" 20. For Saint Augustine, the most intimate and decisive thing in man is charity, the tendency to good, and in that depth subsoil works divine grace to heal its roots and produce fruits of justice. In summary: the names of illumination and inspiration designate the two forms of influence that God exercises on the understanding and will of man to elevate his works to a category of higher justice. Which does not mean that the first Cause cannot act or does not act in other lower faculties, such as the imagination and the sensitive appetite, just as there are also external graces, which are given even using other creatures, whose action is ordered by divine Providence for the sanctification of its chosen ones. And what is the extent of this divine influence and divine help in man? According to Saint Augustine, good and just action in the supernatural sense is subject to this influence in its entirety, that is, in its three moments: before operating, in the course of the operation and at the end of it. Such is the result of the division of grace into prevenient, exciting or operative, into adjuvant, or cooperating or concomitant, and the final, or perseverance. God is at the beginning, in the middle and at the end of the good work. It acts from outside and inside with deep intimacy and strength. External graces such as preaching, good examples, salutary counsels, fears of conscience are sterile without the secret and immediate influence of God. As the illuminator of consciences, He is the inner Teacher 22. The fundamental and first stone of the supernatural building must be laid by God, from whom come the aids that are called prevenient, exciting and oppressive grace. God prevents, anticipates, awakens and acts when man is unprepared, asleep or lazy for action. Mercy eius praeveniet me. Saint Augustine supports his doctrine in this passage of the psalm: "He anticipated to heal us and will continue to intervene later so that we achieve our development; he came forward to call us and will follow us until we achieve glory; he provided for us to live piously, because without Him we can do nothing" 23. Without prevenient grace, not only is the work not completed, but it is not even begun on our part. This passage offers us a beautiful analogy to glimpse these mysteries of divine and creature action. The Pelagians considered human nature as a boat moved by the oars of free will, which take it to the port of beatitude. By himself, man can do all good and deserve eternal life. But, according to the Catholic and Augustinian conception, man is like a boat with rows and sail, for whose healthy movement personal effort is not enough, but the wind of grace and favor from God is also necessary, which communicates its impulse. Without the help and help from above, the poor human boat remains immersed in the sand of the flesh and is lost among the waves, without arriving at the port of its fortune. Grace, anticipating the movement of the oars, fills the sails of the spirit, gives it a certain impulse and motion to good, with which free will stretches and encourages itself. Then man can do two things: either despise the first motion of the heavenly and favorable wind or second it and move the oars and direct with his own effort where the superior action impels him. In this case, the wind does not stop blowing, and combining with the action or consent of the free creature, it moves to its end. And this movement is action and passion at the same time, because the soul moves. and it is moved, with an operation that is not only attributed to God, as the first mover, but also to the soul itself. And here grace is cooperating, because it is seconded by the free consent of the creature. Throughout the journey it does not lack this auxilium gratiae, which by virtue of the Holy Spirit is communicated to us for our help in each of the acts: Subministratione Sancti Spiritus datur, ut ad nostros singulos actus adiuvemur2S More. especially at the entrance to the port, in the trance of death, full of more dangerous reefs and storms, a special gift is granted, called magnum perseverantiae donum, the great gift of perseverance.
Thus, divine help prevents or anticipates, and is prevenient grace; It helps and cooperates, adding to the creature's own efforts, and it is cooperating grace, helper or Serm.

The combination of the two forces, rowing and sailing, presents us with the difficult problem of free will and grace. The so-called cooperating grace involves human cooperation. Against Protestants and fatalists of all kinds, this is an uncontested principle of the Augustinian theology of grace. Saint Augustine was not only the Doctor of Grace against the Pelagians, but also the defender of free will against the Manichaeans and their modern disciples Luther and Jansenius. He always denounced at this point the pitfalls that must be avoided: that of Pelagianism, or excessive confidence in healthy and natural forces, and that of fatalistic and passive distrust, which nullifies all personal effort, because it denies free will. Oars and sail must be given to the man. "No one, then, dares to give so much thought to free will that he insists on annulling the prayer we pray: Do not lead us into temptation. Likewise, no one dares to deny the discretion of the will, nor dare to excuse sin. Let us rather listen to the Lord, who commands us and helps us; he commands us what we must do and helps us to do it. For some, excessive confidence in their own will made them arrogant; and others, excessive distrust. in his will he threw them into negligence. Those say: "Why pray to God so that temptation does not overcome us, if that is in our power? "These say: "Why strive to live well, if that is a thing of God?" Oh God, oh Father, do not let us fall into either of these two temptations, but deliver us from evil." 29. God does not annul any good principle of nature, but rather with his action he adjusts to its style and way of being, necessarily moving beings that do not have freedom and freely those that are free. "God is called our helper, and He cannot be so if the one who is helped does not spontaneously put in some effort of his own. Because God does not work salvation in us as if we were insensitive stones or things created by Him without reason or will. But why He helps one and not the other, why more so-and-so than So-and-so, and this one in one way and that one in another, that is an arcana, and in it is the reason for such hidden justice and the excellence of such power" 30.

In the light of three epithets we must illustrate the effects of grace in us: Grafía delectans, sanans, liberans. The holy Doctor says: "There were, however, in the Old Testament men who lived not only under the faith that intimidates, argues and punishes, but also under grace, which delights, heals and liberates: Sub gratia delectante, healing, liberating" 35. God acts in man, healing him, freeing him, delighting him. There is a gratia sanans and a gratia liberatrix. "Man perished by his free will; the God-Man came with the grace of liberation": Venit Deus homo per gratiam liberatricem3e. Far from opposing freedom, grace breaks its bonds and removes it from the tyrannis cupiditatis, from the servitude of greed and disordered desires. Christ with his grace is the universal medicine: Nemo itaque liberat a vulneribus illius trucidatoris, nisi huius gratia Salvatoris42. In concrete terms, the two main wounds on whose healing Saint Augustine so insists are the tumor superbiae and putredo concupiscentiae. When exposing the Augustinian doctrine, extraordinary importance is usually given to what we are going to call concupiscentialism, as if it were the first or main wound of man. Without denying the seriousness of concupiscence, there is another earlier and more pestiferous evil, namely, the internal tumor of pride, which affects the spirit, as concupiscence affects the flesh more. Pride is also a kind of lust of the spirit or morbid complacency in oneself, in one's health and strength, rejecting the voluptas Creatoris, the clean and elevated joy of the Lord. Therefore, in the divine plan of redemption, the extirpation of pride constitutes one of the primary purposes of the incarnation of the Word, who has come, as an omnipotent Physician, to cut us and cure us of the Pe'lagian tumor, and the excessive confidence in the force of nature and free alphaedrium: Venit sanare tumorem nostrum magnus Medicusis. Once the swelling of the spirit has subsided, temperance easily comes, or let's say, the humility of the flesh. From both wounds the man bleeds, losing the vital energies of his being. Therefore, as consequences, ignorance and difficulty also follow (ignorantia et difficultasj. Pride darkens the spirit, separating it from the sources of divine light, and leaving it in its own dark terrestrial mansion, and sensuality exhausts and weakens the energy of the will, creating in it a state of indolence and laziness for all virile and noble action.

There is a decisive psychological factor: bad habits, which, when they are strong and dominate us, constitute a moral necessity 51. Man's weakness comes from his mortal origin and his assiduity in indulging in pleasures. The first derives from original sin, and the second, from the punishment of multiplying personal sins. The first is an inheritance of birth; the second, ballast and addition to life. Both things, like nature and custom united, make concupiscence very robust and invincible, and that is what he calls sin and says that it dwells in the flesh, that is, that it exercises as a certain empire and kingdom 62. Spiritual slavery imposes diabolical domination as a consequence, because man, as a creature ontologically weaker than pure spirits, upon emancipating himself from the divine omnipotence, which protects him, falls into the hands of the devil, who with his perversity and envy aspires to counteract the kingdom of God. Slavery to sin and diabolical slavery mean the same thing, because the devil held us in bondage with sins: Non enim tenebat nos nisi vinculis peccatorumBS. With the remission of sins comes freedom: Remissa iniquitate liberarissi. Diabolical slavery is punishment for desertion from God. He who does not want to serve the good King must necessarily go to the galleys of the devil: "God condemns man for vice, which dishonors his nature, not for nature, which is not destroyed by vice. It is therefore not surprising nor does it suppose any injustice that man remains subject to the impure spirit not because of his nature, but because of his uncleanness, which he contracted with the original stain and comes from the human will. For even the impure spirit itself is good as a spirit, evil as impure. The first is the work of God, the second of his own will. Therefore, a stronger nature, that is, angelic, brings subject with the bondage of vices to an inferior nature, that is, the human one. Grace also frees us from the wrath of God, which also contributes to bondage and captivity. All religions admit a very peculiar fear of the holy, caused not only by the ontological distance that separates the creature from the Creator, but also by sin, enmity or the wrath of God. Whoever is at enmity with God lives under the torturous pressure that embitters life, like a fugitive criminal, for whom there is no refuge that will free him from the face of the Omnipotent. Only grace, reconciling him, can restore his joy and freedom: Attulit gratiam Dei, abstulit irarn Dei 5fl. "Nothing saves us from this wrath except the grace of God." Humanity is compared to a coin that is originally engraved with the image of a heavenly sovereign. But how did this image and likeness of God remain in man after sin? The expressions that Saint Augustine uses do not imply a total deterioration or a complete disappearance, but rather a tarnishing (decolor amt eam), an invasion of dust and dirt that has diminished the vividness and splendor of the features and divine beauty. The coin, with the friction of the earth, has lost its primitive luster and the shine of its prerogatives, the holy decorum of its innocence, the reflection of the sovereignty of God, and Christ, with his grace, restored it to its ancient glory, strength and royal dignity. But it is convenient to give these metaphors a more proper and clear meaning. And first of all we exclude the hypothesis of a total corruption of human nature as held by Protestants. The man was stripped of supernatural goods and wounded in natural ones. Through guilt "God does not completely take away what he granted to nature, but takes away something and leaves something, so that there is no shortage of those who regret what he has lost. INTRODUCTION *

The anti-Pelagian epistle, written by Saint Augustine to the Roman presbyter Sixtus, who later occupied the Chair of Saint Peter, gave rise to the Doctor of Grace to enrich his abundant production with the book De correptione et gratia. In the aforementioned letter he formulated many of the truths for which he fought, as a theologian of the City of God: v. gr., the existence of free will and grace, its supernatural nature, the justice of God in the salvation of the good and condemnation of the evil, the depth of divine counsels, the merits of the just, the hardening of sinners, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the distribution of heavenly gifts, the value of prayer in the economy of grace, the cooperation of free will, the supernatural origin of the initium fidei, the smallness of the man, who cannot raise his voice before the Most High; the inexcusability of the sinner, the fate of infants who die without baptism. Likewise, the doctrine of predestination and reprobation and the allegory of the dough with which vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath are made to manifest the mercy and justice of God appear there. Some passages of the letter promoted uproar and confusion in the monastery of Hadrumeto, currently Sousse, in the Byzantine province of Africa (Tunisia). It was around the year 426, when the life of Saint Augustine was already declining. Floro, a young religious from that convent, made a trip to Uzala, where one of the oldest and most faithful friends of Saint Augustine was bishop: Evodio. There a copy of the aforementioned letter fell into his hands, and considering it a treasure, with the help of his traveling companion, named Felix, he transcribed it for the library of his monastery. Florus continued his journey to Carthage and Felix returned to Ha* The chronological order in which the treatises contained in this volume should be read is as follows: De spiritu et littera. De natura et gratia, De gratia Christi et peccato originali, De gratia et libero arbitrio, De correptione et gratia, De praedestinatione sanctorum, De dono perseverantiae. Reading the precious document aroused lively curiosity and opposing interpretations, as two sides were formed: five or six monks believed that with such a doctrine free will and human works and even the truth of divine judgment were annulled; others agreed on both things, grace and freedom. When Floro returned he found the peace of the monastery disturbed, and he immediately notified the abbot, who knew nothing of that internal dissension, so harmful to a religious community. Desiring to restore order, the abbot sent a commission to Uzala so that his bishop could declare the meaning of the letter. Evodio wrote to the monastery exhorting them to harmony and explaining the thought of Saint Augustine. The response of the bishop of Uzala was not satisfactory, and so they decided to consult the same author. And, in fact, two contradictors of Augustinian doctrine, Cresconio and Felix, left Hadrumeto for Hippo in order to meet with their bishop, who after receiving them very charitably, gave them the necessary explanations to calm them down, reconciling both things, grace and free will, in accordance with the truth of the divine Scriptures. He also wrote a letter to the abbot explaining how the two proper titles of Christ, Savior and Judge, demonstrated the existence of both truths. And although the monks were in a great hurry to return to their convent to celebrate Easter, at last, at the request of the Saint, they stopped to celebrate it with him. He took advantage of that stay to inform them of the anti-Pelagian literature, of the minutes of the councils of Carthage and Milevi, of the documents addressed to Pope Innocent and his responses, of the correspondence with Pope Zosimus, of the canons of the council of Carthage held in the year 418. At the same time he wrote a new book, entitled Be gratia et libero arbitrio, addressed to the abbot and his monks. With this rich treasure the travelers joyfully returned to their convent, where peace was restored with the news and documents they received from Hippo. They were confused by the generosity and marvelous wisdom of Saint Augustine, who seemed angelic to them. The abbot wrote him a letter full of gratitude and praise, rejoicing that he had contributed with his ignorance to the copious wealth of Catholic doctrine contained in the new book.
However, new difficulties and applications of the doctrine of predestination arose.

Some had drawn this consequence: if God works in us to will and act, it seems that all corrections from superiors are unnecessary. If the Creator is the one who cooperates perficit quod operand incepit; If not only the initiative, but also the completion of the work belongs to God, the superiors must be content with instructing us and praying so that we do not lack the grace to fulfill his commandments, but they cannot neither deny us nor impute any fault to us, when we are deprived of help that God grants to whomever he wills. Such a consequence was extremely dangerous for religious life and contrary to the doctrine of Christ and the apostles. Insubordination, fatalism, and spiritual inertia would spread everywhere. To resolve these difficulties, the Bishop of Hippo wrote the book De correptione et gratia, composed in the year 426 or 427, and sent it to the community of Hadrumeto through Florus. The monks' objections are presented vividly, and the Bishop of Hippo responds to all of them with texts from divine Scripture, with the doctrine of the apostles and the arguments of reason. OF CORRECTION AND GRACE

Grace does not destroy, but preserves the heritage of natural goods: "Ut in melius commutati, quod in nostra natura bonum fecit, impletum summo bono in eius naturae bonitote servemus" T. So that, transformed into a more flourishing state and filled with the highest good, we preserve in the goodness of his nature the good that he worked in ours. Going against a good with which the Creator has endowed his creature is repugnant to the supernatural providence of God, as conceived by Saint Augustine. The insurmountability that the Saint speaks of in the cited passage should not be related to an alleged enslaving action of God, but rather to the strength that divine help imprints on the weak will to resist the most violent contrasts presented by the world, the devil and the flesh. Calvin - supposes the free movement of the creature to be incompatible with divine omnipotence. Saint Augustine also highlights the sovereignty of divine power, which can bend human wills wherever it pleases; But, precisely because it is all-powerful, it saves the ontological rights of the creature, helping it to produce a vital and free movement with a loving lordship, to which all violence and oppression is foreign. In the same Calvinist and Jansenist sense these words have been interpreted: "Nunc vero posteaquam est illa magna peccati merit amissa libertas, etiam maioribus donis adiuvanda remansit infirmitas" s. The great and privileged freedom alluded to in the previous passage is not human free will, as it exists today, but the freedom of innocent man in the vigorous balance of his powers, without the contradiction and fight of sensuality. Human freedom has undergone a historical process whose moments should be noted. In the innocent state man enjoyed perfect freedom, exercising his right of choice without any pressure or flattery from the disordered passions, which were unleashed with the first guilt. Only an easily overcome external suggestion was possible for him. But, once the first and serious fault had been committed, a double inclination towards himself and the sensible world took over, with the consequent deviation from the higher kingdom of eternal goods. Before, he could not sin and preserve the treasure of integrity with which he came into the world; Later, sin became a burden and necessity, viscous for the wings of the spirit, a burden for the carnal and haggard soul. And this burdened, weakened freedom, diminished in its indifference and in its orientation to supraterrestrial values, is free will, which subsists in man as the faculty to cooperate with grace, now responding to the first stimuli, now striving with the help of God to fulfill his commands and deserve eternal life. The first freedom was lost in paradise, the second is the one that remains, diminished in its dominion by other antagonistic forces that militate against it. When Saint Augustine affirms that man has lost freedom, he alludes to vera libertas, also recalled in the following passage: "Sicut ergo non est opus sanis medicus, sed male habentibus, ita non est opus liberis Liberator, sed servis, ut ei dicat gratulatio libertatis: Salvasti de necessitatibus animam meam. Ipsa enim sanitas est vera librrtas. quae non perisset, si bona permansisset voluntas; felixque necessitas" 9. The Jansenists also use this passage to defend their system, but without reason. Augustinian thought is clear. There are degrees in the enjoyment of freedom, as there are in knowledge and love and in bodily health itself. There is an innocent freedom, which does not know sin, and a freedom of the sinner, who has eaten the forbidden fruit, losing the righteousness of the first justice, and a freedom of the redeemed, imperfect and combative man, and a final and victorious freedom, which the righteous possess in glory. In the present state, man, subjected to the yoke of sin and the tyranny of sensuality, enjoys a medium and weak freedom even until he achieves perfect health, which is also true freedom: "Ipsa enim sanitas est vera libertas." He who rejects correction and only admits prayers in his favor must be corrected in that very case so that he also implores divine favor for himself. For that pain that insults him in his own eyes, when he feels the sting of correction, awakens him to a more fervent desire to ask, so that, receiving from the mercy of God an increase in charity, he may abandon the iniquity that insults and debases him and perform works worthy of praise and congratulation. Here is the convenience of correction that is used healthily, proportioning it to the diversity of faults, and then achieves its effectiveness, when the divine Physician looks with eyes of mercy. When they heard him preach the Gospel and say: I tell you, then, brothers, that the Gospel that I preached to you is not according to man, since I did not receive it from any man, but by revelation from Jesus Christ, they could have answered him: Why, then, do you bother us, forcing us to receive and learn what you have not learned or received from any man? He who gave you such a gift is also powerful to do the same to us as to you. Then, if they do not dare to respond in that way, but rather consent to the Gospel being preached to them by a man, even though it can be communicated to man by God, let them also confess that they must be rebuked by their superiors, who are in charge of preaching the doctrine of Christian grace, even without denying that God can, without any intervention from anyone, himself correct whomever he wants and communicate to him with the force of his mysterious and highly effective medicine the pain of penitence. And just as we should not interrupt prayer in favor of those whose conversion we desire, even knowing that, without anyone praying for Peter, the Lord changed him with a look from Him and filled him with contrition for his sin, so we should not omit the rebuke of the guilty, even when God, those He loves, changes their lives without using correction. For this only benefits man when the Lord accompanies it with his mercy and grace, who can convert those he wants without needing to rebuke them. Why these are called to the reform of customs in one way, and those in another, and the others in another, in diverse and innumerable ways, that is not for the clay to judge, but for the potter 1. 9. Our adversaries insist: "The Apostle says: Whose is the gift with which you excel? What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why boast as if you had not received it? Why, then, are we corrected, argued against, rebuked, accused? What are we going to do, if we have not received?" Those who use this language want to appear blameless even for the disobedience they show to God; For certainly obedience is a gift from God, as it is necessarily linked to the one who possesses charity, which, without a doubt, flows from God and is given by the Father to his children. "We have not received charity," they say: "Why then are we rebuked as if we could give it to ourselves and at our discretion we do not want to give ourselves this gift?" And they do not notice that, even in those who are not yet regenerated, there is a first cause why, when they are rebuked for their disobedience to God, they feel disgust with themselves, because God created the righteous man at the beginning of creation, and God cannot be blamed for being unjust. And, consequently, man is responsible for the first evil with which he departs from submission to God, since he lost, through the inclination of his ill will, the righteousness in which he was originally created, and he perverted himself. Should this depravity not be corrected in man, since it is common to all, and not personal, to the one who is rebuked? Rather, let each one also correct what is common to all. Well, just because no one is free from it does not mean that it is no longer personal and unique to each person. In truth, these sins of origin are called foreign sins, because each one inherits them from his parents; and with reason they consider themselves equally ours, because all have sinned in that one man, according to the Apostle. The condemnable origin must therefore be rebuked, so that the pain produced by correction engenders the desire for regeneration; if the corrected one is a child of the promise, so that, as the crack of the scourge and rebuke sounds externally, God infuses the secret of the soul, by mysterious inspiration, with the effective will. And elsewhere he says: O depth of the riches, wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are your judgments and how unsearchable are your ways! As, therefore, he deigns to make known to us his judgments, let us give thanks to him; and if He hides them from us, let us not murmur against His advice, but believe that a very healthy medicine is hidden here too. And you, whoever you are, enemy of the grace of God, who ask such questions, what do you yourself say? Well, you don't deny that you are Christian and you claim to be Catholic. If, then, you confess that perseverance until death is the gift of God, I believe that you are in the same ignorance as I as to why this one receives such a gift, and the other does not; For both of them, God's judgments are impenetrable. Or if you believe that persevering or not persevering in good depends exclusively on man's free will, which you defend not in accordance with divine grace, but to the detriment of it, perseverance not being the gift of God, but the effect of human will, what will you oppose to the words of the Savior: I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail? Will you dare to say that, despite Christ's prayer that Peter's faith would not fail, she would have suffered brokenness if Peter had wanted it, that is, if he had refused to persevere to the end, as if there were a contrast between Peter's will and the prayer of Christ, who prayed that he would want to persevere? Certainly, no one is unaware that Peter's faith would have failed if he had plundered his will, for which he was faithful, and that he would have to remain firm in it if it stood. But since the Lord prepares the wills, the prayer of Christ could not be fruitless for him. Well, when he prayed that his faith would not be broken, did he ask for anything other than that he would have a very free, very strong, most invincible and most persevering will? See, then, how the freedom of the will is very well harmonized with grace, it does not go against it. For the human will does not obtain grace with its freedom, but rather with grace freedom, and to persevere in it, a willing permanence and insurmountable strength. 18. It is certainly a wonderful thing and very worthy of admiration that God does not grant perseverance to some of his children regenerated in Christ, after giving them faith, hope and charity, while he forgives the children of the unbelievers so many crimes and, giving them grace, adopts them as his children.
Who will not be amazed at this? Who is not filled with great astonishment at such a fact? Nor is it any less to be admired, because it is true and something so manifest,

Let us not be surprised that we cannot investigate its impenetrable ways. For, even omitting other innumerable goods that God, our Lord, distributes to some and denies to others to men, without any respect of persons, neither are goods such as agility, strength, freshness of health, bodily beauty, wonderful wits and mental aptitudes for many arts; or those that come from outside, such as opulence, nobility, honors and the like, whose possession is subordinated to divine power; also passing in silence the baptism of infants, which no one can deny is a supernatural good, unlike those mentioned, and without trying to find out why it is given to one and denied to another, when both things are in the hands of God and that sacrament is essential to enter the kingdom of heaven; Leaving and omitting these things, let us examine a little the class of people here alluded to. We are dealing with those who do not have the good of perseverance, but who die after having deviated from the good path due to a defect of their will. Let our adversaries answer, if they are able, why God did not rescue these men, when they lived in faith and piety, from the dangers of the world so that evil would not change their thoughts and illusions would not deceive their souls. Did he perhaps lack the power to do so or the knowledge of his future evils? It would be grave perversity and insipidity to defend either of these two statements.
So why didn't he do it? Let those who mock us respond when, when dealing with such ineffable mysteries, we exclaim: How inscrutable are His judgments and impenetrable!

Will those mentioned by the Gospel be numbered among the disciples, where, after the Lord intimates the precept of taking his flesh and drinking his blood, it is said: This he said while teaching in a synagogue in Capernaum. After hearing it, many of his disciples said: How hard these words are! Who can admit them? When Jesus knew that his disciples were murmuring about this, he said to them: Does this scandalize you? Well, what will it be like to see the Son of God rise to where he was before? The spirit is what gives life, the flesh is of no use. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life; but there are some of you who do not believe. Because Jesus knew from the beginning who were those who did not believe and who was the one who would betray him. 26. Here another important question arises, which I must try and resolve with the help of God, in whose hands we and our words are. Regarding this gift of perseverance in good to the end, I am asked my opinion about the first man, who was created in righteousness and innocence. I do not say: If he did not persevere, how was he without defect, lacking such a necessary divine gift? The answer to this question is simply: he did not have perseverance, because he did not remain in that good, which included exemption from all vice. This began with his fall: then, prior to the fall, he was certainly without vice. Because it is one thing not to have vice and another not to remain in the innocent and vice-free state. We do not say that he was never without vice, but rather that he did not persevere without vice; and, for the same reason, we say that for some time he was innocent and we reproach him for not having persevered in that state. But a more satisfactory answer must be investigated and given to those who say: "If in the righteousness in which Adam was created, without vice, he obtained the grace of perseverance, without a doubt he persevered in it; and if he persevered, then he did not sin or depart from the first justice and from God." But the truth proclaims the opposite and that it lost its original righteousness and innocence. Therefore he did not obtain the grace to persevere in that innocent state: and if he did not have it, he did not receive it either. Well;. How would I have received the grace of perseverance without persevering? Therefore, if he did not have it, because he did not receive, why is he who did not receive the gift of perseverance blamed for not persevering? Can't you say? who did not receive it, because he was not separated from the mass of perdition by the rarity of divine grace. Perhaps because the latter goods will be more important and better, were those first ones null or of little importance? 34. It is also important to distinguish aid. Because one is the help without which a work is not done, and another is the help with which something is done. For example, without food we cannot live, but even if we have it, it is not enough for someone who insists on dying to live. Therefore the help of food is essential to live, but they do not make us live. But when the happiness that he lacks is given to man, he will immediately be happy. There is, therefore, not only a help without which something is not done, but also a help with which the thing for which it is given is done. Happiness belongs to this case: with it one becomes happy and without it one cannot be happy. When happiness is granted to man, he immediately becomes happy; and if it were never given to him, it never will be. On the other hand, food does not make man live, although he cannot live without it. To the first man, then, who, created in original justice, had received the faculty of being able not to sin, being able not to die, being able not to abandon goodness, was granted not the help that would make him persevere, but the help without which he could not persevere using his free will. But now to the saints, predestined for the kingdom of God, by divine grace is given not only help to persevere, but also the grace of perseverance itself; They are not only given the gift without which they cannot persevere, but the gift by which they actually persevere. In fact, Christ, after saying: Without me you can do nothing, added: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you so that you would go and bear fruit and your fruit would remain.

For who among the multitude of Christians, during this mortal life, will flatter themselves at finding themselves among the predestined? The Savior used the same language with the apostles: If you remain in me, knowing his future perseverance. Because of the usefulness of this secret, so that no one boasts of himself, let everyone fear, even those who run well, because they do not know who will arrive; Because of the usefulness, I repeat, of this mystery, it must be believed that some sons of perdition, without receiving the gift of final perseverance, begin to live according to the faith that inspires works of charity, and temporarily practice justice and piety, and then fall, being taken from this life before rising. If some cases of this kind did not occur, men would have the very healthy fear with which pride is subdued until they attained the grace of Christ, the foundation of the pious life; but once this was achieved, they would live in complete security not to fall again. Now, such presumption is not appropriate in this place of trial, where weakness abounds and security itself favors pride. In the end this certainty will not be lacking either; but, like angels now, men will have it then, when they are invulnerable to pride. The number, then, of those chosen for the kingdom of God by divine grace, thanks to the final perseverance, which will also be granted to them, will not suffer any decrease there and will be preserved in all its integrity and most blessed glory until the end by the work of the mercy of their Savior, both when they convert and fight and when they are crowned. 41. Therefore, the mercy of God is also necessary there, who beatifies those who are already immune from guilt. But even in that just judgment there will be room for mercy according to the merit of good works, because by saying: He who was not merciful will be judged without mercy, it is implied that, for those who did good works of mercy, the judgment will be merciful, and, consequently, that the same mercy is given for him merit of good works. This is not the case now, when without previous merits of good works, but rather, with many bad ones, his mercy comes before men, freeing them from the evils that they have done and those that they would do if they were not governed by divine grace, as well as from the eternal punishments that they would suffer if they were not torn from the power of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of the beloved Son of God. Notwithstanding what has been said, since the Apostle gives the name of grace to eternal life itself, which is certainly given as a reward for good works, this being a free gift and not due to works, we must confess that eternal life receives such a name because it is given as a reward for the merits achieved by men with grace. And such is the meaning of the Gospel's expression grace upon grace, which means, for these merits that grace has won for us. 42. On the other hand, those who do not belong to this number of the predestined, whom divine grace leads to paradise, pray when they do not have the use of free will, pray because they have corresponded to grace with free will, which is then truly free, when it has been liberated by grace; Those who, as I say, do not belong to this most certain and blessed number, will receive the very just sentence that they have deserved. In effect, they either lie under the yoke of original sin, and, in solidarity with a hereditary guilt, they leave this world without having been remitted to them by baptism. Or they also added new sins with free will; I say free will, but not liberated; free from justice, but a servant of sin, which drags them to their guilty passions, some more, others less; but they are all evil, and their punishments will be proportionate to the seriousness of their crimes. Or they receive divine grace, but they surrender to the current of the world and do not persevere, they abandon and are abandoned.

THE LETTER KILLS AND THE SPIRIT LIVIFIES

Saint Augustine remembers this Pauline passage (to Cor. 3, 6), which gave the title to his book De spiritu et littera, directed against the Pelagians. According to its author, knowledge of the law is not enough without the help of God, who makes us love the commandments and fulfill them. Pelagius also admitted doctrine and law: Non vult alliad accipi qíuzm legem et doctrinam, qua naturalis possibilitas adiuvetur (De gratla Christi, 6,8: P L 44, 364). The prohibition of a thing rather irritates the desire for evil, auget prohibindo desiderium malum, similar to the dam, which with its repression increases the impetus of the water, so that it rushes with greater violence (De spiritu et litt., 16, 6: P L 44, 204). In this aspect, the law, far from suppressing sin, gives it new flavor and multiplies it. Iubet enim magis quam iuvat; Docet morbum esse, non sanat. Hence its main usefulness: it makes one's own helplessness and misery known so that one turns to the doctor and medicine: Et haec ostendatur legis utilitas, quoniam quos facil praevaricationis reos, cogit confugere ud gratiam liberandos, et ut concupiscentias malas superent adiuvandos (De grat. Christi, 8, 9: P L 44, 365). The old law was not useless or harmful, because it served to prepare the ways of the Messiah. By expanding man's moral conscience, he persuaded him of the need for higher help. Saint Augustine had to combat two extreme conceptions of the law: the Manichaean and the Pelagian. The Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament as contradictory and inspired by the spirit of evil. The old law is evil, because it has a perverse origin. On the contrary, the Pelagians exalted it as they suppressed grace; The law is enough, God's help is not needed: Callidissime legem contra gratiam laudant (Cont. duas ep. peí., IV, 5, 10: P L 44, 616). With a great copy of reasons and a redundant style in all their disputes they want to identify grace with the law, affirming that we receive from God the help of knowledge (adiutorium cognitionis), with which we know what must be done, not the inspiration of love to do with pleasure what we already know, and this is properly grace (ibid., n. 11: P L 44, 617). Against the Manichaeans Saint Augustine defends the value and pedagogical usefulness of the ancient law; against the Pelagians, their insufficiency to justify man, because simple knowledge inflates,
PROPHETIC, APOSTOLIC AND CATHOLIC DOCTRINE

Saint Augustine characterizes the three fundamental aspects of the doctrine of grace. There is internal grace, with which God helps the weakness of the human will to do good; There is also free will, and grace and free will harmonize with each other. This is a prophetic doctrine, announced in the books of the Old Testament, mostly by the prophets and the Psalms; It is apostolic doctrine, taught above all by Saint Paul; and Catholic doctrine, professed by the Church, spread throughout the world. Far from being a novelty, the doctrine of grace has the oldest and most certain testimonies of revelation. 3.

tin in these passages for supporting the double vocation in the Apostle's doctrine: to faith without perseverance and to faith oerseve-ante. There are two categories of calls: some, according to purpose or design, and they are those who persevere to the end and are predestined to glory; others, who temporarily embrace the faith, and reject it or do not live according to it and are condemned. The Pauline expression "prothesis tou Teou": propositum Del (Rom. 9, n), means, according to the holy Doctor, the effective, congruous or according to design vocation. «This word prothesis designates in Saint Paul an eternal act of the divine will, consistent and absolute, which is related to a particular benefit; for example, the effective vocation» ÍPRAT, Theologic de Saint Paul, I, 511). It is not an act of will that commands, but rather one that disposes in advance. In it is hidden for Saint Augustine the ultimate and definitive reason for persevering grace. 18.
THE TEST OF FREEDOM (10, 27).—'«In this way he ordained

"Creator of the life of angels and men, who first wanted to show them the value of their agency and then the benefit of grace." These words refer to the three categories of free creatures, or three processes of created freedom; There are innocent and perfect beings who always remained united to the Creator: the good angels. Using their will well, they have achieved perfect bliss. There are others who are perverse, who loved themselves more than God, and were condemned to eternal punishments, deserved for their pride. Finally, there are other creatures who occupy a middle ground: for abusing their blissful freedom they were temporarily condemned to penalties; but divine mercy, surpassing justice, has given them the power to repair their fall and become children of God by grace. In the former the vigor of free will and the force of grace shine; in the second, the rigor of justice; and in the third, justice and mercy. Thus, God and the creature reveal all their depths in salvation, damnation and redemption. Human redemption points to the most perfect revelation of God and, at the same time, the profound tragedy of created freedom. Without the fall, we probably would not have Christ, that is, the unsearchable riches of God's omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness.

ADDITIONAL NOTES ss.).--Begin

here the exposition of the doctrine of the two helps, in whose interpretation two excesses must be avoided: that of the Semi-Pelagians and that of the Jansenists. The former considered it a depressing and fatalistic doctrine: Deinde moleste ferunt ita dividí gratiam quae vel time primo homini data est, vel mine ómnibus datur (Epist. 126, 6: P L 33, 1010).

The effectiveness of grace does not nullify free will. The gentle hand of God helps man by freeing him, not by oppressing him. On the contrary, Jansenius exaggerates when he says: Haec est enim vera clavis qua aditus in eius scripta aperiendus est; et sine qua qui ea molitur ingredi, velut caecus palpabit in meridie. Father Merlin corrects this exaggeration and writes: cIf the distinction of the two aids is the basis, the key, the thread, the principle of the doctrine of Saint Augustine, this Father, in the space of twenty-five years, has published his writings while trying to hide his intelligence from the whole world; He wanted the basis on which his doctrine rests to be known neither by Catholics nor by Pelagians; and it gave them reason to believe that such a foundation was ruinous" (Vérilable clef des ouvrages de Saint Augustin, 913: P L 47). Both aids, which Father Cayré translates as efficient grace and non-efficient grace, should not be identified with effective and sufficient grace. Adam in the innocent state had need of a glacis, but of less influence or strength than fallen man. Being endowed with a right will, the purpose of grace was not to produce the valle bonum, because it already existed, but rather to help maintain primitive righteousness, or the posse perseverare. But in the fallen man inclined to evil, grace must first produce the rectitude of the will, the velle bonum, and the vellc persevere in the midst of great temptations and combats. The previous distinction was excogitated by Saint Augustine to respond to the objection of the Semi-Pelagians: "If the grace of perseverance is a gift, and Adam did not receive it, since we know that in reality he did not obtain perseverance in the innocent state, how can he be accused of guilt, having lacked the help of God, indispensable for this?" Saint Augustine responds: "He did not lack help to persevere, but it was very different from that which the children of grace now receive through the mediation of Christ." The first man needed minor help, because he was internally healthy and vigorous, planted in righteousness and justice.

He was sailing on a calm sea, and with a gentle breeze from God and a slight movement of the oars of free will he could have continued or persevered in the same bliss. • But his children navigate an inconstant and stormy sea, with weak oars and among innumerable reefs; the wind of God must be stronger and its direction more effective to come out alive and towards happy eternity; such is the auxílium quo, that is, a different, more abundant and effective grace, as a gift from Christ, our Mediator, given to a helpless and miserable creature. "Jansenius pointed out well the different value of both aids or graces, which correspond to two different situations of man; but he was wrong to consider the auxilium quo as nullifying the freedom.

In both states this faculty or freedom of indifference subsists; But God knows that with the auxilium quo the human creature will resist and move forward with his plans of redemption. 20. VICTORIOUS GRACE (11, 29).—Ponder in these passages the victorious force of grace, which gave rise to Jansenius for his fatalistic and anti-Augustinian doctrine: Gratiam Dei Augustinus ita victricem statuit supra voluntatis arbitrium (Augustinus, 3, 400). These words express the thought of Jansenius, inspired by Calvin. The victory of grace is related to the human will, which it forces and despotically dominates. But in the mind of Saint Augustine, victory is not over free will, but over concupiscence and temptations. Grace is given to free will so that it may strengthen itself and overcome the suggestions of sin: In tali certamíne laborantes ac periclitantes dari sibi pugnandi vincendique virtutem per Christi gratiam poscunt (De cor. el grat., 11, 29). It does not defeat free will, nullifying it, but rather strengthens it and gives it very effective forces against its enemies, world, devil and flesh: Praebendo vires efficacissimas voluntati (De grat. et lib. arb., 16, 32). It does not, therefore, go against free will, but rather in its firmness and support. Grace reduces the pressure that his enemies exert on him, that is, it frees him and arms him to sustain the war against concupiscence until the definitive capitulation; l'raelium contra concupiscentiam carnis, per Sancti Spiritus adiutorium us, que ad victoriae pacem (Opus imp. contra luí., 2, 217: P L 45, 1236). In this aspect it is the struggle of one delight against another delight: Donat ut delectatio peccati iustitiae delectatione vincatur (ibid-, 2, 217: ibid). 21.
EXEMPLARY AND SOURCE OF ALL GRACE

expounding the Catholic doctrine of grace, Saint Augustine does not take his eyes off Christ, who is the true torch of Catholic soteriology. The incarnation is the sovereign example of grace: Summum exemplum gratiae (De civ. Dei, 10, 29: P L 41, 308). The hypostatic union is not a reward for previous merits, but rather a gift of divine benevolence. That is why he refutes here the opinion of the Pelagians, according to whom Christ deserved to be the son of God by the prior good use of free will and just works: Natus ex Virgine, suae postea voluntatis virtute projecit et fecit ut a Verbo Dei susciperetur (Op. imp. contra Iuiiánum, 4, 84: P L 45, 1386). This error leads directly to Nestorianism, or accidental and moral union of the Word with human nature. But a gift as sovereign as Christ cannot be deserved by any merit, if it is not the fruit of God's favor, and therefore, a model of free predestination and grace (cf. Enchiridion, 36, 11: P L 40, 250). 22.
GRACE AND FREE WILL (I I, 31).—"Free will

It is sufficient by itself to do evil, but it is weak for good if omnipotent goodness does not lend it its help. This truth was well shown in the process of the two falls, the angelic and the human. The land of free will may bring forth thorns and thistles; but

Healthy flowers and plants must be planted by the generous hand of the Creator. That is to say, the creature, precisely because it is a creature, is in a metaphysical poverty that only the Creator can remedy. JJnde homini bona vita, nisi a fonte vitae? Unde homini illuminatio, nisi ab aeterno lumine?... Fons est vitae. Si non influat lile, siccus eris (Serm. 284, 1: P L 38, 1288). Where can good life come to man if not from the source of life and light, from eternal light? He is the source; If He does not send his water, you will be a wasteland. Such is human free will; In itself it is a wasteland for good without the communication of heaven's favors. Man can have no meritorious thought about himself if help for it does not come from above. The best goods, the perfect gifts, descend from above and are derived from the Father of lights. Virtues, good works, spiritual goods, are gifts and gifts from God. 23. THE TWO GRACES (I I, 31).—St. Augustine ponders here the diversity of the two kinds of graces: that granted to innocent man and that granted to those redeemed by Christ. The second grace has been more excellent and powerful than the first, because the conditions of Adam and his children were very different. These lack the righteousness of the will in which their father was created; For the same reason, his free will lacks intimate vigor and freedom, because of the pressure that passions and bad inclinations exert on him. Great is the grace possessed by the first man, and with it he could have persevered in the good received until the end; but greater is that which is granted to the children of the New Testament to triumph over the many enemies that surround them. The first gave the power to do good, the second gives the act of doing it, being more effective than the first. The help sine quo was sufficient for Adam, given the original vigor of his will; the help that is effective grace or that brings about good in Christians, overcoming the obstacles opposed by the devil, the world and the flesh. 24.
THREE STAGES OF HUMAN FREEDOM (12, 33-34).—Alluded to here

Saint Augustine to the three stages or stages through which human freedom has passed in the innocent man, in the fallen and in the redeemed. In the first, freedom enjoyed a very singular privilege: posse non peccare, the power not to sin. Then man had true and perfect freedom; but Adam did not reciprocate the privilege, and introduced sin into the world, and humanity became a massa peccati, a mass of sin. The privilege of posse non peccare was lost and the empire and kingdom of sin entered, sin as a bond, necessity and servitude. But fallen man did not lose the ability to return to God through repentance and forgiveness. V freedom passed to a new state of liberatum arbitrium, removed from the bondage of sin by the work of the Mediator between God and men, Christ. He thus returns, in a certain way, to recover the privilege of posse non peccare, albeit restricted, or rather that of freeing himself from sin through superior help.

THE ABANDONMENT OF GOD (13, 42).—Deserunt et deseruntur.

The cause of not persevering in the good begun is the sin or aversion to God to guiltily adhere to creatures. But God's aversion brings in turn divine desertion. God does not abandon if he is not abandoned first. Here is a postulate of the doctrine of grace in Saint Augustine. Te nenio amittit, nisi qui dimittit (Conf., 4, 9). Non deseritur amor, si ipse non desemt (ibid., 4, 11). Misericordia eius et gratia... non deserit eos qui ex eius Jiote vivunt, eurnque pie colunt. The Council of Trent formulates the same principle in Augustinian words: Deus namque sua gratia semel iustificatos «.non deserit, nisi ab eis prius deseratury, (sess. 6, chapter 11: Denz., 8041). The words in quotation marks were taken from the book De natura et gratia, 26, 29: P L 44, 261. Even by the title of Creator, Saint Augustine admits universal assistance and help, which is extended with particular providence to souls: Tu enim aditivas qui condidisli, i ti non descris qui creasti (Enarrat. in Ps., 26, 17: P L 36, 708). «You help your creatures, because you gave them being; you do not abandon them, because you created them. 29.
CERTAIN NUMBER OF THE PREDESTINED (13, 40).—The semi-pela-

Gians rejected the doctrine of the certain and fixed number of the predestined, denying the perfection of divine science: Inde est quod et illud pariter non accipiunt, ut electandorum reiizandorumque esse definitum numerum nolint (Epist. 226, 7: P L 33 1010). In his system, salvation is due to the initiative of the creature rather than the Creator. God's election follows foreknowledge or simple knowledge of each person's merits; even in infants who die without baptism. He has foreseen what they would be following the movements of their will and snatches them from the world. For Augustinian and Catholic theology, the number of the predestined is fixed and certain. Infallible and certain, divine science at this point cannot admit failures or errors; Otherwise, an imperfection would be introduced that is irreconcilable with the very being of God: «God is deceived if any of the predestined perish; but none of them perish, because God is not subject to error. From all eternity the predestined are inscribed in the secret archives of the heavenly Father": In memoriali Patris sai inconcussa stabilitate conscripti (De corrept. et grat., 7, 14; 9, 20). To say with Cassian that Judas was among the elect before his fall is to seriously compromise the infallibility of the science of God. 30.

conveys the saving will of God to the predestined, explaining in a relative sense the Pauline text 1 Tim. 2, 4: Qui vult omnes hotnines safe fieri.

Neither God nor Christ have had an absolute and effective will to save everyone. It is evident that they could convert all sinners and entirely save today's humanity. Posset plane. Cur ergo non fecit f Quia noluit. Cur noluent penises ipsum est (De Gen. ad lit., n, 10-13: P L 34, 434). As a theologian was tortured by Saint Paul's text, it shows evident breadth, and the fact that many condemned themselves not only for their personal sins, but also for hereditary or original sin. The Apostle's omnes homines limits it to "many" {Epist. 217, 6, 19: P L 33, 1005), or he understands it by all kinds of men (Enchir., 103: P L 40, 280), or he restricts it to those who are saved, since all of them are saved by the will of God {De praed. sanct., 8, 14: PlL 44, 971). This exegesis is based on two facts: the incontrovertible sovereignty of God, whose absolute will cannot be frustrated by any obstacle or creaturely malice, and the certainty of the condemnation of many. For the Semi-Pelagians, this limitation was scandalous, as Saint Prosper and Hilary of Marseille made it known to them from the south of France. The universal salvific will was one of the postulates most precious to Semi-Pelagianism to enhance the goodness and mercy of God: Bonitas in eo apparet, si neminem repellat a vita, sed indifferenter velit Universos Salvas fieri et in agnitionem veritatis vinoe (Epist. 225, 4: P L 33, 1004). Saint Augustine does not admit divine indifference towards all men, but rather the principle of predilection, with which he freely chooses many for glory. For the semi-Pelagians, the saving will of God is subordinated to the favorable or adverse response of the human will. The initiative is taken from God and placed in the creature, who has to receive the gifts offered by the Creator or reject them. The key to the solution of this problem is in the distinction of the divine will in antecedent and consequent, the first being universal and the second limited. «Certainly, as A. Jacquin says, there are traces of double will in Saint Augustine, but nothing more. If he had had a clear notion of the distinctions that theologians used after him, he would not have done the prodigies of ingenuity to save the text: Qui vult omnes homines saved fieri.

Faithful to his method, he stuck to the concrete, taking care above all to attribute salvation to God and his loss to the name" (La prédestination d'aprés Saint Augustin: "Miscel. Agost", I I, 869). According to Tixeront, Saint Augustine also admits the universal salvific will, since it is evidently understood from a good number of passages, especially when he affirms that Jesus Christ died for all and offers sufficient graces to all {Histoire des dogmes, I I, 505-0). Above all, he cites as classic the passage from the book De spiritu et littera, 58: Vult autem Deus omnes homines safes fieri et in agnitionem veritatis vinore, non sic tamen ut eis adimat liberum arbitrium, quo vel bene mate utentes iustissime iudicentur. Saint Prospero already began this method of conciliation and interpretation of difficult passages by resorting to great principles such as this: Deus impossibilia non iubet, sed iubendo monet et faceré

THE SECRET OF PREDESTINATION (15, 4Ó-48>.—Reuter andHar -

nack have formulated the following reproach against the Augustinian doctrine of grace and predestination: it renders the Church useless as an organism dedicated to the salvation of souls. If these are predestined ab aeterno, the ecclesiastical hierarchy has no reason to exist. Quietism is the term and result of such a way of thinking. These rationalists of our time follow the semi-rationalists of the time of Saint Augustine, that is, the semi-Pelagians, for whom the word "predestination" was equivalent to the fatum of the ancient religions. Men are pure mechanical toys, not free beings moved by the springs of their own will. The Christian sense rejects these fatalistic deviations of the ancients and moderns. Humanity is not divided into two masses

or groups, separated by barriers of high privilege. A deep secret veils the designs of God and the destiny of each creature. In the last years of his anti-Pelagian polemic, Saint Augustine gave great emphasis to the secret of predestination. All men are guided to eternal destinies under the direction of a loving providence that flutters over them: Circumvolabat super me fidelis a Ion ge misericordia tua (Con/., 3, 11). The same heavenly rain falls on the roses and the thorns, on the wheat and the tares. No movement of pride should trouble the hearts of the Lord's chosen ones, who only know who the sheep of his pasture are. The sheep themselves do not know themselves. "But the Shepherd knows them according to this predestination, according to this foreknowledge, according to this election made before the foundations of the world were laid": Secundum istam ergo praescientiam Dei et praedestinationem qitam múltete oves fotis, quam mrtlti lupi intiis! el qítammulae oves intiis et quilín multi lupi foris! According to this foreknowledge and predestination of God, how many sheep are outside and how many wolves are inside! And how many sheep inside and how many wolves outside! I mean, how many who are ravaged by lust now will be chaste later! How many blasphemers today will believe more in Christ! How many drunks today will be sober tomorrow! However, now they are other people's sheep and follow other shepherds. Likewise, how many who now praise God in the Church will blaspheme Him later, how many chaste people will become lighthearted, how many sober people will lose their moderation in drinking, how many who are now standing will fall! Non sunt oves: "They are not of the number of the sheep" (Tract. 4$ in Ioan.,\2: P L 35, 1724). This great secret ordained by divine Providence must fill everyone with dread and humility. No one should be preferred to anyone; No one can despise another, because today's sheep can become a wolf tomorrow, and the fiercest wolf today can be the gentle little sheep of Christ. With this, the Church is not useless, but necessary with its hierarchy, its sacraments and its pastoral zeal. And keep a. profound sense of that Augustinian advice: Nondum traheris? Ora ut traharis. Pray that you may be drawn, pray that you may make effective with your cooperation the decree of eternal predestination (Tract. 26 in loan., a: P L 35, 1607).

The book Liberty and Grace that we offer translated to BAC readers corresponds to the one that Saint Augustine wrote with the title De gratia et libero arbitrio in the year 426 and directed to Valiente and his monks, who lived in a monastery in Hadrumeto, a city on the Tunisian coast. In this book he proves the absolute gratuitousness of God's gift, without the freedom of man suffering anything. We could say that this little work is the second intervention of the Saint in the Semi-Pelagian controversy. Pelagius and Celestius were condemned on January 27, 417 by Pope Innocent I; but certain problems had been left floating in the air that had only been touched upon in passing in the Pelagian controversy; such, for example, the gratuitousness of grace, predestination and perseverance, the discussion of which later received the name of the Semi-Pelagian controversy. For this reason, in the year 418 Saint Augustine wrote a letter to Sixtus, priest of Rome, who later became Sixtus HE, insisting on free predestination to grace and refuting the Pelagians, who attributed this to the possible merits of men. The monks of Hadrumeto learned of this letter and began to discuss it, so some of them let the Saint know what was happening in their monastery. To clarify these problems, Saint Augustine wrote the book De gratia et libero arbitrio.

OF GRACE AND FREE WILL

1. We have already spoken and written much—as much as the Lord was pleased to grant us—because there are some who so highly praise and defend freedom, that they dare to deny and try to ignore the divine grace, which calls us to God, which frees us from sins and makes us acquire good merits, by which we can reach eternal life. But because there are others who, when defending the grace of God, deny freedom, or who when they defend grace believe they deny free will, I determined, driven by charity, oh brother Valentine!, to address this writing to you and to the others who serve God with you. Well, I have heard from you, brothers, from some of your own congregation who came to see me from there and from those who sent you this writing. Tell me that there are dissensions among you regarding this problem. Therefore, dearly beloved, so that the darkness of this matter does not disturb you, I warn you first of all that you give many thanks to God for the things that you understand; And in relation to those that you have not yet penetrated, ask the Lord to make you understand them, but maintaining peace and charity among yourselves, and insist on the purpose until God leads you to the penetration of what you do not understand. This is noted by the apostle Paul, who, when saying that he was not yet perfect, shortly after adds: We who are perfect, let us live this; That is to say, we are so perfect that we have not yet reached the perfection that belongs to us, and then he adds: And if you understand anything differently, this also the Lord will reveal to you, but let us live what we understand. By fulfilling this, we will be able to reach what we do not understand, because God will reveal to us if we understand something differently, as long as we do not abandon what he has already taught us.
