2. The Lord revealed to us through his holy Scriptures that man has free will. How, then, he revealed it, I remind you not with human words, but divine ones. First, because the divine precepts themselves would be of no use to man if he did not have the freedom to fulfill them, and thus reach the promised prize. For this purpose they were given, so that man would not excuse himself out of ignorance. And thus, the Lord says in the Gospel of the Jews: If he had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but thus, they have no excuse for their sin. What sin does he speak of if not that execrable sin that he foresaw as the future when he spoke thus, and that is to say that they would kill him? Because before the incarnation of Jesus Christ, they were guilty of no sin. Furthermore, the Apostle says: The wrath of God is manifested from heaven against the impiety and injustice of men, who retain the truth of God in iniquity, whenever the knowledge of God is manifested in them, since God manifested it to them. His invisible things, after the world was created, understood by the things made, become visible, as well as his power and divinity, so that they are inexcusable. What excuse does he call them inexcusable but the one for which human pride usually says: "If I had known it, I would have done it; I didn't do it because I didn't know it"; or also: "I would do it if I knew; precisely I don't do it because I don't know"? This excuse becomes vain to them when they are commanded or the way not to sin is shown to them.

CHAPTER V 10. When God says: Return to me, and I will return to you, it seems that one of these propositions belongs to our will—that we return to Him; and the other, however, corresponds to grace—that He returns to us. And the Pelagians could see in them their thought, by virtue of which they affirm that the grace of God is conferred on us according to our merits. What Pelagius certainly did not dare to maintain in Jerusalem of Palestine when he was heard by the bishops. Because, among other things that were reproached to him there, he was affirming that the grace of God is conferred on us according to our merits, which is so foreign and contrary to Catholic doctrine and the grace of Christ, that if he had not detested such a proposition, he would have been excommunicated from there. But he falsely detested it, since his later books, in which he defended nothing else, show that God's grace is given to us according to our merits. They gather such thoughts from sacred testimonies, such as the one adduced at the beginning of this chapter: Return to me, and I will return to you, as if the merit of our conversion to God were the measure of grace, by which the Lord returns to us. And those who think like this do not realize that, if our conversion to God were not his grace, we would not say to him: God of virtues, return us to you; and God, you,

19. And from here arises another problem of no small importance, which, with the grace of God, we must solve. If eternal life is given to good works, as the Scripture clearly states: For God will give to each one according to his works, how can eternal life be grace, if grace is not given by works, but freely, according to the Apostle: He who works, his wages are not counted as grace, but as debt? And in another place: At the present time a remainder has been left by virtue of a gracious election; and then: But if by grace, it is no longer by works, for in this case grace would no longer be grace. How then will eternal life be grace, if it responds to works? Or perhaps the Apostle does not call eternal life grace? What's more, he says it so clearly that it is completely undeniable. If faith only affected the free will and gift of God, why pray for those who do not want to believe so that they may believe? We would do this in vain if we did not believe, and with great reason, that omnipotent God can return even the most perverse and contrary wills to faith. Human free will is exhorted in those words of the Psalm: If you hear his voice today, do not harden your heart. If the Lord could not deliver us from hardness of heart, would he not say through the prophet: I will remove your heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh. The Apostle clearly shows that such words of the New Testament were spoken: You are my letter, written not with ink, but with the spirit of the living God; not on tables of stone, but on the tables of flesh that are your hearts. What was certainly not said so that those who must live spiritually may live carnally, but that because they do not feel the stone, a hard heart is compared to it, and to the sensitive flesh, on the other hand, a generous heart. This is how it reads in the prophecy of Ezekiel: And I will give them another heart and put in them a new spirit, I will remove their heart of stone from their body and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may follow my commandments and observe and practice my laws and be my people and I may be their God. Thus, in chapter 36, 22-27, he says: I do not do this for your sake, house of Israel, but rather for the honor of my name, which has been profaned for your sake from among the nations to whom you have gone. I will sanctify my great name, profaned among the nations because of you in their midst, and the nations will know that I am God, says the Lord, when I will sanctify myself in you in their sight. I will take you from among the nations, and I will gather you from all the lands, and I will bring you to your own land. And I will sprinkle you with pure water and purify you from your impurities, from all your idolatries. I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you. I will tear out that heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my spirit within you and make you follow my commandments and observe my precepts and do them. Who will be so blind that he does not see and so stone that he does not realize that grace is not conferred according to the merits of good will, when the Lord himself attests to this when he says: I do not do it for your sake, house of Israel, but rather for the honor of my name? Why, then, did he say: I do it only for the honor of my holy name, but so that no one would believe in the collation for good merits, which the Pelagians are not ashamed to affirm? And not only that they totally lack good merits, but that their bad merits come before them, he demonstrates this by saying: for the honor of my name, profaned among the nations for your sake. Who will not see a horrendous crime in the profanation of God's holy name? However, for the very name of mine, he says, which you have profaned, I will make you good, not for your sake. And I will sanctify my great name, profaned among the nations because of you among them. He says that he will sanctify his name, which he previously called holy, the same thing that we pray in the Sunday prayer when we say: Hallowed be your name, so that hallowed may be in men that which in itself is always and without a doubt holy.

Finally, he adds: And all nations will know that I am God, says the Lord, when I will be sanctified in you in their sight. Being, therefore, He holy, He sanctifies Himself, however, in those to whom He gives His grace, tearing out the heart of stone, by which they profaned the name of God.

31. So that one does not think about the uselessness of free will by men, it is said in the Psalm: Harden your hearts. And by the same prophet Ephcekiel: Cast upon yourselves all the iniquities that you commit and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you want to die, house of Israel? That I do not want the death of the one who dies. Convert and live. Let us notice that it says: Convert and live, to whom we say: Return us to you, Lord. Let us remember that it says: Cast all iniquities from upon you. Being thus that He is the one who justifies the sinner. Notice that it says: Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, who on another occasion assures: I will give you a new heart and a new spirit. How, then, does he assure us that he will give us what he says to us: Be done? Why does He command us, if He will give it to us? Why does he give it, if man has to do it, if not because he gives what he commands when he helps to fulfill what is commanded? We always, therefore, enjoy free will; but this is not always good; because either it is an hour of justice, if it serves sin, or it is an hour of sin, if it serves justice, and then it is good. But the grace of God is always good and makes the man who previously had a bad will have good will. Through it it is achieved that the same good will that was initiated increases and grows so much that it becomes able to fulfill the divine precepts, when it desires it with complete effectiveness. Refer to this what was written: If you want, you can keep his commandments, so that if someone wants and is not able, he may know that he does not yet want with full effectiveness. Pray, then, in order to achieve as much will as is necessary to fulfill the commands. Thus, everyone is helped in the fulfillment of the precepts, since will is worth when we can and power is worth when we want; because what would be the use of willing, if we cannot, or power, if we do not want?

33. He who, therefore, desires to fulfill God's command and cannot, already has a good will, but it is still weak and mean. You can when you have it strong and firm. When the martyrs fulfilled those great commands, they fulfilled them very willingly, that is, with great charity; of which the Lord said: Greater love has no one than this to lay down one's life for one's friends. For what the Apostle says: He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law, for you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet and any other precept, in this sentence it is summarized: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love does not cause harm to others, because love is the fulfillment of the law. The apostle Saint Peter did not have this charity when he denied the Lord three times out of fear. Charity has no fear, as Saint John says in his Epistle, but perfect charity casts out fear. But even a little and imperfectly, he already loved, because he said: I will give my life for you. He believed he could do what he felt he wanted. And who had begun to give this love, even small and imperfect, but he who prepares the will and by cooperating perfects what he begins by doing? Because truly He begins to work so that we want, and when we want, He cooperates with us to perfect the work. Therefore, the Apostle says: I am certain that he who began a good work in you will carry it out until the day of Christ Jesus. Therefore, for us to want, it begins to act without us, and when we want and willingly to act, it cooperates with us. However, if He does not work so that we want or does not cooperate when we want, we can do nothing in the way of good works of piety. Of God's action so that we will it is written: God is the one who works in you to will; and of the action with which he cooperates when we want and act voluntarily, the Apostle said: We know that God makes all things work together for the good of those who love him. What does that mean all things except the terrible and violent passions themselves? Because the burden of Christ, which is heavy for illness, is made light by charity. Christ told those who live that their burden was light, as it was for Saint Peter when he suffered for Christ, not when he denied him.

37. All these precepts of love, that is, of charity, are of such a nature that if man believes he has done something good, but without charity, he is totally mistaken. And these commands would be given to man in vain if he did not enjoy free will. But who, if not God himself, gives men this love of God and neighbor, which is commanded by the old and new law? It is well to note that the grace promised in the old is given in the new, and that the law without grace is a letter that kills; With grace, however, it is a spirit that gives life. If charity does not come from God, but from men, the Pelagians are right; but if it comes from God, we have defeated the Pelagians. Let us sit, then, all3 around the apostle Saint John, and let him tell us: Dearest friends, let us worship one another. And when in these words the Pelagians begin to see the dawn of their triumph and say: "Why are we commanded to love one another if not because it depends on us?", Saint John continues, and confusing them says: Because charity comes from God. It does not come, then, from us, but from God. And if we are told: Let us love one another, because charity comes from God, it is, without a doubt, to warn our free will that we should seek the gift of God. Which would certainly be without any fruit if he were not first given some charity, so that in the precept itself he would already find strength to fulfill it. When we are told: Let us love one another, we have a law; when it is added: Because the charity of God proceeds, grace is announced; because the wisdom of God carries law and mercy in its words. And that is why it was written in the Psalm: The lawgiver will give a blessing. 38. Let no one therefore deceive you, my brothers; We would not love God if He had not first loved us. Saint John says this without ambiguity: Let us love God, because He loved us first. Grace makes us lovers of the law, and the law without grace, prevaricators, which is evident from the words of Our Lord: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you. If we had been the first, He would love us because of our merit; We first choose Him to deserve to be chosen by Him. But God, who is the same truth, says something else, which is openly opposed to the vanity of men: You have not chosen me. If, then, you did not choose, without a doubt you do not love-

Of this spirit the Apostle says writing to the Romans: We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience; patience, proven virtue, and proven virtue, hope will not be confounded, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts by virtue of the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

That tribulation, therefore, does not end patience, but rather produces it, is not due to us but to the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us; to that charity gift of God, as the Apostle teaches: Peace, he says to the Ephesians, to the brothers and charity with faith. 40. And this is no wonder if the light shines in the darkness, but the darkness does not embrace it. In Saint John the light says: See what love the Father has shown us, that we are called children of God; and in the Pelagians, darkness says: "Love for us comes from ourselves." But if they had the true, that is, Christian charity, they would know well where it comes from, because Saint Paul writes: We have not received the spirit of the world, but the spirit of God, so that we may know the gifts that God has given us. And Saint John in his first letter writes: God is charity. The Pelagians affirm that they possess God not by the grace of the Lord, but by their own virtue; and although they confess that the knowledge of the law comes to us from God, charity, on the other hand, they believe they possess 'by themselves. And they do not hear the Apostle, who says: Science inflates, only charity deifies. And can anything else be conceived without. reason and far-fetched and alien to the sanctity of love than to estimate that science comes from God, which without charity inflates, and charity from ourselves? And the Apostle saying that the charity of Christ surpasses all science, how dare they say that science, inferior to charity, comes from God, and that charity, which surpasses all science, comes from men? But true faith and sound doctrine teach that both come from God, for it is written: From the countenance of God come knowledge and understanding; and also: Charity comes from God; and spirit of wisdom and intelligence; and spirit of strength, love and temperance. Charity is a greater gift than science, since, when it occurs in man, it needs charity to not become swollen. Charity is not envious, it is not boastful, it is not puffed up.

41. I think I have already spoken enough against those who fight the grace of God, which does not annul the human will, but rather makes evil good and then helps it. Better said, rather than me, it has been the same sacred Scripture that has shared eloquent testimonies of truth with you. And if you diligently study these divine Scriptures, you will see that God not only makes bad wills good and directs them to eternal life for the sake of honest acts, but that the will of men is always in the hands of God. He inclines it where he wants and when he wants, either to render favors or to inflict punishments, according to his pleasure and in accordance with his most hidden judgments, yes; but full of reason. We sometimes find that sins are punishments for others, like the vessels of wrath, fit for the perdition of which Saint Paul speaks; or the hardening of Pharaoh, a means for the Lord to show his power; or the flight of the Israelites before the enemy from the city of Gai; Fear took hold of their spirits and they fled, and so it came to pass that the sin of the people would be avenged with justice. Therefore the Lord said to Joshua: The children of Israel were unable to resist their enemies and turned their backs on them. What does it mean that they have not been able to resist? Why, being free, was their will overcome by fear and they fled, if not because the Lord reigns over the wills of men and plunges those whom He loves into terror? Did not the enemies of Israel fight of their own free will against the people of God, commanded by Joshua? David said to Abishai and all his followers: "You see that my son, coming from my womb, seeks my life; much more so that the son of Benjamin. Let him curse, for God has commanded him to do so. Perhaps God will look at my affliction and will repay me with favors for today's curses." Who will be the wise man who can understand how the Lord told this man to curse David? He did not tell him this by commanding, for in that case we would have to praise him for his obedience, but rather, by a hidden and just plan, God inclined the will, vitiated by his own evil, towards sin, and that is why it is written: The Lord said to him. If it were a matter of obedience to the Lord, there would be more reason to praise him than to punish him, as for this sin we know that he was later afflicted. And on this occasion the reason why the Lord told him to curse David or, in other words, why the Lord let that man's evil heart fall into sin, is not left silent. Maybe God will look at my affliction and repay me with favors for today's curses. And from this story it is clear that the Lord uses evil wills for the praise and help of the good. Thus, he employed Judas when he betrayed Christ, and thus, he employed the Jews who crucified Christ. And how many good things followed to the believing people! And also in a very wise way the Lord uses our terrible enemy in order to exercise and test the faith and piety of the good. The Lord seeks nothing for himself, who knows and knows everything before it comes to pass; but for us, who need to go through this or that. Did not Absalon freely choose the counsel that suited him? And yet he did so, because the Lord had heard his father's prayer, which is why the Scripture says: Because God had decided to thwart the wise counsel of Ahithophel, so that God would bring evil upon Absalom. He said correctly because at that moment it benefited his cause, which was to put an end to his father, since he had rebelled against him, and certainly he would have succeeded if the Lord, working in Absalon's heart, had not dispelled the good advice of Ahithophel, so that Absalon rejected it and chose what was in no way convenient for him.

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, despised the salutary advice of the elders, not to treat the people harshly, and agreed to that of the young men, responding with threats to those who owed gentleness. And didn't he act with complete freedom? But for this reason ten of the tribes separated from him, and took Jeroboam as king, thus fulfilling the will of the angry God, who had thus predicted it. What does the Scripture say? Therefore, the king ignored the people, because this is what the Lord ordained, to fulfill the word that MI had spoken through Agias of Shiloh to Jeroboam, son of Nabat. This was accomplished by the will of man, but by God's will. Read the book of the Paralipomena: Then God aroused against Joram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabs, who lived near the Ethiopians, who came up against Judah, invaded the land and captured all the property that they found from the king's house. It is discovered in such words that the Lord raises up enemies who destroy countries worthy of such punishment. Did the Philistines and Arabs go up unintentionally to the land of Judah, or if they did so willingly, is it falsely written that the Lord awakened the spirit of those enemies? Rather, both feelings are right, because of their free will they ascended, and yet the Lord awakened their spirit. What we can reverse by saying that God awakened their spirit, and yet, by free will they rose. The Almighty impresses in the hearts of men a movement of his own wills, so that he who never knew how to want injustice does whatever he wants. What did the man of God say to King Amaziah? If you go with them, even if you make courageous efforts, God will make you fall before the enemy, because God has the power to lift up and to tear down. How is it that the power of God helps some in war, and makes others flee with terror, but because in heaven and on earth he accomplishes everything he wants and still works?

With these divine testimonies and other similar ones that it would take a long time to enumerate, it has become very clear, in my opinion, that God works in the hearts of men in order to incline human wills where He wants, now with mercy towards good, now in accordance with His merits towards evil, always by virtue of His plan, sometimes clear, other times hidden, but without just remission. Indelibly engraved in your heart you must have that in God there is no injustice. And for this reason, when you read in the sacred books that God seduces men or that he hardens or dulls their hearts, be sure that their evil merits have been the cause of everything they suffer, and certainly with reason; and never do what the Proverbs of Solomon condemn: The foolishness of man twists his ways and then he blames God. Grace, however, is not given according to merit, since otherwise grace would no longer be grace. In fact it is called grace because it is given for free. If God is so powerful that he can work through good or bad angels, or by any other means, in the hearts of the evil ones according to their merits, keeping in mind that their malice is not God's work, but comes from original sin or from one's own will, will we marvel that through the Holy Spirit he works good in the hearts of his chosen ones who made them good out of evil hearts?

Saint Augustine, tireless defender of the Catholic faith in all areas and under all aspects in which it was fought, reaches the summit of his greatness in the Pelagian controversy; This is also where that subtlety of ingenuity is shown in all its splendor, which very few have achieved and perhaps none surpassed, in unraveling the sophistry and in discovering the misunderstandings and artinuiflim in which the proud Breton heretic appeared so skilled, neither side of the deepest humility and that supreme charity with which he loved those very ones whom he fought with so much zeal from the first moment in which this error was born, until, lacking strength, the pen fell from his hand prostrate on the bed of pain. For him there was no work when it came to defending the Church and the honor of its divine Founder, since charity was the spring of all his undertakings. The fight was hard, because the enemies, tenacious, obstinate and fruitful in all kinds of resources, did not neglect any opportunity that could give them any advantage; All their weapons were good, even lies and slander; The Saint multiplied his activity: new treatises, new epistles and new sermons appeared every day to combat error, taking from the adversaries one by one their positions with the weapons of the truth of the cause he defended, and since he was not able to convert those obstinate heretics, at least ensure that their errors were not the cause of the perdition of other souls, for all of whom he was willing to sacrifice every moment of his existence and his life itself. It was a great day for the holy Bishop of Hippo when Pope Zosimus, finally discovering the tricks and bad faith of Pelagius and Celestius, solemnly excommunicated them and once again condemned their errors. Saint Augustine had worked hard to reveal them, already in his books, and in the councils that had met for this purpose in Africa, but at last he managed to see his most ardent desires fulfilled: the

heretics were unmasked, the Church was now free of those dry and useless members, and Christians knew what to expect. This condemnation surprised many Christians in the East, where Pelagius was then, since he was considered a man of an austere life and impeccable customs; Furthermore, this cunning heretic, with his continuous reservations and reticences, sowed confusion in upright and well-intentioned souls who were unaware of his ambiguities and the abuse he made of certain Catholic formulas, and because of this he was considered a true Catholic. Saint Melania was also in the East, where she had arrived not long ago with her mother and husband; These illustrious Christians, who showed Pelagius, a former friend of Saint Paulinus of Ñola, a certain deference, having had an interview with the heretic following his condemnation, obtained from him a satisfactory declaration on grace and original sin, in their opinion, impractical in the ambiguities that Pelagius so abused, satisfactory, and they immediately communicated it to their great friend Augustine. The Saint, who knew perfectly well the heresiarch's tricks, judged such statements insufficient, too general and not very explicit, which could have had the same meaning in the mind of their author as others made previously. The holy Bishop had reflected a lot on the works of Pelagius to unravel his obscure theories expressed under Catholic formulas, although completely distorting their meaning, to allow himself to be dazzled by some words said to get out of the embarrassing situation in which the zeal of these pious Christians had placed him. And so, to prevent those illustrious friends from becoming involved in the networks and sophistry of Pelagius, and even more so to make known in the East, where the heretic had numerous supporters and sympathizers, the true doctrines and the entire process of the Pelagian controversy, Saint Augustine addresses them with the present treatise, where he analyzes this confession and compares it with the works recognized as his own by Pelagius himself. with the profession of faith that he had sent to Pope Innocent. Before giving a brief summary of the content of the work, we are going to give some news about its recipients.

Saint Melania was born around 383; His father, Valerio Publicóla, belonged to the gens Valeria, descendant of that famous Valerio Publicóla, one of the founders of the Republic and companion of Brutus in the Consulate; His mother, Albina, also of noble family, was a member of the Cetonia gens, to which the emperor had belonged.

dor L.. Vtero. Still very young, Melania, to obey her parents, had married the noble Piniano, and by common agreement, the two children they had had having died in their tender years, they resolved to live from now on in chastity like two brothers, consecrating themselves entirely to God. In the first months of 404, her father, leaving her an immense fortune, the largest in the Empire, died as a Christian, recanting in his deathbed the opposition he had until then made to his daughter's plans to retire from the world to follow the life of austerity and mortification that her illustrious grandmother Antonia Melania led in the Holy Land. After overcoming great difficulties that opposed his purpose, he managed to obtain the power to sell his immense possessions; He spent six or seven years selling off those properties scattered throughout the Empire. Fabulous amounts of money came to them from everywhere, which they immediately distributed to the poor, to the churches and monasteries; They freed multitudes of slaves: 8,000 had been manumitted, and they were not done yet, far from it. When Rome was sacked by the Goths, August 410, they were in Sicily, where, after selling the beautiful estates they owned there, they headed to Africa. They set up residence in Tagaste, and Saint Augustine, who was unable to meet them, sent a messenger carrying a letter of welcome "to the illustrious brothers in the Lord and most beloved for their holiness and most esteemed Albina, Piniano and Melania" {Epist. 124). Very soon they would undoubtedly go to visit him in Hippo, where they would talk about Publicóla and Antonia Melania, who had also died by this date, so that the Saint could narrate to them the cries of this mother, her resignation and her prayers for her dead son, when she was still in Africa on her way back to the Holy Places. But above all, what these friends, in love with the perfect life, were looking for in Hippo was advice for directing their vocation; and who could give it to him more fully than Augustine? Two great monasteries were founded in Tagaste on the recommendation of the Saint: one for men, the other for women; Melania retired to this, where she lived the five or six years that they remained in Africa consecrated to the most absolute poverty, to the most rigorous penance and to continuous prayer and reading of the Bible.

In one of the visits that Melania and Piniano, accompanied by Saint Alypius, made to the holy Bishop of Hippo, a scene took place in which Saint Augustine found himself in an extremely embarrassing situation for his guests.

The years from 420 to 431 were spent by Melania in complete solitude in a rough and narrow cell that her mother had built for her on Mount Olívete; In this year he left his retirement to found a monastery, where he soon had the consolation of seeing more than ninety nuns gathered together, whom he wisely and prudently directed until his death. Not long after his mother's death, which occurred in the same year 431, he also followed her to the

Piniano tomb, silently and darkly as he had lived, always supporting the initiatives of the heroic Melania in everything. Shortly after, she began to build, in the place where the remains of her loved ones rested, a monastery for men, "so that I may still live, she said, to see the regular services celebrated in this church and the bones of my mother and my husband chilled with the psalmody that the religious here raise to heaven." He still makes a trip to ConsUintiritiplu in order to convert his uncle Volusiano, a noble and generous spirit, who unfortunately still lived in the HoInbras of gentility. Having achieved his objective, after suffering great setbacks and sufferings, he returned to Jenmulén to his beloved nuns, and on December 31, 439, after receiving the Eucharist for the third time in that same day, faithful as always to the Roman liturgy, my pure and generous soul flew to heaven to receive the reward promised to the poor in spirit. Poor clothes, which holy hermits of Egypt had given her, and which she had preserved as precious relics, served as a shroud for that body exhausted by penance, in which she had surpassed the most austere ascetics of the wasteland. Such is, broadly speaking, the life of the last and most glorious heiress of the illustrious family of Ion Valerios. The present treaty was composed in 418; and determining more, it had to be in the period of time that goes from June to mid-September; During all this time and also throughout May the Saint remained in Carthage, where the work was written, as seen in the first chapter. From the second book we know that Pelagianism had already been condemned by Pope Zosimus, and this took place at the end of May of that year; Furthermore, in the book of the Retractationes he reviews this work immediately before that of the minutes of the conference with Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, which took place in Caesarea on September 20 of the same year 418. It cannot, therefore, be doubted that it was written during this time. If we wanted to estimate more, we would be inclined to believe that it would have been in August or the first half of September. The interview of the three pious Christians with Pelagius had to take place after the latter's condemnation, as seems to be indicated in several passages of the work, and clearly in one (c. 8, 1.

I I ), in which Saint Augustine tells us that Pelagius complains of having been included in the same condemnation as Celestius; and it seems that it is not too long to take two months for the news of the condemnation to reach the East, for the interview to take place and for Saint Augustine to receive it. The recipients are the three illustrious Christians Albina,

Piniano and Melania; The treaty is dedicated to them; but Saint Augustine knew these illustrious characters too well, their great faith and zeal for orthodoxy; They were not the ones who needed an extensive and complete refutation of the heresy; Those whom Saint Augustine has in his mind when writing this work are the numerous young men of the East who had adhered to the errors of Pelagius or who, attracted by the rigid asceticism of the heretic or deceived by the cunning and misunderstandings and by the way of expressing himself, in the appearance of a true Catholic, were about to be dragged to perdition. "It was very important," says Poujoulat, "that these countries, visited every year by a multitude of pilgrims, knew the entire truth about Pelagius and Celestius, about the writings and acts that motivated and preceded their condemnation. These two books were true to everything and made the East fully aware of the matter." The content of this treatise, briefly stated, is as follows: The first book, which is entitled On the Grace of Christ, is dedicated to refuting Pelagius' concept of grace, exposing in contrast the true doctrine of the Church on this issue. It begins with the declaration that the heretic made to the pious Roman Christians. "I anathematize," he declared to them, "everyone who denies, by word or deed, that the grace of God, by which Christ has come into this world to save sinners, is necessary not only at all times, but also for each of our acts; and that those who work to destroy it receive eternal punishment." Whoever reads this confession, continues the Saint, and has not read his works, will accept this declaration as the expression of Catholic sentiment; but whoever knows the works that he himself admits as authentic will consider this same statement very suspicious; for Pelagius always understood by grace the forgiveness of sins, the sublime example of Christ or; its divine doctrine, very well in the mind of its author these words may have this same meaning; since the generality and imprecision in which they are conceived lend themselves wonderfully to such explanations.

He then analyzes his most recent work De libero arbitrio, copying numerous and very significant paragraphs in which he talks about grace, but always either limits himself to generalities or, when expressed more precisely, it is seen that he understands by grace either free will itself or the law, or at most, the revelation of wisdom through the illumination of the understanding, but it is never found in

the works of Pelagius that God immediately influences the will of man and cooperates with him in the execution; But it is not only this: whatever this heretic understands by grace, he strictly assures that we can deserve it with our good works; Furthermore, convinced of the robustness or integrity of free will, he defends with great aplomb that even this same grace is not necessary for us, but only useful, since with it we can more easily execute the precept, which without it we would also execute in the same way, although with more difficulty. The Saint refutes all these errors through the work with numerous texts from the holy books. Similar to this declaration is also the one he made in the profession of faith that he sent to Pope Innocent, in which, having expanded on other dogmas of the Church, about which no one accused him, when he came to the question in which his orthodoxy was doubted with such serious and well-founded reasons, he limited himself to this brief and imprecise statement: "In such a way we confess free will, that, nevertheless, we maintain that we are continually in need of help. divine", since we do not know what he means by this help. He then quickly examines the heretic's other treatises, all of which he confesses to have read, except a brief epistle, and in none of them has he found that they speak of true Christian grace, nowhere has he found that grace means for Pelagius "a help for good action added to nature and doctrine by the communication of the most ardent and most luminous charity." And this is the grace that Pelagius must confess, if he wants to be a true Christian. And he ends this first book by quoting several paragraphs from Saint Ambrose in which he vigorously defends the traditional doctrine of the Church on grace; and since the heretic had paid him great praise, believing that he could support his errors in some passages of the works of the holy Bishop of Milan, he correctly explained such texts and exhorted Pelagius to imitate the faith and humility of such a great man and vindicated him of his praises, which to true Christians would make the name of such an excellent bishop suspicious, in view of their origin. The second book, which is titled On Original Sin, is dedicated to defending the transmission of the first sin. In the same interview, Pelagius found it necessary to say something regarding this issue.

"Children, he continued, must also be baptized under the same formula with which adults are baptized." No one would suppose, continues Saint Augustine, that original sin was denied under these words; but certain statements of

Celestius, more determined than Pelagius, has made known to us the true feelings of Pelagius on this matter, since it is no mystery to anyone that Celestius is nothing more than a front man for the ideas of this outright heretic. And everyone knows, and he is not shy about hiding it, that Celestio denies that children contract original sin. In a synod held in Carthage, from which he copies a long quotation, he did not dare, it is true, to deny it, although otherwise he could not in any way be made to admit it; but in a writing that he presented to the Church of Rome he admitted the need to administer baptism to children in remissionem peccatorum, but at the same time he flatly denied that children had any sin. Pope Zosimus, believing he saw signs of good faith in Celestius and having some hope that he would return to the right path, treated him for some time with great indulgence and commiseration; but having discovered the bad faith and obstinacy of this heretic, he launched a solemn excommunication against him, including Pelagius in the same anathema. And although he complains of having been included in this condemnation, the examination of the Council of Diospolis where, due to his evil arts, he managed to deceive the Fathers, the examination of some proposals of works that he published after this Council, the oral teachings that he propagated among his disciples and, finally, the same profession of faith sent to Rome, in which his only objective was to deceive the Apostolic See, although he was in no way able to achieve this, all of this proves, without leaving any room for doubt, the justice of the ruling pronounced against him. These heretics, in order to erase the stigma of heresy from their foreheads, resorted to defending that this question was one of those about which in the Church the pro or he against can be defended without any damage to the faith; This statement gives Saint Augustine the opportunity to explain which doctrines directly touch the faith and which others, not having such a connection with it, can deny or doubt or err about them without detriment to the faith by which we are Christians; It is not one of the latter that of original sin; Well, in the cause of those two men, one of whom with his disobedience has subjected us to sin, involving us all in his own perdition, while the other with his obedience has rescued us from sin and in himself has made us saved, in these two men, Adam and Jesus Christ, lies the entire foundation of the Christian faith.
And dividing men according to how they have lived before the law, under the law and after the coming of Jesus Christ, in order to exclude the help of the grace of Christ to those of the two first.

In this book Saint Augustine teaches that Pelagius tries to deceive with his confession of the step, since he makes it consist either in nature and free will, or in law and doctrine. Pclagio also affirms that divine grace helps only what he calls the possibility of will and action, not the will itself and the action; and he believes that even this same grace is given by God according to the merits of men and that it only helps them so that they can more easily fulfill the divine precepts. Saint Augustine examines the passages of the heresiarch's treatises in which, as he boastfully said, he explicitly exalted the rank of God; and shows that these passages can be interpreted from the law and from the doctrine or from the divine revelation and from the example of Oristo, which is also reduced to the doctrine, or the remission of sins, and that it is not in any way clear whether Pelagius admits Christian grace, that is, a help to do good added to the natural and to the doctrine by the communication of the most ardent and most luminous charity; and finally, she exhorts Pelagius to listen doubly to the great man, since he so exalts him, to Saint Ambrose, who has spoken so eloquently in praise of divine grace.

Anyone who hears these words and ignores his way of feeling, which he has expressed clearly enough in his books, not in those that, as he says, were stolen from him before he had given them the last hand or denies at all that they are his, but in those that he mentions in the letter he sent to Rome, will undoubtedly believe that Pelagius thinks in accordance with the truth; but whoever knows what is stated in them more clearly, will also consider even these words suspicious. For if you make the grace of God, by which Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, consist in the remission of sins, you can adapt those words to this sense by saying that for this reason grace is necessary for each hour, for each moment and for each of the acts, so that, always retaining in memory and continually keeping in mind this forgiveness of sins, we do not sin from now on, strengthened not by the communication of some strange virtue, but by the forces of our own will, which remembers in each one of acts what was granted to him for the forgiveness of sins.

3. But what is strange about it? For Pelagius himself having condemned in the episcopal acts without any protest those who affirm that the grace and help of God is not given to us for each act, but consists in free will or in law and doctrine; and we believed that all his misrepresentations on this matter had been destroyed there, since he condoned even those who teach that the grace of God is granted to us according to merit; Despite this, in the books he has published in defense of free will, which he mentions in the letter he sent to Rome, it is clear that he does not think anything different from what he was believed to have condemned. For it makes the grace and help of God, with which we are helped not to sin, consist either in nature and free will or in law and doctrine; namely, he wants it to be believed that, when God helps man to avoid evil and do good, he does so by revealing to him and showing him what must be done, but in no way by cooperating with man and inspiring him with charity so that he can do what he has known should be done. 4. Because Pelagius, establishing and distinguishing three things, by which he says that we fulfill the divine precepts: possibility, will and action; the possibility, by which man can be just; the will, by which it wants to be, and the action, by which it is; confesses that the first, namely, possibility, is granted to us by the Creator of nature and that it is not in our power, but that we possess it even against our will; but the other two, that is, will and action, he affirms that they belong to us and attributes them to us in such a way that he categorically assures that they depend only on ourselves. Finally, he says that divine grace does not help these two, will and action, which he wants to be exclusive.

Here is the entire dogma of Pelagius, clearly explained in the third book in defense of free will, where these three things: one, which is power; another, which is willing, and the third, which is being, that is, possibility, will and action, with such subtlety he took care to distinguish that, when we read or hear that he confesses the help of grace to avoid evil and do good, whether he makes it consist of law and doctrine, or elsewhere, we understand what he says and we do not err by understanding him in a different way than the one who thinks. For we must know that he does not believe that our will and action are helped by divine help, but only the possibility of will and action, which is the only one among these three things, as he says, that we have from God, as if what God has placed in our nature were weak; but the other two that Pelagius wanted to attribute to us were so strong and robust and so self-sufficient that they did not need any help from God; That is why it does not help us to want, nor to act, but it only helps us so that we can want and act. The Apostle assures the opposite: With fear and trembling work out your own health. And so that they would understand that they are helped by God not only in terms of being able to act (since they had already received this in nature and in doctrine), but also in terms of acting, he does not say: God is the one who works the power in us, as if they by themselves had the power to will and act and had no need, regarding these two things, of divine help; but says: For it is God who works in you to will and to finish, or as we read in other codices, and especially in the Greeks: to will and to act. See how the Apostle, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, anticipated long before the future adversaries of the grace of God and affirmed that God works in us these two things, namely, willing and acting, which he so wanted to depend on us as if they were not helped by the help of divine grace.

This is making the grace of God consist of the law and the doctrine.

CHAPTER XI 12. But what shall I say about the revelation of wisdom? It is not easy for anyone to hope to be able to reach in this life the sublimity of the revelations of the apostle Saint Paul; and what else are we to believe that was used to be revealed to him but things relating to wisdom? Without a doubt, if the Apostle had already then possessed the highest charity that could not be increased nor could he be conceited, would it be necessary for the angel of Satan to slap him to repress the pride that might exist in the greatness of the revelations? But whoever knows what should be done and does not do it, that person has not yet learned from God according to grace, but according to the law; not according to the spirit, but according to the letter. But many seem to execute what the law orders for fear of punishment, not for love of justice; and this justice that comes from the law the Apostle calls his own, since it is as it were commanded, not given. But if it is given, it is not called natural justice, but from God, because in such a way it becomes ours that, nevertheless, it comes to us from God. For he says: That I may find myself in Him, not having a righteousness of my own, which comes from the law, but that which comes from faith in Jesus Christ, the righteousness that comes from God. So great is the distance between the law and grace that, even though we do not doubt that the law comes from God, nevertheless, the justice that comes from the law does not come from God, but the justice that is consummated by charity does come from God. For what is called legal justice is that which results from the curse of the law, but what is called the justice of God is that which is given for the benefit of grace, so that the precept may not be terrible, but gentle, as requested in the Psalm: You are gentle, Lord, and in your gentleness teach me your justice; that is, in such a way that I am not forced to be slavishly under the law for fear of punishment, but that I delight in being embraced by the law through free charity. For he freely fulfills the precept who willingly fulfills it; and everyone who learns in this way, executes absolutely everything that he has learned to do.

CHAPTER XIV 15, Of this way of teaching the Lord also says: Everyone who has heard my Father and has learned comes to me. After him who does not come, it will not be possible to say with truth: He certainly heard and learned that he should come, but he does not want to execute what he learned. To speak in this way about the way in which God teaches by his grace would be absolutely wrong. Well, if, as the Truth says, everyone who has learned comes to me, whoever does not come is, without a doubt, who has not learned. But who does not see that coming or not coming is a matter of the free will? But this agency can be alone, if it does not come; but if he comes, he cannot help but be helped; and so helped that he not only knows what he should do, but does what he has learned.

OF THE GRACE OF JESUS CHRIST

And for this reason, when God teaches not by the letter of the law, but by the grace of his Spirit, he teaches in such a way that what has been learned is not only seen with the intelligence, but is also desired with the will and is executed with action. By this divine way of teaching, not only the natural possibility of willing and acting is helped, but also the will itself and action. In fact, if only our power were helped by this grace, this is what the Lord would have said: Everyone who has heard my Father and has learned can come to me. But he did not say this, but: Everyone who has heard my Father and has learned comes to me. The power to come, Pelagius places in nature, or also, as he recently began to say, in grace, as he understands it, "with which—as he says—possibility is helped"; On the contrary, coming depends on will and action. But just because someone can come, it does not follow that he also comes, unless he wants to and does so. But everyone who has learned from the Father not only can come, but comes; where the effectiveness of the possibility, the affect of the will and the result of the action are already found.

And if this has been said of the eyes of the spirit, from there it truly comes to the eyes of the flesh both seeing good and evil, since it is not spoken here in the same sense as when it is said that those who look with healthy eyes see well, and those who are sick with them see badly; But here we say that they see good to help and evil to covet. For although through the external eyes we see the poor man who is helped and the woman who is desired, nevertheless, mercy and concupiscence, to see good or evil, come from the interior. Why then is it said to God: Turn away my eyes from seeing vanity? Why do we ask for what is in our power, if God does not help our will?

OF THE GRACE OF JESUS CHRIST

CHAPTER XVI 17. "That we can speak, he says, comes from God; but whether we speak good or bad comes from ourselves." He who speaks well does not teach this. Because it is not you, he says, who speak; but the Spirit of your Father speaks in you. "And to encompass all things in general, the fact that we can act, say and think all good comes from him who this power granted us and helps him." He repeats here the same meaning that he explained previously: that of the three things, that is, possibility, will and action, only possibility is helped. Finally, to complete what he intends, he then said: "But that we act, speak and think well is our own." Here he passed on what he had corrected above, where, after having said: "Therefore, the glory of man consists in his good will and in his good action," he added, saying: "YET more, that of man and that of God, who gave him the possibility of will and action." Why in these examples did he not remember the same thing again, in such a way that, at least at the end of them, he said: The fact that we can act, say and think all the good belongs to him who gave us this power and helps him, but the fact that we act or say or think well is ours and God's? He didn't say that, and if I'm not mistaken, I think I see what he feared.

18. Well, wanting to declare why it belongs to us, he said: "Because we can also convert all these things to evil." Then the reason for not saying that it is ours and God's was that he feared that someone might reply: If the fact that we act, speak and think good belongs to us and to God, because He has granted us this power, for the same reason, it is ours and God's that we act, speak and think evil, because He granted us that power for one or the other; and so, far from us such a thought, just as we are praised together with God in good works, so we must also be blamed together with Him in bad ones. In fact, this possibility that he granted us means that we can do both good and bad.

19. About this possibility, Pelagius, in the first book in defense of free will, speaks in these terms: "We have the possibility of both things granted by God, like a certain root, so to speak, fruitful and fertile, which from the very will of man generates and produces various fruits and can, at the will of the cultivator himself, either shine with the flower of virtues or be bristling with the thorns of vices." Where, without reflecting on what he says, he establishes good and evil as one and the same root, against evangelical truth and apostolic doctrine. The Lord says that neither the good tree can produce bad fruit, nor the bad tree, good; and the apostle Saint Paul, when he says that the root of all evil is greed, warns us that charity must be understood as the root of all goods. If the two trees, the good and the bad, are two men, one good and the other bad, what is the good man if not the one with a good will, that is, the tree with a good root? And what is the bad man if not the one with bad will, that is, the tree with bad roots? Mine are the fruits of these roots and of these trees: the works, the sayings, the thoughts; and those that come from a good will are good, and those that come from a bad will are bad.

CHAPTER XIX 20. Man makes the tree good when he receives the grace of God. For evil is not made good by itself, but from that, through that and in that which is always good; and not only to be a good tree, but also to produce good fruit, it must be helped by the same grace, without which it cannot do any good. For he who externally waters and cultivates through some minister and internally gives the increase by himself contributes to the fruit on good trees. On the contrary, man makes the tree evil when he makes himself evil, when he departs from the unchangeable good, since the separation of that good is the origin of bad will. But this separation does not give rise to another evil nature, but vitiates that which was created good; but, once the vice is corrected, no evil remains, because the vice was attached to nature, but it was vice, not nature.

So to get to God's help you run to Him without His help; And to be helped by God, by being united with Him, will we become united with Him without His help? What greater gift or what similar thing can grace itself obtain for us, if without it we have been able to become one spirit with the Lord only through the freedom of our will?

Stop saying: "The fact that we can act, say and think all the good belongs to him who granted us and helps us with this power, but the fact that we act or speak or think well is exclusively ours." Cease, I say, from speaking thus. For God not only gave us our power and gives him his help, but also works in us to will and to act. Not because we do not want or do not act, but because without his help we neither want anything good nor do we do it either. How can one say: "That we can do good belongs to God, but that we do it is our own," when the Apostle says that he prays to God for those to whom he wrote so that they would do nothing evil and do what is good? In fact, the Apostle does not say: "We ask" that you may not do anything evil, but that you do nothing evil; nor does he say, That you may do good, but that you do good. For those of whom it is written: All who are moved by the Spirit of God are children of God, evidently, to do what is good, are moved by him who is good. How does Pelagius say: "That we can speak well we have from God, but that we speak well is exclusively ours," when the Lord says: It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you? He does not say: It is not you who have given yourselves the power to speak well, but he says: It is not you who speak. Nor does he say: "It is the Spirit of your Father" who gives you or has given you the power to speak well, but rather he who speaks in you; Jesus Christ does not indicate the help of possibility, but rather expresses the effect of cooperation. How does the conceited defender of free will say: "That we can think well is from God, but that we think well is our own"? And the humble preacher of grace responds: Not because we are capable of thinking something, as of ourselves, but our sufficiency comes from God. It doesn't say "being able to think", but rather "thinking".

Very healthy and very true sentence. For we would have no where to love Him if we had not received it from Him by loving ourselves first. What good could we do if they did not love us? Or how can we not do good if we love? For even though it seems that at times God's command is carried out not out of love, but out of fear, yet where there is no love, no good work is taken into account, nor, strictly speaking, can it be called a good work; because everything that is not according to faith is sin, and faith works through charity. And for this reason, the grace of God, by which the charity of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, must be confessed in such a way by those who truly want to confess it, that they do not doubt that without it no good that is related to piety and true justice can be carried out at all. "Let me justify," he says, "before your beatitude this letter, in which I plainly affirm that we, in order to sin and not to sin, possess, without any injury, free will, which in all good works is incessantly helped by divine help." You see, according to the intelligence that God has given you, that these words of his are not enough to resolve the issue. For we still ask by what help he says that free will is helped, lest, as usual, he wants the law and doctrine to be understood. And if he is asked why he said "always", he can answer: Because it is written: And he will meditate on his law day and night. Then, having interspersed a few words about the state of man and his natural possibility to sin and not to sin, he added, saying: "And this power of free will is universally possessed by everyone, Christians, Jews, and even Gentiles. By nature, free will is equal in all, but only in Christians is it helped by grace." Again we ask: Why grace? And he will still be able to answer us: By the law and by Christian doctrine. 34. Furthermore, whatever I understand by grace, he affirms that it is given to Christians themselves according to merit, despite the fact that in Palestine, I have already recalled before, he condemned in his famous justification those who maintain this. Here are his words: "In those, he says, the excellence of their condition is naked and defenseless"; refers to those who are not Christians. Then, continuing the rest, he says: "But in those who belong to Christ, it is strengthened by his divine help." You see that it is not yet indicated with what aid she is helped. But he continues still about those who are not Christians, and says: "Those must be judged and condemned, because, possessing free will, through which they could come to faith and merit the grace of God, they misuse the freedom granted. So it is clear that Pelagius affirms that grace, whatever its nature, since he does not expressly declare it, is granted to us according to merit. 36. Who would have believed that a contrary meaning was hidden beneath this almost obvious confession, if Celestio had not expressed it? Well, this one, in his little treatise that he alleged in Rome in the ecclesiastical records, admitted that "children are also baptized into the remission of sins", but denied "that they had any original sin." But now let us see not what Pelagius thought about the baptism of children, but rather what he thought about the help of grace in the book of the profession of his faith that he sent to Rome. "In such a way," he says, "we confess free will, that, nevertheless, we maintain that we continually need the help of God." And again we ask what help he confesses we are in need of; and again we find his words ambiguous, because he can answer us that he speaks of the law or of the Christian doctrine, by which natural possibility is helped. But we in the confession of the followers of Pelagius seek that grace of which the Apostle says: God has not given us the spirit of fear, but the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of charity and the spirit of continence. For it does not follow that he who has the gift of science, by means of which he knows what he must do, also has the gift of charity to execute it.

CAPUT XXXVIII 42. item alibi in eadem epistle: "Nam si etiam ante legem, inquit, ut diximus, ac multo ante Domini nostri et Salvatoris adventum, iuste quídam et sánete vixisse referuntur; quanto magis post illustrationem adventus eius nos id posse credendum est, qui instaurati per Christi gratiam, et in meliorem hominem renati sumus, qui sanguine eius expiati atque mundati, ipsiusque exemplo ad perfectionem incitati iustitiae, meliores illis 'esse debenmus, qui ante legem fuere?" 42. In another passage of the same letter he also says: "For if even before the law, as we have already said, and long before the coming of our Lord and Savior, some are said to have lived justly and holyly, how much more after the splendor of his coming should it be believed that we, who have been renewed by the grace of Christ and have been reborn to a new and better class of men, who have been completely purified by his blood and encouraged by their example to the consummation of justice, and how much better than those, who lived before the law, must we be?" See how here also, although with different words, he made the help of grace consist in the remission of sins and in the example of Christ. Then he adds: "We must also be better than those who lived under the law, since the Apostle says: Sin will not dominate you, for you are not under the law, but under grace. And since we have spoken about this, as I believe, sufficiently, let us now form a perfect virgin, who, always inflamed by both things, with the sanctity of her customs will attest together to the excellence of nature and that of grace." In these words you must notice that that is why he wanted to close this phrase in this way, so that we understand by the good of nature what we received when we were created; and by that of grace, when we contemplate the example of Christ; as if their sin had not been forgiven. those who lived or live under the law because they did not have the example of Christ or because they do not believe.

43. Hoc autem istum sapere, et alia eius verba ostendunt, non in hoc libro, sed in tertio pro libero arbitrio, ubi ad eum loquens contra quem disputat, quoniam ille posuerat verba Apostoli dicetis: Non quod voló ago, et, Video aliam legem in membris meis repugnantem legi mentís meae, et cetera quae ibi dicuntur; iste responded, atque ait: "Hoc enim quod tu de Acostólo intelligere cupis, omnes ecclesiastici viri ín peccatoris-et sub lege adhuc positi asserunt eum dixisse persona, qui nimia vitiorum consuetudine velut quadam teneretur necessitate peccandi, et quamvis bonum appeteret volúntate, usu tamen praecipitaretur in malum. In persona autem, inquit, hominis unius, designat populum sub vetere adhuc lege peccantem; quem ab hoc consuetudinis malo dicit liberandum esse per Christum, qui credentibus sibi primo omnia per baptismum peccata_ dimittit; vitiorum consuetudinem virtutum vincit exemplo". Bcce quomodo vult intelligi adiuvari eos, qui sub lege peccant, ut per gratiam Christi iustificati liberentur, tamquam eis non sufficiat sola lex, propter nimiam peccandi consuetudinem, nisi Christi accessat, non inspiratio caritatis per Spiritum Sanctum, sed intuendum et imitandum in doctrina evangélica virtutis eius exemplum. Et certain maxim hic erat causa exprimendi, quam dieeret gratiam, ubi locum ipsum de quo respondert, sic conclusit Apostolus, ut diceret: Infelix ego homo, quis liberated me from corpore mortis huius? Hanc iste eum constituat, non in virtutis eius auxilio, sed imitationis exemplo, quid amplius de illo sperare deben, ubicumque gratiae nomen sub ambigua generalitate commemorat?
OF THE GUIDANCE OF JESUS CHRIST

43. That is how Pelagius understands it; Other words of his also declare it, not in this book, but in the third of his defense of free will, where, addressing the one against whom he disputes, when opposing him the words of the Apostle: I do not do what I want, and I see in my members another law that resists the law of my spirit, and the rest that is said there, Pelagius responds, saying: "This is what you understand to be said by the Apostle, all I03 ecclesiastical men maintain that he said it in the person of the sinner and of him who still lives under the law; who, by the great habit of vices, is, so to speak, dominated by a certain need to sin, and although he desires good with his will, yet he is drawn to evil by custom. The Apostle, then, continues, in the person of one man designates the people who still sin under the old law; who, first through baptism, forgives all the sins of those who believe in Him, then stimulates them to perfect holiness by imitation of Him, and overcomes the habit of vices by the example of His virtues." See how I want it to be understood that those who sin under the law are helped, so that, once justified, they may be set free by the grace of Christ; Since the law alone is not sufficient for them, because of the excessive habit of sinning, it is necessary that they add not the inspiration of Christ's charity, through the Holy Spirit, but the contemplation and imitation of the example of his virtue, as found in the evangelical doctrine. And truly here was a good occasion to declare what he calls grace, where this same place, about which Pelagius answers, the Apostle concluded with these words: Woe to me! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Making it consist not in the help of the virtue of Christ, but in the example of his imitation, what more are we to expect from him whenever he mentions the name of grace under ambiguous generalities?
OF THE GRACE OF JESUS CHRIST

44. item in eodem libro ad virginem sacram, unde iam etiam supra disseruimus, ubi ait: "Subditi simus Deo, eiusque fazando voluntatem, divinam mereamur gratiam, et facilius nequam spiritui, Sancti Spiritus auxilio, resistamus." In quibus eius verbis certe manifestum est, ita eum velle nos adiuvari gratia Spiritus Sancti, non quia sine illo etiam per solam naturae possibillitatem non possumus resistero tentatori, sed ut facilius resistamus. Quod tamen qualeeumque et quatulumcumque adiutorium, eum credibile est in hoc constituere, quod nobis additur scientia revealing Spiritu per doctrinam, quam vel non possumus, vel difficile habere possumus per naturam. Ista sunt quae in libro, quem scfipsit ad virginem Christi, advertere potui, ubi videtur gratiam confiteri; quae profecto qualia sint, utique cernitis.

44. Likewise, in the same booklet to the sacred virgin, about which we have also already discussed, it says: "Let us be subject to God, and, by fulfilling his will, we will deserve divine grace and more easily we will resist, through the help of the Holy Spirit, the evil spirit." In these words of his it is very clear that he wants us to be helped in this way by the grace of the Holy Spirit, not because without it we cannot also resist the tempter by natural possibility alone, but so that we resist him more easily. Which help, however, of any kind and however small, it is credible that he establishes it in that, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, he communicated to us through doctrine a science that we either cannot or can hardly obtain by nature. These are the places that I have been able to notice in the book he wrote to the Virgin of Christ, in which he alludes to grace; You, without a doubt, see what its importance is.

CHAPTER XLI 45. "Read also, he says, the recent short story that in defense of free will we have recently been forced to publish; and you will know how unjustly they enjoy infaming us for denying grace, who in almost the entire course of the work fully and sincerely confessed both free will and grace." in order that he execute by will and by action what he has learned that he must act. It does not deviate in any way from its well-known principle in which it establishes those three things: possibility, will and action; in which he affirms that only possibility is incessantly helped by divine help, but he judges that will and action do not need any help from God. The very help, by which he affirms the natural possibility is helped, he makes it consist of the law and the doctrine, which he confesses are also revealed to us by the Holy Spirit, and for this reason he grants that we should pray. He judges that the times of the prophets also had this help of law and doctrine; but that the help of grace, taken in the strict sense, consists in the example of the Savior, which, as you see, is included in the evangelical doctrine that is preached to us; as if it were a path that we must walk, since, once indicated, we are enough for ourselves with the forces of free will, without needing any other help, not to deviate from it; although he assures that the path itself can also be found by nature alone, but more easily with the help of grace.

46. ​​This is what, to the best of my knowledge, I have been able to understand in the writings of Pelagius when he mentions grace. And you see that those who think this way, ignoring the justice of God, want to establish their own; and they are far from that which comes to us not from us, but from God, which they should notice and know mainly in the holy canonical Scriptures. As you read them according to your own feeling, in reality you do not even see what is manifest. 47. "The blessed bishop Ambrose," he says, "in whose books the Roman faith primarily shines, shines like a beautiful flower among the Latin writers, and whose faith and very clear understanding of the Scriptures not even the enemy has dared to censure." See how and with what great praise he celebrates this man, who, although very holy and learned, is in no way to be compared with the authority of the canonical Scriptures. Whom he praises in this way because he believes that in some passage of his works he can use him as a witness to prove that man can live without sin; But this is not the question now, but we are dealing with the help of grace, by which we are helped not to sin and to live righteously.

48. Listen, then, to that venerable prelate when he says and teaches in the second book of his Exposition of the Gospel according to Saint Laica that the Lord also cooperates with our wills. "So you see," he says, "that everywhere the virtue of the Lord cooperates with human efforts; so that no one can build without the Lord, no one can keep without the Lord, and no one can begin anything without the Lord. And for this reason, according to the Apostle: Whether you eat, or whether you drink, do everything to the glory of God." You see how Saint Ambrose, even what men usually say: "We begin and God finishes," excluded it with these words: "No one can even begin anything without God." Likewise, in the sixth book of the same work, when dealing with the two debtors to a single creditor, it says: "According to men, perhaps the one who owed the most offended more; but by the mercy of God the cause is changed, so that the one who owed the most loves more, provided, however, that he obtains grace." See how the Catholic Doctor proclaims very clearly that charity itself, for which one loves more, is also attributed to the benefit of grace.

49. Blessed Ambrose also affirms in the ninth book of the same work that penance itself, which is undoubtedly a work of the will, comes to fruition through the mercy and help of the Lord; It goes like this: "Good tears are those that wash away guilt. Therefore, those whom Jesus looks at, they cry. Peter denied for the first time, and did not cry, because the Lord had not looked at him; he denied a second time, and neither did he cry, because the Lord had not yet looked at him; he denied yet for the third time, Jesus looked at him, and he wept very bitterly." Let these read the Gospel, and they will see that the Lord was then inside while he was judged by the chief priests, and that the apostle Saint Peter was outside and below in the court next to the fire with the servants, now sitting, now standing, as stated in the most truthful and agreeable narrative of the evangelists. That is why it cannot be said that the Lord would have looked at him, visibly admonishing him with his bodily eyes. And, therefore, what is written there: The Lord looked at him, was realized within, was realized in his spirit, was realized in his will. By his mercy, the Lord helped him invisibly, touched his heart, brought back his memory, visited Peter with his interior grace and moved the inner man to the point of shedding external tears and making love flow. Here is how he assists our wills and actions with his help; Here is how willing and acting work in us. 50. Saint Ambrose himself also says in the same book: "For if Peter fell, who had said: Even though others be scandalized, I will not be scandalized, who can justly boast of himself? Finally, David, who had said: I said in my abundance: I will never be moved, declares that his own presumption harmed him, saying: You turned away your face and I was troubled." Let this one hear the teaching of such a great man, imitate the faith of him whose doctrine and faith he exalted. Humbly listen to him, faithfully imitate him and do not stubbornly boast about yourself so that you do not perish. Why does Pelagius want to sink in that sea from which Peter was freed by the stone?

51. Listen to the same priest of God in the same sixth book of the same work when he says: "The evangelist himself expressed why they did not receive him, saying: Because he gave it to understand that he was going to Jerusalem. For the disciples longed to be received in Samaria. But God calls those with whom he is pleased, and whom he wills, he makes religious." What an expression of this man of God, drawn from the very source of divine grace! "God, he says, calls those whom he pleases, and makes religious whom he pleases." See if this sentence is not prophetic: I will have compassion on whoever has compassion on me and I will grant mercy to him to whom I am merciful; and this other apostolic: Thus, then, it is not of the one who wants nor of the one who runs, but of God, who has compassion. Because as your man of our time also says: "He whom he deigns, he calls, and whomever he wants, he makes religious." Will anyone dare to say that he is not still religious "he who runs to the Lord and desires to be directed by Him and subordinates his will to the will of God, and who, being constantly united with Him, becomes, according to the Apostle, one spirit with Him"? But all this excellent work of a religious man "can only be realized, according to Pelagius, through the freedom of free will." On the contrary, the blessed Ambrose, so exaltedly praised by him, says: "The Lord God, whom he deigns, calls, and whom he wills, he makes religious." Then so that he runs to the Lord and desires to be directed by Him, and subordinates his will to the will of God, and, being constantly united with Him, becomes, according to the Apostle, one spirit with Him, God, whom He wills, makes religious; and all this is done only by the religious man; Therefore, if it is not the work of God that all this is done, whose is it? •

If, then, it agrees with us that not only the possibility that subsists in man, although he neither desires nor acts good, but also the will and the action themselves, that is, the fact that we will and act well, things that are only in man when he wills and acts well; If, as I say, Pelagius agrees that the will itself and the action are also divinely helped, and are helped in such a way that without that help we desire or do no good, and agrees that this is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in which he makes us just by his justice and not by ours, so that this justice that comes to us from him is truly our justice, there will no longer be, as I believe, any dispute between us regarding the help of the grace.

53. The reason why Pelagius praised Saint Ambrose is, without a doubt, because in his writings he found among the praises of Zechariah and Elizabeth that man could dwell in this life without sin; Although it cannot be denied, if God so wills, to whom all things are possible, nevertheless reflect more carefully on how this was said. Because, in my opinion, he said it according to a certain plausible and praiseworthy way of life among men, upon which no one could justly bring any rebuke or accusation. And this life is said to have been had in the presence of God by Zechariah and his wife, because in it they deceived men with no dissimulation, but as they appeared before men, so they were known by the eyes of God. But this was not said according to that perfection of justice, in which we will live truly and absolutely blameless and blameless. For the apostle Saint Paul also said of himself that, according to the righteousness that comes from the law, he had lived blamelessly; and the life of Zechariah was blameless in that same law; but he considered this justice to be dung and waste in comparison with the justice we hope for, and of which we must now be hungry and dry.
