54. Finally listen to the same venerable prelate, who, when expounding the prophet Isaiah, says that "no one in this world can live without sin." And in this passage it cannot be maintained that it says "in this world" in this sense: in the love of this world. In fact, he was talking about the Apostle, who said: Our life is in heaven. Thus, explaining this sense, the illustrious bishop said: "The Apostle assures that there are many who, even living in this life, are perfect together with him, who, if we set our sights on true perfection, could not be. For he himself also said: Now we see through a mirror and darkly, but then we will see face to face; now I know only in part, but then I will know as I am known. And thus, they are immaculate in this world and will be so in the kingdom of God; although, if examined more particularly, no one can be found immaculate, because there is no one without sin." Therefore, that testimony of Saint Ambrose that Pelagius uses in favor of his sentence, or is a certain way of saying certainly acceptable, but not examined with all rigor; or at least, if that holy and humble man judged that Zechariah and Elizabeth had possessed the supreme and perfect justice, to which nothing could be added, upon a more detailed examination, he corrected his sentence.

CAPUT I 1. Iam nunc diligenter advertite, de baptismate parvulorum quam caute debenatis audire homines eiusmodi, qui ñeque aperte illi aetati lavacrum regenerationis, et peccatorum remissionis audent negare, ne hoc christianae aures ferré non possint; et tamen opinionem suam, qüa putant peccato primi hominis carnalem generationem obnoxiam non teneri, tueri et defensere persistunt, quamvis eis baptismum videantur in peccatorum remissionem will grant. Niempe ipsi a Pelagius vos praesente scripsistis audisse, recitante vobis de libello suo, quem etiam Riomam se misisse asserebat, quod "iisdem sacramenti verbis—dicant—deberé baptizan infantes, quibus et maiores." Quis post illa verba putaret, eis de hac re ullam movendam esse quaestionem?

St. Augustine proves that, on the question of original sin and the baptism of children, Pelagius disagrees absolutely nothing with his disciple Celestius, who, for not wanting to confess original sin, or, even more, for having dared to deny it openly, has been condemned, first in Carthage and then in Rome, by the episcopal synods. It also proves that this question is not one of those in which one can err, as these heretics wanted, without danger to the faith, but that, on the contrary, this error attacks the very foundations of the Christian faith. He then refutes those who affirm that the dogma of original sin undermines the goodness of marriage and insults God himself, who creates man through marriage.

1. Now diligently warn with how much caution you must listen, regarding the baptism of children, to men of such a condition that, on the one hand, they do not dare to openly deny at that age the bath of regeneration and the remission of sins, lest Christian ears cannot bear it, and, on the other hand, nevertheless, they continue to support and defend their opinion, according to which they judge that the carnal generation is not subject to the sin of the first man, even though It seems that they grant them baptism in remission of sins. You yourselves have written to me that you heard Pelagius in person, reading to you from a book about which he claimed that he had sent him to Rome, that he and his supporters maintain "that children should be baptized with the same words with which adults are baptized." Who after these words would have thought that they would raise any question on this matter? Or if he had, would he

Nam verba eius ista sunt: "Infantes autem—inquit—deberé baptizari in remissionem peccatorum, secundum regulam universalis Ecelesiae, et secundum Evangelii sententiam, confitemur; quia Dominus statuit regnum caelorum nonnisi baptizatis posse conferri 1; quod iquia vires naturae non habent, conferri necesse est per gratiae libertatem". scripsistis, sic vobis responderes Pelagium: "quod eisdem quibus et maíores sacramenti verbis baptizantur infantes";

5. But in the writing that he published in Rome, and that was there alleged in the ecclesiastical records, he speaks in such a way on this matter that he states that he is convinced of what he had said here that he doubted. For these are his words: "We confess that children, he said, must be baptized into the remission of sins according to the norm of the universal Church and according to the sentence of the Gospel; because the Lord established that only the baptized could be conferred the kingdom of heaven; since, since they lack natural forces, it must be granted to them by the liberality of grace." If he added nothing more on this matter, who would not believe that he admitted that children also had their original sins forgiven when he said that it is necessary to baptize them for the remission of sins? This is why we have preferred to reflect more carefully on the words that, as you wrote, Pelagius answered you: "that children are also baptized with the same words of the sacrament with which the elderly are baptized", which filled you with joy for having heard what you wanted.

6. Attendite itaque quid Caelestius apertissime dixerit, et ibi videbitis quid vobis Perugius occultaverit. Caelestius quippe adiungit, et dicit: "In remissionem autem peccatorum baptizados infantes, non idcirco diximus, ut peccatum ex translate firmare videoamur; iquod longe a catholico sensu alienum est. Quia peccatum non cum homine nascitur, quod postmodum exereetur ab homine; quia non naturae delictum, sed voluntatis esse monstratur. Et illud ergo confiten congruum, ne diverse baptismatis genera faceré videamur, et hoc praemunire necessarium est, ne per mysterii occasionem, ad Creatoris iniuriam malum antequam fiat ab homine, tradi dicatur homini per naturam. 6. Therefore, pay attention to what Celestius has said very clearly, and there you will see what Pelagius hid from you. Well, he goes on to say: "We have said that children must be baptized in remission of sins in order to make it appear that we affirm sin by inheritance, which is something completely foreign to Catholic sentiment. For sin is not born together with man, but is executed later by man himself; because it is proven that there is no crime of nature, but of the will. It is, therefore, convenient to admit this, so that it does not seem that we do different kinds of baptism, and it is necessary to prevent this, not whether on the occasion of a mystery it is said, with insult to the Creator, that evil is transmitted to man through nature, before it is executed by man." CAPUT VII 8. Hanc eius praelocutionem venerabilis papa Zosimus tenens, egit eum homine, quem false doctrinae ventus inflaverat, ut ea quae illi a deacon Paulinus fuerant obiecta damnaret, atque ut Sedis A'postolicae litteris, quae a sanctae memoriae suo praecessore manaverant, praeberet assensum. At ille noluit quidem diaconi obiecta damnare; sed beati papae Innoeentii litteris non est ausus obsistere; imo "se omnia quae Sedes illa damnaret, damnaturum esse promisit"; atque ita yelut phreneticus, ut requiesceret, tamquam leniter fotus, a vinculis tamen excommunicationis nondum est creditus esse solvendus. Sed interposito duorum mensium tempore, doñee rescriberetur ex África, resipiseendi ei locus sub quadam medieinali sententiae lenitate concessus est. Quoniam revera, si deposita pervicaciae vanitate, quod promiserat vellet attendere, et easdem litteras, quibus se consensurum esse responderat, diligenter legeret, sanaretur. Sed posteaquam ex Africano episcoporum concilio rescripta direct sunt, quid fuerit consecutum, ut iustissime in eum sententia proferretur, cuneta legite, quia cuneta transmísimus.

CHAPTER VII 8. Taking into account this warning from Celestius, the venerable Pope Zoslmus ensured that this man, whom the wind of false doctrine had inflated, condemned everything that the deacon Paulinus had objected to and granted his assent to the letter of the Apostolic See, which had been written by his predecessor, of holy memory. He indeed refused to condemn the deacon's accusations, but he did not dare to oppose the letter of the blessed Pope Innocent; On the contrary, he promised to "condemn everything that that See condemned"; And so, as if he were frantic, he was treated gently, so that he would calm down; However, it was not yet considered appropriate that he should be absolved from the bonds of excommunication. For two months, while a response was received from Africa, he was given the opportunity to come to his senses under the medicinal softness of this sentence. Because in reality he would be healed if, having abandoned his stubborn vanity, he wanted to reflect on what he had promised and carefully read that same letter, with which, according to his response, he would agree. But after the response was sent from the council of African bishops, you can read what happened so that a sentence was justly pronounced against him, since we have transmitted everything to you.

9. Unde etiam Perugius, si se ipsum et sua scripta sine dolo cogitat, non recte dicit, eadem sententia se non debuisse teneri. Fefellit enim iudicium palaestinum; propterea ibi videtur esse purgatus; Romanam vero Ecclesiam, ubi eum esse notissimum scitis, fallere usquequaque non potuit; quamvis et hoc fuerit utcumque conatus; sed, ut dixi, minime valuit. Recoluit enim beatissimus papa íZosimus, quid imitandus praecessor eius de ipsis senserit gestis. Attendit etiam quid de illo sentimentet praedicanda in Domino Romanum fides 1, quorum adversus eius errorem pro veritate catholica, studia consonantia concorditer flagrare cernebat; Inter quos ille diu vixerat, et quos eius dogmata latere non poterant; qui Caelestíum eius esse discipulum sic noverant, ut fidelissimum et firmissimum possent de hac re testimonium perhibere. Quid ergo of Palaestinae synodi gestis, quibus se Perugius absolutum esse gloriatur, sanctus papa Innocentius iudicarit, quamvis et in litteris eius, quas nobds rescriptit, legere possitis, et commemoratum cum venerabili papae Zosimo synodus Africana respondit, quod vestrae caritati cum ceteris instructioníbus misimus, tamen nec in hoc operate praetereundum videtur.

9. Pelagius, too, if he honestly examines himself and his writings, without reason says that he should not have been included in the same condemnation. In effect, he deceived the Palestinian court; and for this reason it seems to him that he was justified there; but he could not in any way deceive the Roman Church, where you know he was very well known, even though he tried as much as he could; but, as I say, he in no way succeeded. The most blessed Pope Zosimos recalled the opinion that the minutes themselves had earned his predecessor, worthy of all praise. The opinion of both of them is contained regarding children, who, according to them, are born without any contagion from Adam's sin. Therefore, it is not surprising that Celestius did not want to condemn those who affirm that "Adam's sin only harmed him and that children when born are in the same state as Adam before the prevarication"; but what causes great admiration is the impudence with which Pelagius condemned him. For if, as it says, "evil is not born with us and we are born without guilt, and if before the action of self-will only exists in man what God has created," without a doubt, Adam's sin only harmed him, since it did not pass on to his descendants. Indeed, it cannot be said that sin is not an evil, or that sin is not a vice, or that God created it. But he says: "Evil is not born with us and without vice we are born, and only those who are born have what God has created." And for this reason, judging very consistently, according to this doctrine of his, "that the sin of Adam only harmed him and not the human race," why did Pelagius condemn this opinion except to deceive the Catholic judges? In the same way, it can also be argued: "If evil is not born with us and we are born without vice, and there is only in man at birth what God has created", without a doubt, it follows "that children when born are in the same state as Adam before the prevarication", in which there was then neither evil nor vice, and only what God had created existed in him. And yet, Pelagius anathematized "those who defend or have defended at some time that newly born children are in the same state as Adam before the prevarication", that is, without any evil, without any vice, only having what God had created. Why, then, did Pelagius also condemn this opinion if not to deceive the Catholic synod and to avoid being condemned as a new heretic?

It is objected to them that they do not want to admit that unbaptized children are subject to the condemnation of the first man and that original sin has passed to them, which must be erased by regeneration, since they maintain that they should only be baptized so that they can receive the kingdom of heaven, as if outside of it those who, without the participation of the

CHAPTER XIX 21. He says this in vain, but that does not mean he is justified. Not even they themselves have ever affirmed that children without baptism can enter the kingdom of heaven. But it's not about that, it's about the destruction of original sin in children. Whoever does not want to admit that the bath of regeneration has something to purify in children can justify this. So, let's pay attention to the rest he's going to say. After having interspersed the testimony of the Gospel that whoever is not reborn of water and the Spirit will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven, about which, as we have said, there is no dispute with God, he continued saying: "Who will be so impious as to prevent a child, whatever his age, from the common redemption of the human race?" This is also ambiguous, what is meant by redemption: whether it is the transition from bad to good or from good to better. For Celestius in Carthage also confessed in his booklet the redemption of the children, and yet he refused to confess that Adam's sin had been transmitted to them.

CAPUT XX 22. Sed quid deinde iste subiungat, warn: "Et in perpetuam—inquit—certamque vitam renasci vetet eum qux natus sit ad incertam?" id est, quis tam impius est, ut vetet renasci ad perpetuam icertamique vitam eum qui natus sit ad incertam? Haec verba quando primitus legimus, credidimus eum incertam vitam istam voluisse dicere temporalem: quamvis nobis videretur magis eam mortalem dicere debuisse, quam incertam, eo quod certa morte finiatur. Tamen quamdiu ducitur, quoniam momentis omnibus esse non dubitatur incerta; nihil aliud eum putavimus, quam istam mortalem vitam maluisse dicere incertam. Ac per hoc, quamvis aeteraam mortem parvulorum sine baptismatis sacramento ex hac vita migrantium aperte noluerit iconfiteri; tamen de illo sollicitudinem nostram quasi certa ratioeinatio solaba tur. Dicébamus enim: Si perpetua vita, sicut confiten videtur, nisi eorum qui baptizati sunt non potest esse; prefect eos iqui non baptizati moriuntur, mors perpetua consequetur. Quod nulla iustitia potest accidere his, a quibus in hac vita nu'lla peccata commissa sunt, nisi origínale peccatum.

CHAPTER XX 22. But notice what Pelagius later adds: "And does it hinder being reborn to a perpetual and certain life for him who is born for an uncertain life?", that is: Who will be so impious that he hinders being reborn to a perpetual and certain life for him who is born for an uncertain life? When we first read these words, we believed that he had meant to call this temporary life uncertain; although it seemed to us that it should have been called mortal rather than uncertain, since it is limited by certain death. However, since it cannot be doubted that this life at every moment of its duration is uncertain, we believed that nothing else had been preferred to be called uncertain more than this mortal life. For this reason, although he would not have wanted to openly confess the eternal death of children who leave this life without the sacrament of baptism, nevertheless, an almost conclusive reasoning alleviated our concern on this matter. Well, we said to ourselves: If perpetual life, as you seem to confess, can only be that of those who have been baptized, without a doubt those who die without having been, obtain perpetual death. Since by no means can this occur to those by whom no sin was committed, unless they have original sin.

CAPUT XXI 23. Sed postea non defuerunt fratres, qui nos admonerent, hoc ideo dicere Pelagium potuisse, quia de ista quaestione ita perhibetur solitus respondé quaerentibus, ut diceret: "Sine baptismo parvuli morientes, quo non eant, scio; quo eant, nescio"; id est, non iré in regnum caelorum scio; quo vero eant, ideo se nescire dice'bat, aut dicit, quia dicere non audebat in mortem illos iré perpetuam, quos et. hic nihil mali commississe sentiebat, et originale traxisse peccatum non consentiebat. Itaque et ista eius verba Romam pro magna eius purgatione transmissa, tam sunt ambigua, ut possint eorum dogmati praebere latibula, unde ad insidiandum prosiliat haereticus sensus, iquando nullo existent qui valeat respondere, tamquam in solitudeine aliquis invenitur infirmus.

CHAPTER XXI 23. But there were later brothers who warned us that Pelagius could very well have said this, because it is stated that he has usually responded in such a way to those who ask him about this question, that he has said: "Children who die without baptism I know where they do not go, but I do not know where they go"; That is, I know that they are not going to the kingdom of heaven; But he said and still says that he does not know where they are going, because he did not dare to say that those who, on the one hand, saw that they had committed no evil here were going to eternal death and, on the other, did not admit that they had contracted original sin. Thus, even these words, sent to Rome as his solemn justification, are so ambiguous that they can offer refuge to their errors, from which heresy springs to lay snares when, there being no one capable of refuting it, it encounters someone thus abandoned like a sick person in solitude. 24. On the other hand, in the profession of his faith that he sent to Rome together with this same letter to the same Pope Innocent, to whom he had also written the letter, much more evidently, in his desire to conceal himself, he revealed himself by saying: "We profess one baptism, which we maintain should be administered to children with the same words of the sacrament with which it should also be administered to adults." He did not at least say: With the same sacrament; and even what he would have said would still be ambiguous; but he said: "With the same words of the sacrament"; as if the remission of sins were told to children by the noise of words, and were not brought about by the effect of things. However, for the moment it was believed that he was saying something that was in accordance with the Catholic faith; but he could not deceive the Apostolic See until the end. In fact, after the decisions of the council of the province of Africa, to which in truth that pernicious doctrine had stealthily reached, Hnyque had not invaded it very extensively nor had it penetrated into it very deeply, in the city of Rome, where Pelagius had lived for a very long time and where he had previously occupied himself in these practices and discussions, other things of this became evident, published at the request of the faithful, which, as worthy of execration, Pope Zosimus added, as you can read in the epistle he wrote to be disseminated throughout the Catholic world. Pelagius, in what is intended to be an exposition of the Epistle of the apostle Saint Paul to the Romans, argues by saying: "If the sin of Adam has also harmed those who do not sin, then the justice of Christ also benefits those who do not believe in the same way." and other things of the same kind, all of which have been refuted and dispelled, with the help of God, in the books we have written about the baptism of infants.

And although in these alleged expositions he has not dared to object to these things for himself, he nevertheless said this where he was well known to many and what he thought and said could not be a secret; and in those books, the first of which I recalled some phrases above, he defends, not covertly, but with all clarity and with all the dialectical rigor he can, that in no way should human nature be believed to be vitiated in children by heredity; and thus, by attributing health to it, it denies the savior.

35. The Scripture certainly does not declare whether before Abraham righteous men or their children were marked with any corporal and visible sacrament. In any case, Abraham received the sign of circumcision as a sign of righteousness by faith. And he received her in such a way that from then on he was also ordered to circumcise all the boys in his house on the eighth day after their birth; in such a way that also those who could not yet believe in justice would nevertheless receive the sign of justice by faith. And this was commanded under such a serious threat that God announced that the soul of anyone who had not been circumcised on the eighth day would be excluded from his people. If we inquire into the justice of this dreadful punishment, will not all their argument, however subtle it may be, about free will, about the great vigor and purity of nature, vanish, dissolved and pulverized? For what evil, I ask, has a child committed of his own free will that, due to another's negligence in circumcising him, he himself is condemned with such a rigorous sentence that that soul is excluded from his people? For he is not threatened with temporary death, since of the righteous at his death, then it was rather said: And he was gathered to his people; or also: He was reunited with his parents, since from now on the man would not fear any temptation that could separate him from his people if his people were the very people of God.

As if the excellence of the nuptials were the disease of concupiscence, by which those who do not know God love their wives, something that the Apostle prohibits; and not rather conjugal modesty, by which sensuality is reduced to the good use of the right procreation of children; or what is still more, as if man could not be God's brother not only when he is born of a marriage, but also when he is born of fornication or adultery. But in this question, in which we inquire not about what needs a creator, but what needs a savior, we must not look at the good that exists in the procreation of a nature, but at the evil that exists in sin, by which it is evident that nature has been vitiated. For both things, nature and the vice of nature, propagate together; the first of which is a good, the second an evil. The former is received from the liberality of the Creator, the latter comes from the condemnation of the origin; The former has as its cause the good will of the supreme God, the latter the bad will of the first man; the former declares God as the creator of the creature, the latter as the avenger of disobedience; Finally, Jesus Christ himself, in order to create it, is the author of man, and in order to heal it, he became man.

i Saint Augustine's fight against Pelagianism, which began in the year 412, was to last until the last days of his life. Like all the great questions that have disturbed human conscience, that of grace and freedom was evolving and being elucidated in the heat of fierce and prolonged controversies. If it is true that Pelagianism soon scandalized pious souls due to its radical character in terms of the absolute denial of grace, the same did not happen with the moderate doctrinal tendencies that emerged from the fight against Pelagianism. Many spirits did not correctly interpret the doctrine of Saint Augustine and blamed him for sinning by the opposite extreme to that of Pelagius, that of annulling the action of free will under the influence of grace, despite the passages in which the Saint saves the independence of the former. It was, therefore, a matter of establishing an intermediate doctrine in which the two forces seemed to balance, divine power and human power, the action of grace and that of freedom. This is how semi-Pelagianism arose. This moderate attitude in solving the problem seduced many. Their multiple points of contact with the truth obscured their understanding so as not to see the error. That is why Saint Augustine's intuition, in perceiving the falsity and danger of such an attitude, has a value no less transcendental than that of extreme Pelagianism in the history of heresies. Without the brilliant intuition of Saint Augustine, semi-Pelagianism would undoubtedly have achieved a much more lasting fortune in the field of Catholic controversies. But the hammer of the heretics also wounded him to death. After the discredit of the Pelagian doctrines, caused by the anathemas of the Church and by the formidable attacks of Saint Augustine, the discussions about grace took different directions. Among them he came to occupy a position

main, if not central, the doctrine of predestination. The Bishop of Hippo, in the letter to Sixtus, a Roman priest (Epist. 194: PL 2, 874), later the third pope of that name, and in his books to the monks of Adrumeto (De gratia et libero arbitrio, De correptione et gratia), had established with most courageous audacity a purely gratuitous predestination. This doctrine was considered new and uniquely personal. The abbot John Cassian, Valentine and Vital of Carthage, Hilary, bishop of Arles, and other illustrious writers disagreed with Augustine on this point and influenced the opinion of many thanks to his authority, combined with the prestige of his name. Parallel to the semi-heretical position adopted by the monks of Adrumeto, under the direction of Vital, in Carthage, a theological movement of identical semi-Pelagian tendency arose in the south of France, mainly in Marseille and in the entire region of the Gaules. Since among the followers of these doctrines there were monks of great austerity of customs and exemplary life, some of them prelates and even bishops, such as Hilary of Arles, the error threatened to spread among the mass of simple people. Understanding it in this way, two lay monks, but learned and faithful disciples of Saint Augustine, Prospero and Hilary, raised their voices against the dangerous advances of the new errors. Both agreed to address the Bishop of Hippo and inform him of the doctrinal atmosphere prevailing in the Gaulas regarding the theological issues recently defended by him. The letters of Prospero and Hilario constitute a monument of true value and of maximum interest to appreciate the theological opinions that agitated the Gaula region around the doctrines of Saint Augustine and Pelagius. Two truly important and definitive works of Saint Augustine on grace are due to them: De praedestinatione sanctorum and De dono perseverantiae. Therefore we will give below a brief summary of both epistles. H THE LETTER OF PROSPERO (Epist. 225).—Prospero, whom some call a saint, was from Aquitaine. He has been described as a deeply religious man and a talented writer. In the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine, several of his pamphlets and a short Latin poem are preserved. When the Semi-Pelagians argued and refused to accept the doctrines of Augustine, Prospero found himself retired in

Marseille, where John Cassian directed the abbey of Saint Victor, founded by him and the main center of those theological discussions. After the death of Saint Augustine, "his illustrious disciple of Aquitaine," writes Poujoulat, "continued victoriously the fight" against Semi-Pelagianism. Here is the greeting with which Prospero addresses the Bishop of Hippo: "Prospero, to the most happy lord and pontiff, ineffably admirable, incomparably venerable and most excellent teacher, Augustine. Although I am unknown to you in person, I am not completely unknown to you in spirit and word, if your memory has not forgotten it; for by the deacon Leontius, my pious brother, I have previously sent you other letters and I have received them of you. But now I have the audacity to write again to your holiness, not only for the sake of a respectful greeting, as then, but also for the zeal of faith, which is the life of the Church. Since I know your most vigilant concern for all the members of the body of Christ and the invincible value of the truth with which you combat all the snares of heretical doctrines, I have judged that I should not be ashamed nor would it bother you or bother you. importunate in a matter that concerns the spiritual good of many and that, therefore, also affects your pity; on the contrary, I would consider myself guilty if in these things, which I consider to be most pernicious, I did not address him who is a special defender of the faith. Prospero then relates how the monks of Marseille, after having read Augustine's writings against the Pelagians, did not agree at all with the doctrine of predestination held by the Bishop of Hippo, considering it contrary to the opinion of the Holy Fathers and the sentiments of the Church. At the height of these disputes, the book Of Correction and Grace, written by Augustine to dissuade the monks of Adrumeto from their errors, reached the Gaulas. Prospero found this book "full of divine authority" and hoped that its reading would calm restless spirits, "since you have answered," said the pious monk to the holy Doctor, "so completely to all the questions about which we wished to consult you, as if you had studied them especially to compose the quarrels that existed between us." But reality did not confirm these hopes of the zealous monk of Marseille.

Although the reading of Augustine's work served as instruction to those who already followed his doctrines, it further inflamed the spirits of the dissidents. From which, according to Prospero, two great evils were to be feared: one, for the
OF PREDESTINATION

The same enemies of Augustine, since some of them being men of great virtue and yearning for greater perfection, ran the risk of incurring Pelagian impiety, and another, that, moved by his example and the prestige of his virtues, ignorant and simple people would equally follow his error. Here is how Prospero details the various opinions that were professed in the Gaulas: all men sinned in Adam and no one can be freed without grace; The propitiation of the blood of Christ is offered, without exception, by all men, so that whoever wishes to receive faith and baptism can be saved; God knew in his foreknowledge, before the creation of the world, all those who were to believe and persevere in faith with the help of grace, and these are the ones who, freely called, because they were to become worthy of the divine election and leave this world with a happy end, have been predestined to the kingdom of heaven. So that no one despairs of attaining eternal life, every man is invited to faith and good works, since eternal reward is reserved for voluntary piety. For this reason they rejected the distinction between the elect and the reprobate according to a decree of God, according to which, freely predestined before the creation of the world or at the moment of its creation, some would be vessels of honor and others vessels of ignominy, since such predestination would remove the diligence to rise from those who have succumbed and would plunge the righteous into inertia. For both concepts, all efforts of will would be useless, since neither the reprobate could enter the kingdom of heaven nor the elect be excluded from it. In a word, the Gaula semi-Pelagianists continued to support all of Julian's objections, raised and refuted by Augustine in the book De correptione et gratia. According to Prospero's letter, there were some who still openly followed the same doctrines of Pelagius. Regarding the predestination of children, God saves or condemns them according to the foresight of the merits they would acquire if they had reached the use of reason or lived longer. As for the people who have come to know the truth or remained in error, God knew in his foreknowledge those who would believe or those who would not believe. He sends missionaries and preachers to the former, denying them.

The monks of the Gaulas insisted, above all, on the convenience of saving the fruit of preaching, which could not be achieved by admitting free predestination prior to all merit and effort of the will. Thus, when the time came for the use of freedom, two things were

necessary to achieve health: the grace of God and the obedience of man; but they claimed that human obedience to divine grace should precede. The beginning of health had to come first from the one who is saved, not from the one who saves. Having learned through the mercy of God and through the teachings of Augustine the perversity of these errors, and not considering himself to have sufficient authority to refute them, given that illustrious men placed in the dignity of the priesthood held this opinion, the holy monk of Marseille begs the Bishop of Hippo to deign to answer and resolve the proposed difficulties. He especially desired the conversion of Hilary, bishop of Arles, whom he described as a saint, who also disagreed with Augustine on this point of predestination, although he followed and admired him in other matters and wished to correspond with him. "Since by the grace of divine Providence," Prospero exclaims enthusiastically before the venerable figure of Augustine, "you are the glory of this century and our decadence has placed its hopes in the power of your charity and wisdom, do not deny your instruction to the humble nor your rebuke to the proud" (Epi.it. Prosperi, n. 9: PL.10, 946). THE LETTER OF HILARIO (Epist. 226).—Hilario was also, like Prospero, a lay monk. What is not certain, nor does Saint Augustine allude to it, is whether he is the same one who wrote to the holy Doctor from Syracuse in the year 414, proposing the solution of some questions about the Pelagian doctrine, and to whom Saint Augustine responded with an extensive epistle (Epist. 1457), which achieved great fame and was read by Orosius at the Council of Jerusalem (year 440), with Pelagius present, and in the from Diospolis. Poujoulat identifies the monk of Marseille with the monk of Syracuse. Hilary's epistle, although inferior to Prospero's in elegance of diction, is no less important in understanding the atmosphere of uncertainty and theological unrest that reigned in the south of France. Hilary, after declaring to the Bishop of Hippo that he hopes his communication will be pleasant, goes on to propose to him the questions that were discussed in that region. In a not very different way he states the same opinions that Prospero, although he clarifies more accurately the passages of Saint Augustine that the Semi-Pelagians of the Gaulas contradicted.

Thus they intended to prove their doctrines with the authority of tradition and with that of Augustine himself, whom they accused of having held a similar doctrine in the response given to Porphyry (Epist. 102, q. 2, n. 14) when dealing with the time of religion.

Christian and in a passage of the commentary on the Epistle of the Romanians (Rom. 9, 19) (Expos. quor. proposit. ex Epist. ad Rom., proposit. 60, 62). As for the gift of perseverance, they did not admit that it was entirely free, but that it could be earned through prayer and good works or lost through resistance to grace. They rejected as deuterocanonical the passage from the Book of Wisdom (Wisdom 6, 11) adduced by Saint Augustine to support his doctrine of predestination. They did not admit the difference established by the Saint between the grace of being able to persevere granted to the first man in paradise and that granted to his descendants of effective perseverance (De correptione et gratia, c. 11 et 12). They judged that this imposed on the predestined a fatal necessity in acting or, as it is a grace that is ignored, a tendency to despair. They also rejected the doctrine about the fixed number of the elect and the reprobate, "for God wants all men to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth", a salvific will that Saint Augustine restricts to only those predestined to grace (De corrept. et gratia, ce. 13-14). The Massilians also rejected as invalid the testimonies of the Book of Kings and the Paralipomena (1 Reg. 10, 26; 1 Par. 12, 18), adduced by Saint Augustine to demonstrate how God freely inclines, in a wonderful and ineffable way, human wills to carry out the same thing that He has determined, working in them up to the very act of willing. Regarding the predestination of children, they considered it wrong that they were placed on the same line as adults, since they lack freedom. They accused Saint Augustine himself of having doubted about this question (De libero arbitrio, 1. 3, c. 23). The monk Hilary, like Prospero, did not consider himself to have authority to resolve these questions, and so, stimulated by a holy zeal and charity towards his brothers, he addressed himself with affectionate solicitude to the indisputable authority of Augustine, whose virtues and wisdom were the astonishment of all Christendom. "Here, my Father," exclaimed the pious monk at the end of his letter, "are the questions that, along with many others, so as not to hide my best wishes from you, I would have preferred to bring to you personally.

Since I have not deserved such a great honor, I would have liked at least to compile with more space all the issues that are discussed, to hear from your mouth to what extent everything that is controversial in these matters should be refuted, or, if this were not possible, tolerated. But since neither one nor the other has depended on me, I have preferred,

As far as I have been able, I will send you a summary of these questions, leaving in absolute silence the great opposition with which some contradict them. For there are among them people of such prestige that it is the obligation of the laity, in accordance with the custom of the Church, to pay them the most respectful veneration. Which I have accomplished in such a way that, when necessity has demanded it, I have not failed to say in relation to these things what the shortness of my wit has suggested to me. But now I have summarily explained all these things to you as soon as the urgency of the mail carrying this letter has allowed me. It is up to your wisdom to determine what is appropriate to do to refute or moderate the opinion of so many respectable men. But I judge that it would be of little use to them if you explained these matters to them if the weight of an authority that the disputing spirits could not oppose was not added to it. Well, speaking plainly, I must not omit here, as far as you are concerned, that, except in this single question, everyone admires your actions and your words. And, therefore, it is up to you to define to what extent his opposition should be tolerated." Hilario concludes his letter by asking the holy Doctor for some writings that had not yet reached his hands. He confesses himself to be his disciple and begs him on behalf of his brothers to answer the questions proposed. Fearful of not having declared them worthily or of having omitted some important one, he informs him that he has come to an agreement with Prospero, "an illustrious man both for his customs and for his eloquence and studies".

m THE RESPONSE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE.—The books Of the Predestination of the Saints and Of the Gift of Perseverance were Augustine's worthy response to the letters of Prospero and Hilary. Both works were probably written at the beginning of the year 429, since by this time he had already reviewed all his previous writings (De praedestinatione, c. 3, n. 7). Although he judges that he has already written enough on the subject, Augustine yields to the requests of his disciples, whose charitable and fraternal concern he praises, not disdaining to repeat, like the Apostle, the same things for the good of his brothers (iPhil. 3, 1). He rejoices that they have already confessed some truths in accordance with the doctrine of the Church, although they are still wrong regarding predestination. For this reason
FROM A.I. PREDESTINATION OF EOS SANIOS

Trust that God will enlighten you as you walk sincerely in the truths you have already come to confess. Create an obligation to exercise with them the ministry of your teaching, serving them in the free charity of Christ, because perhaps God wants to convert them completely to the truth through your mediation. The Doctor of Grace addresses, above all, the fundamental point denied by the Semi-Pelagians: faith, both in its beginning and in its increase, is a gift from God. The Gaulas monks judged that the scriptural texts adduced by Saint Augustine only demonstrated that the increase in faith was a supernatural grace, but not the beginning of faith itself. The holy Doctor makes them see the inconsistency of such a doctrine, by which they come to incur the same error as Pelagius. If the beginning of faith is the work of human will and by this initial act we deserve the increase of faith itself, the entire treasure of grace becomes a retribution for that first merit. Saint Augustine's argument is radical and incontrovertible. The semi-Pelagian doctrine falls at its base. "It must be taken into account—the holy Doctor reasons—that if something is done in us in such a way that grace was given to us for our merits, such grace would no longer be grace. For in such a concept what is given is no longer given freely." Because if man can acquire what he did not have, so that he himself increases what he acquired, I fail to understand why all the merit of the work should not be attributed to man: "cur autem non totum tribuatur homini, ut qui sibi potuit instituere quod non habebat, ipse quod instituit augeat, omnino non video" (n. 6). The Saint supports his doctrine on various testimonies of Scripture (Rom. 11, 33, 36; Phil. 1, 29; 1 Cor. 7, 25; 2 Cor. 3, 5). Saint Augustine had at some time thought in a similar way to the Semi-Pelagians. These claimed their doctrine as the Saint had defended it in 394 in the Exposition of some passages of the Epistle to the Romans (propositions 60 and 62; Epist. Hilarii, n. 3). The Saint modestly confesses his error, which he had already retracted in 397, writing to Simplician, bishop of Milan, in the principles of his episcopate (De diversis quaestionibus), a rectification that he later confirmed in the Retractations (Retract., 1. 1, c. 1, n. 3, 4; 1. 2, c. 1). The holy Doctor recommends that his opponents read those books.

The most careful and profound consideration of this text of the Apostle: What tempt you that you have not received it? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? (1 Cor. 4, 7),

commented by Saint Cyprian (Ad Quirinum, 1. 3, c. 4), he was saved from that error. "I had not yet inquired," he says, "with all diligence nor had I managed to find out what the election to grace consists of, which, certainly, is not grace if it is preceded by some merit" (n. 7). Saint Augustine distinguishes between being able to possess faith and actually possessing it. Being able to possess it is a natural grace, common to all men; In scholastic terms, we would say the obedience power so that the name can be elevated to the order of grace. Effectively possessing faith is already the work of grace itself. There can be nothing on the part of man that merits faith, not even in its beginning, because this is already a supernatural gift. The Saint prevents an objection: "Many hear the word of truth; of these, some believe it, others contradict it. Therefore the former want to believe and the latter do not want to." “No one can deny this,” answers Saint Augustine. But how is the difficulty resolved? The Doctor of Grace gives us a solution that has not stopped being discussed. "We must distinguish," the Saint affirms, "what comes from God's mercy and what comes from his justice, since in some the will is prepared by the Lord and in others it is not." Regarding the letter of three biblical texts related to the question at hand (Rom. 11, 7; Is. 6, 9; Ps. 68, 23), the Saint comments: "Behold divine mercy and judgment: mercy, in the election that achieved divine justification; judgment, however, in those who were hardened in their blindness. And yet, those, because they wanted to, believed; these, because they did not they wanted, they did not believe. The mercy and judgment of God have been verified in the same wills. Such election is, therefore, a work of grace and not, certainly, of one's own merits" (c. 6, n. 11). On this divine mercy and judgment Saint Augustine has based his rigorous thesis of the predestination of the elect and the reprobate, considered excessively rigid by some theologians. Read carefully number 16, where the Saint summarizes his exposition of the preceding chapters (6, 7 and 8). Thus it is verified that faith is an absolutely free gift, since otherwise there would be no possibility of freeing oneself from the bonds of semi-Pelagianism, which is nothing other than a rearguard entrenchment of the doctrine of Pelagius. The biblical texts and commentaries accumulate under the tireless pen of the Doctor of Grace (Rom. 5, 10; lo.

6, 28-29. 36. 37. 43, 45; Eph. 2, 8-9). In addition to the action of grace on the will - which does not destroy free will - an ineffable and mysterious illumination also influences the intelligence of the

man to come to faith. This is what Saint Augustine calls the teaching or school of the Father, or, if you like, of the Trinity, since none of the three persons teaches separately: "Inseparabilia quippe didicimus esse opera Trinitatis." But this school in which God is heard and teaches is very far from the bodily senses. "We see that many come to the Son, because we see that many believe in Christ; but how they hear or how they learn we do not see. It is a most secret grace; but who can doubt this grace?" (no. 13). The exposition of Saint Augustine has undoubtedly provided the basis for establishing the theory of effective grace, since, according to the holy Doctor, the elect, according to the decree of God, must infallibly do good: 'Haec itaque gratia, quae occulte humanis cordibus divina largitate tribuitur, a nullo corde respuitur.' These words and those that follow them are so definitive that they leave no room for doubt. The scriptural texts are for the Saint of very evident clarity (Ez. 11, 19; Rom. 9, 18. 23; 1 Cor. 1, 18; lo. 6, 44-46). repugnare" (n. 16). The semi-Pelagians of the Caulas argued against Saint Augustine himself, blaming him for having changed his sentence on predestination held in the booklet against Porphyry (Epist. 102, 2, n. 14). The Bishop of Hippo replies that it had not been his intention to establish the doctrine of grace there, a question that required a more detailed and diligent study and that he hoped to carry out more forward or that it was carried out by others. He claims his ancient doctrine as reconcilable with that which he now establishes, provided that it is understood that divine election precedes all merit of the will, "they have never been lacking in the Christian religion," said Augustine in the booklet to Porphyry, "for those who have been worthy of it; Therefore, if someone has been lacking, it is because he has not been worthy." The entire discussion consists—the holy Doctor now adds—in inquiring where that dignity comes from. Some claim that it comes from human will; but we maintain that it comes from divine grace and predestination. Answering another of the opinions expressed by Prospero, the Saint distinguishes between "predestined" and foreknowledge. The former cannot occur without the latter, but the latter can without the former.

No one can help but admire the originality of his doctrine and the wonderful lucidity of understanding with which he expounds it at the age of seventy-five. On the eve of his death, the venerable and elderly Bishop of Hippo could still combat the insistent attacks of heresy with a firm and calm pulse. Who did not hesitate to solve those terrifying problems about grace and freedom? Saint Augustine himself was forced to rectify his old error, born from not having yet properly considered such an intricate question. Although long before his struggles with the Pelagians the Bishop of Hippo had retracted his error, nevertheless, the very difficulties of the problem, the deep penetration of his genius, together with the greatness of his holiness and his incomparable knowledge of the divine Scriptures, made him create a predestinationist system so consistent and luminous that it has been and will not cease to be the admiration of the wise. The Supreme Pontiffs and the Councils have not hesitated to proclaim him the spokesperson of Catholic doctrine on this matter. Augustine's doctrine of grace is the voice of the Church; The doctrine of the Church is the voice of Augustine. In this book On the Predestination of Saints he admires and astonishes the precision and certainty with which Augustine refutes the Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian Objections, the inflexible logical rigor with which he maintains the doctrine of free predestination, a brilliant creation of his thought; the intuition and skill in the interpretation of biblical texts, the vigor and maturity of his intelligence, the energy and charity combined to correct the error of those who professed it in good or bad faith. Therefore, if God is the author of our faith, working in our hearts in a marvelous way so that we may believe, is there any reason to fear that he is not weak enough to work faith completely, so that man arrogates to himself the beginning of faith in order to fully deserve the increase of it from God? Keep in mind that if anything is worked in us in such a way that the grace of God is given to us for our merits, such grace would no longer be grace. For in such a concept, what is given is not given freely, but is repaid as something due, since it is due to the one who believes that God increases his faith, and in this way the increased faith is nothing more than a salary for the faith that has begun. It is not noted, when such a thing is stated, that this donation is not imputed to those who believe as a grace, but as a debt. But if man can acquire what he did not have, in such a way that he can also increase what he acquired, I cannot understand why the entire merit of faith should not be attributed to man except because it is not possible to distort the most evident divine testimonies, according to which it is clear that faith, in which piety has its beginning, is a gift from God; as the testimony declares in which it is said that God has distributed to each one the measure of faith. And that other: Peace to the brothers and charity and faith from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. And so on other similar ones. Therefore, wanting, on the other hand, to oppose such obvious testimonies and wanting, on the other hand, to ascribe to himself the merit of believing, man tries to reconcile himself with God by attributing to himself one part of the faith and leaving the other for God; but so insolently, that he ascribes the first to himself, granting God the second, and thus in what he claims to be both, he places himself first, and God second.

Now, it would be completely absurd, as far as I understand it, to suppose that in this very clear purpose of the Apostle, by which human pride is combated, so that no one glories in man but in the Lord, and hints at the merely natural divine gifts, either that complete and perfect nature that was given to man in his primitive state or any other vestige of this vitiated nature is understood. Already before, here the Apostle had said: For who is it that gives you advantage over us&T;, and then he added: So what do you have that you have received? In fact, some puffed-up man could say against another: "My faith gives me the advantage," "My justice gives me the advantage"; or any other similar thing. But the holy Doctor confronts such inflated thoughts: "What do you have," he says, "that you have not received? And from whom have you received it but from him who gives you advantage over the other, to whom he did not grant the gift that he has given you? If, then, everything that you have," he adds, "you have received, what do you boast about as if you had not received it?" In the same way, when I affirmed "that the salvific virtue of this religion has not been lacking in anyone who was worthy of it and that the one to whom it was lacking has not been worthy", if it is discussed or investigated why each one is worthy, there is no shortage of those who affirm that due to human will; but we maintain that by grace or divine predestination. Now, between grace and predestination there is only this difference: that predestination is a preparation for grace, and grace is already the effective gift of predestination. And thus what the Apostle says: Not by works, so that no one may boast; What His workmanship we are, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, grace means; But what follows: that God prepared in advance for us to walk in them, means predestination, which cannot occur without foreknowledge, even though foreknowledge can exist without predestination. By predestination God had foreknowledge of the things that He would do, for which reason it was said: He did what should be done. But foreknowledge can also be about those things that God does not do, such as sin, of any kind; and although there are some sins that are punishment for other sins, for which reason it was said: God gave them into the hands of a reprobate mentality, so that they did what was not appropriate, in this there is no sin on the part of God, but just judgment. Therefore, divine predestination, which consists in doing good, is, as I have said, a preparation for grace; but grace is the effect of predestination itself. Therefore, when God promised Abraham the faith of many people in his descendants, saying: I have made you the father of many nations, therefore the Apostle says: And so it is by virtue of faith, that it may be by grace, so that the promise may be firm to all posterity, he did not promise this to him by virtue of our will, but by virtue of his predestination. He promised, therefore, not what men, but what He Himself would accomplish. For if men practice good works in regard to divine worship, it comes from God.

That is certainly not what the Apostle says, but that God promised Abraham children who would follow in the footsteps of his faith; This is stated very clearly. But if God only promised works and not the faith of the Gentiles, since good works cannot exist except by faith—because the righteous live by faith, and everything that is not according to faith is sin, and without faith it is impossible to please God—then the fulfillment of what God has promised depends on the power of man. For if man, without the grace of God, does not do what belongs to him according to his nature, neither will God be able to do what corresponds to divine grace; That is to say, if man does not have faith in himself, God will not fulfill what he has promised, so that the works of justice may be given by God. And, consequently, whether God can fulfill his promises will no longer depend on God, but on the power of man. But if truth and piety are not an obstacle to faith, we must believe, like Abraham, that God is able to fulfill what he has promised. Because God promised Abraham children, who could not be without having faith; Therefore it is God who also grants faith.

Even you yourself are not sure of your own will, and are you not afraid of what is written: Let him who believes he stands take heed that he does not fall? If, then, both wills are uncertain, why does man not rest his faith, his hope and his charity on the stronger one, and not on the weaker one? 22. They will answer us: "For when it is said, If you believe, you will be saved," one of these two things is required of us and the other is offered to us. What is required is in the power of man; the one that is offered, in God's. But why not both in God's, what is commanded and what is offered? Well, it is true that God is asked to grant us what he commands. Those who already believe ask that faith be increased in them, and for those who do not yet believe, they ask that it be granted to them; and thus, both in its increase and in its beginning, faith is a gift from God. That is why it is said: If you believe, you will be saved; as it is also said: If with the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. And here too one of these two things is demanded of us and the other is offered to us. If with the Spirit—he affirms—you put to death the works of the body. Therefore, it is required of us that with the Spirit we put to death the works of the body; but if we have life, it is offered to us. Will it satisfy anyone to say that the death of the works of the flesh in us is not a gift from God, because we see that this is required of us in exchange for the offered prize of eternal life, if we fulfill it? Far be it from us to think that such a response can satisfy those who are already participants and defenders of grace. \ 24. 'For who will have ears to tolerate it being said that infants who die baptized in childhood receive baptism by virtue of the foreknowledge of their future merits, and, therefore, that those who die without being baptized at that same age do so because of the foreknowledge of the future merits of their bad works, whereas God cannot reward their good life or punish their bad life, because both How else are they null? The Apostle has set a limit on this point, which—I will say it in the most discreet terms—must not be crossed by the reckless consideration of man. Because it says this: For all of us must appear manifestly before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the payment of what he has done while living in the body in proportion to what he has done, whether good or bad. Of what was done, he says, and he did not add: "of what was to be done." But from what these men could have deduced the interpretation that future merits, which are never to be realized, in kindergartens are rewarded or punished, I do not know. And why has it been said that man will be judged according to what he has done while living in the body, since many works are not performed by the body or by any bodily member, but only by the soul, and are sometimes of such responsibility that the mere thought of them is due a most just punishment, such as, not to mention other examples, what the fool said in his heart: "There is no God"? What does it mean, then, according to what he has done while living in the body but "according to what he has done during the time he lived in the body", so that by "the body" is understood during the time of the body? Because after the death of the body, no one will be in the body except for the last resurrection; not to acquire any merit, but to receive rewards for good merits, or for bad ones, expiatory penalties. But during this time between the burial of the body and its resurrection, the souls are either tormented or rest in the other life, according to what they would have deserved during their indwelling in the body.

To this time of the indwelling of the soul in the body also belongs what the Pelagians deny, but the Church of Christ affirms, namely: original sin; which, whether remitted by grace or not remitted by the just judgment of God, when children die, either by the merits of baptism, they pass from evil to enjoy eternal goods, or by the merits of original sin they pass from the evils of this life to those of the next. Such is the doctrine that the Catholic faith has come to know and what some heretics already confess without any opposition.

But the saint proves there with very copious and excellent doctrine that in this life there is never a lack of dangers of sinning and that only these will not persist beyond death. And it is in this book where he alleges that testimony of Wisdom: He was taken away so that malice would not pervert his intelligence. Text that, also adduced by me, these brothers of ours have rejected, according to what you have told me, because it was not taken from a canonical book; as if, even leaving aside the authority of this book, the question that I was trying to demonstrate there was not sufficiently clear. For who among Christians would dare to deny that the just, when taken away by death, finds his definitive rest in the afterlife? What man of sane faith would judge otherwise from someone who confessed this? In the same way, if it were affirmed that the just man, abandoning the holy life in which he persevered for a long time and dying impiously, even though he had not lived in impiety, I do not say for a whole year, but not even for a single day: if it were affirmed—I say—that such a person would for this incur the penalties due to reprobates and that his past holiness would be of no use to him, what Christian would dare to contradict such a patent truth? And if, for the same reason, we were asked if this person, had he died when he was in a state of grace, would have found his happy rest in the other life or incurred the penalties of the reprobate, would we hesitate to answer that he would have found his happy rest? For this is the whole reason why it has been said, whoever said it: "He was taken away so that wickedness might not pervert his intelligence." For this was affirmed taking into account the dangers of the present life and not the foreknowledge of God, who had foreseen what was to happen and not what was not to happen; That is to say, that God was to reward the righteous with a premature death, to remove him from the insecurity of temptations, not so that he who would not remain in temptation would sin. About this life, read also in the book of Job: Is not the life of man on earth a militia? But why is it granted to some to be delivered from the dangers of this life when they are in a state of grace, and, on the other hand, other righteous people are preserved in the same dangers during a more prosperous life until they come to decline from their state of holiness?

Who knew the mind of the Lord? And yet, by this same thing, the just are also made to understand that, persevering in the sanctity of their good and pious customs until a ripe old age and until the last day of their life, they should not glory in their own

merits, but in the Lord; because the one who snatched away the righteous man in his adolescent age, so that malice would not pervert his intelligence, is the same one who in any other age, no matter how long it may be, defends him so that malice does not disturb his understanding. But why God preserved in this life the righteous man who was finally going to succumb, and who could have been rescued from it before he succumbed, is something that belongs to the most just and inscrutable judgments of God. 27. Since all this is true, this passage from the Book of Wisdom should not have been rejected, which has deserved to be read in the Catholic Church for so many years with the approval of all who have read it and to be listened to with the veneration due to divine authority, from the bishops to the penitents and catechumens, who were considered the last among the lay faithful. Certainly, if, taking into account the expositors of the divine Scriptures who have preceded me, I were now to undertake a defense of this doctrine, which with more study and erudition than is customary I am forced to advocate against the new error of the Pelagians, that is, that the grace of God is not given to us according to our merits, but is freely given to whom it is given—because it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God, who has mercy—and by the just judgment of God it is not given to whom it is not given—because there is no injustice in God—; If, using—I repeat—the Catholic expositors of the divine Scriptures who have preceded me up to the present, I were to defend this doctrine, without a doubt, these brothers for whom I now write would be fully satisfied, since you have indicated this to me in your letters. But what need do we have to analyze the writings of those authors who, before this heresy was born, did not find it necessary to try to resolve this difficult question? No doubt they would have done so if they had been forced to respond to such difficulties. Hence, only in some passages of their writings did they touch on this matter, briefly and incidentally indicating what they felt about divine grace, stopping, on the other hand, with purpose in defending those issues that were then debated against the enemies of the Church and in the exhortation of those virtues by which worthy worship is paid to the living and true God to achieve true and eternal happiness.

Through the frequent prayers the value of divine grace was simply manifested, for they would not ask God to fulfill the things that He has commanded if it were not granted by Him that they could be fulfilled.

28. But even those who wish to be instructed with the doctrine of the sacred expositors must put before them the same book of Wisdom, in which it is read: He was taken away so that evil would not pervert his intelligence; because also the egregious expositors immediate to apostolic times preferred him and, citing his testimony, believed they were claiming a divine testimony. It is certainly evident how the most blessed Saint Cyprian, to extol the benefit of premature death, defended in his dissertation that those who die, upon leaving this life, in which sin can be committed, are free from all danger of sin. And in the same book he says, among other things: "Why shouldn't you embrace living with Christ, being sure of the promises of Christ, being called to the company of Christ, and rejoice in being free from the bonds of the devil?" And in another place it says: "Children by death are freed from the dangers of lascivious age." And in another: "Why don't we hurry and run to be able to contemplate our homeland and greet our relatives? A huge crowd of parents, brothers and beloved children awaits us there; an innumerable and tight crowd awaits us, already certain of their immortality and even solicitous for our health." With these and other similar expressions, which shine with the most splendid light of the Catholic faith, that holy Doctor shows us that the dangers and temptations of sin must not cease to be feared until it is time to abandon this body; No one afterwards will suffer such dangers and temptations. And even if he did not attest to it, could any Christian entertain any doubt about this truth? Well, how about a fallen man who ends his life miserably in such a state, incurring the penalties due to those who die in this way; How—I repeat—would it not be extremely beneficial for this person that, before succumbing, he had been snatched by death from this place of temptations? 29. And therefore, if we are not moved by the passion of a dispute that is too indiscreet, this question regarding the one who has been carried away may well be terminated here so that evil does not pervert his intelligence.

Nor, therefore, should this book of Wisdom, which has deserved to be read for so many years in the Church of Christ and in which this sentence is read, suffer an insulting contempt, because it is opposed to those who deceive themselves, attributing to themselves merits, contrary to the grace so evidently manifest; which is discovered in a special way in the infants, who, some dying baptized and others not baptized, reveal with complete clarity

The Doctor of Gentiles proclaims it in the beginning of his Epistles: Paul, slave of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, chosen for the Gospel of God, which He had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures about his Son, who was born of the line of David according to the flesh and was constituted the Son of God, powerful according to the Spirit of holiness since his resurrection from the dead. Jesus was, therefore, predestined so that he who was to be the son of David according to the flesh was, nevertheless, at the same time the powerful Son of God according to the Spirit of holiness, because he was born of the Holy Spirit and of the virgin Mary. Such was that singular elevation of man, accomplished in an ineffable way by the divine Word so that Jesus Christ would be called both truly and properly Son of God and Son of man; Son of man, because man was assumed, and Son of God, because the only begotten Word assumed him into himself, otherwise one would not believe in the Trinity, but in a quaternity of persons. Thus that human nature was predestined to such a great, exalted and sublime dignity that no greater elevation of it was possible, in the same way that divinity could not descend or humble itself more for us than by taking our nature with all its weaknesses until death on a cross. Therefore, just as that singular man has been predestined to be our head, so have many others been predestined to be its members. Let the merits that already perished in Adam be silenced here, and let this grace of God reign forever, which already reigns through Jesus Christ our Lord, the only Son of God and only Lord. And whoever finds in Jesus Christ, our head, the merits that preceded his singular generation, let him investigate in us, his members, the merits preceding such multiplied regeneration. For the generation was not repaid to Jesus Christ, but rather donated, so that, free from all ties of sin, he might be born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin.

For if it has truly been said that God knew in his foreknowledge those who were to believe, not because he would cause them to believe, in that case Jesus Christ himself would speak against this foreknowledge when he says: You did not choose me, but I chose you, since it would be rather true that God knew in his foreknowledge that they had to choose him in order to merit that he should choose them. Thus, then, they have been chosen before the creation of the world with that predestination by which God knows in his foreknowledge all his future works and they are taken out of the world with that vocation by which God fulfills everything that He Himself has predestined. For those whom he predestined, those he called; He called them, yes, with that vocation that is in accordance with his plan. "But we affirm—they will reply—that God only had foreknowledge of our initial faith, and that is why he chose us before the creation of the world and predestinated us so that we would also be holy and immaculate by the work of his grace." But listen to what is assured in the same testimony of the Apostle: In whom we have been made heirs by predestination according to the good pleasure of him who works all things. Therefore, the same one who works all things is the one who works in us the principle of faith. Therefore, faith does not precede that vocation of which it has been said: The gifts and vocation of God are irrevocable; and also: Not by virtue of works, but by him who calls, and it could have been said: "By virtue of him who believes"; nor does it precede the election, which the Lord meant when he said: You did not choose me, but I chose you. For not because we believed, but so that we might believe, He chose us, so that we could not say that we chose Him first, and thus this divine oracle would prove false—which is not lawful to think—: You did not choose me, but I chose you. And not because we believed, but that we might believe, we are called; and it is through that vocation, which is irrevocable, that everything necessary for us to come to faith is realized and perfected. But there is no reason to repeat what we have already said amply about this matter. 39. Finally, in the following testimonies confirming this doctrine, the Apostle thanks God for all those who had believed, and not certainly because the Gospel had been preached to them, but because they had believed. So it says thus: In which you also, having heard the word of Truth, the Gospel of your salvation, in which, having also believed, were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance for the recovery of his possession, to the praise of his glory. For this reason I also, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and of your charity towards all the saints, do not cease to give thanks for all of you. New and recent was the faith of those who had heard the preaching of the Gospel, and, having reached the ears of the Apostle, he gives thanks to God for them. For if a man were thanked for a favor merely assumed or certainly not rendered, would it not be flattery or mockery rather than an act of gratitude?

43. I have discussed this matter at length. Perhaps it has been a long time since I have said enough to persuade what I intended, and thus I have spoken to noble minds as well as to rude intelligences, for whom even excessive explanation is insufficient. But I trust in everyone's forgiveness. The interest of such a new discussion forced me to this prolixity. Well, having adduced in my first writings sufficient testimonies to demonstrate that the beginning of faith is also a gift from God, some have found a way to contradict me, affirming that said testimonies were only valid to demonstrate that the increase of faith is a gift from God; But as for the principle of it, by which one comes to believe in Jesus Christ, it is said that it is the work of man and not a gift from God, but that God requires it previously so that the other divine gifts can be obtained through its merit; none of which is granted, therefore, freely, despite the fact that the grace of God, which in no way can be so if it is not free, is attributed to all of them: which—as you see—is totally absurd. That is why I have insisted as much as possible in affirming that the beginning of faith is also a gift from God. And if I have done it with greater prolixity than perhaps those for whose sake I have written this writing would wish, I am willing to listen to their objections, provided that, although I have exceeded the prolixity and caused the annoyance and even boredom of the intelligent, they confess, however, that with what I have done I have achieved my purpose, that is, demonstrated with all evidence that the beginning of faith is also a gift from God, as are chastity, patience, justice, piety and the other virtues, about which there is no doubt that they are divine gifts. I therefore end this book here so that too much prolixity about a single subject does not become tiring.
P. TORIBIO DE CASTRO, O. S.
INTRODUCTION

In this book, the second part of the previously written On the Predestination of Saints at the request of his enthusiastic disciples, Prosper and Hilary, staunch defenders of his doctrines against the Semi-Pelagians of Marseille, and written in the years 428 or 429, when the great Bishop of Hippo had the work of the Retractions in his hands, the holy Doctor continues establishing, on firm and immutable bases, the doctrine of grace and perseverance of the saints. It is the last book he wrote, and, therefore, it contains the Saint's latest and most refined ideas on such important and decisive matters. Those friars of Hadrumeto, subtle and twisted Pelagians, affirmed that "the beginning of faith, the initium fidei, and the final perseverance make them depend on our will and power in such a way that they absolutely deny that they are gifts from God or that He has to do anything in our wills, either to acquire them or to preserve them", hence the constant and haranguing refrain of Saint Augustine about the gratuitousness of said gifts. In the first part he proves that final perseverance is totally free. It would be mocking God to ask him for what we believe he cannot give us. Saint Cyprian shows that in the Sunday prayer we ask the Lord for almost nothing else. Perseverance is not given iuxta praevisa menta, but only through the mercy of God, who gives it to whomever He wants and refuses it ineffably, but justly, to others. Because? Investigabilia sunt iudicia Dei... It extends at length about the famous case of the Tyrians and Sidonians, which it analyzes from all points of view, and humbly adduces the question of Quis es tu qui responderas Deo? This doctrine of predestination is not contrary to exhortations to good: it would not have been preached by Saint Paul, who did not cease to exhort the practice of faith and virtues; On the contrary, it helps us to ground ourselves in humility, so that he who boasts may glory in the Lord. The same objection might be made to the doctrine of divine foreknowledge, which no one dares to deny; but, naturally, one should not preach in such a way as to frighten and frighten the ignorant and less educated, this is modus in rebus! And he ends by exposing that Christ Jesus is the prototype and exemplar of our predestination.

1. Iam de perseverantia diligentius disputandum est; nam et in priore libro, cum ageremus de initio fidei, etiam de hac aliqua diximus. Itaque utrum quisque hoc munus acceperit, quamdiu hanc vitara ducit, incertum est. Si enim prius quam moriatur eadat, non perseverasse utique dicitur, et verissime dicitur. Quomodo ergo perseverantiam, qui non perseveravit, accepisse vel habuisse dicedus est? Nam si habeat aliquis continentiam, et ab ea decidat atque incontinens fiat, si iustitiam similiter, si patientiam, si ipsam fidem, recte dicitur habuisse et non habere; eontinens enim Fuit, vel iustus Fuit, vel patiens, vel fidelis Fuit, quamdiu Fuit; cum vero esse destitit, non est quod Fuit; qui vero non perseveraverit, quomodo perseverans fuet; cum perseverando quisque ostendat se perseverantem, quod iste non fecit? Sed ne quisquam reluctetur et dicat: Si ex quo fidelis quisque factus est, vixit, verbi gratia, decem annos, et eorum medio tempore a fide lapsus est, nonne quinqué annos perseveravit?
