1. Since in the first book (Of the Predestination of the Saints) we have indicated something about perseverance when speaking of the beginning of faith (the initium fidei), we are going to deal in this one, with greater diligence, accuracy and space, of said perseverance. We first clearly affirm that perseverance, with which one perseveres in the love of God and Christ until the end, that is, until this life ends, in which there is only danger of falling, is a free gift from God. Therefore, no one yet knows if he has already received such a gift while living in this earthly life, because if he falls before dying, it is said that he did not persevere, and it is said with all truth; How, then, could he who did not persevere be said to have received perseverance? Thus, if someone has continence and falls, becoming incontinent, or has justice, or patience, or faith itself and loses them, it is truly said that he had them, but he does not have them; He was continent, he was fair, he was patient, he was faithful as long as he was; However, when it ceased to be, it is no longer what it was. He who does not persevere, how was he persevering, if by persevering is how one demonstrates that one perseveres, something that he did not do? And don't tell me that if you lived since you became faithful or accepted the faith, v. gr., ten years, and half of this time he apostatized, did he not persevere for five years? I am not dealing with the materiality of words, by virtue of which this is also called perseverance at that time; of which I speak, of the perseverance with which one perseveres in Christ to the end, in no way can it be said that he who did not persevere to the end possessed it. And it can be better said that the man who was faithful for a year or less had it, if until he died he lived in accordance with the faith, than the other who was faithful for many years, but shortly before death apostatized from the faith.

2. This being well established, let us see if perseverance, of which it is said: He who perseveres to the end will be saved, is a free gift from God. If it is not, how would what the Apostle says be true: It has been given to you through Christ not only that you believe in Him, but also that you suffer for Him? Of these two things, one belongs to the beginning of faith (to the initium fidei), and the other, to the end; but both are a free gift from God, because it is said in the cited text that both have been given; And when does one more truly begin to be a Christian than when he believes in Christ? AND; What better end than to suffer death for Him? Regarding believing in Christ, someone has claimed that the increase or growth of faith is a gift from God, but not the initium fidei, which with the help of the Lord we have already widely refuted. And how is it possible to say that perseverance has not been given to the end to which it is granted to suffer, or better yet, to die for Christ? Saint Peter the Apostle, demonstrating that this is a gift from God, affirms: It is better to suffer while doing good, if such is the will of God, than to suffer while doing evil. By saying whether such is the will of God, he demonstrates that it is the gift of God to suffer for Christ, something that is not given to all saints, and for this reason it should not be said that those who do not have the glory of suffering for Christ do not reach the kingdom of God, do not enter into his glory by persevering to the end in Christ, because God does not want it. And who would dare to maintain that perseverance is not granted to those who, due to a bodily illness or any other accident, die in Christ? Since it is more difficult to persevere where the enemy fights so that one does not persevere, and, therefore, one fights to the death to persevere. That perseverance is more difficult to have, this one is easier, but it is equally easy to give both to those for whom nothing is difficult. God our Lord promised this perseverance, saying: I will put my fear in their hearts so that they will not depart from me. Which is to say: Such will be the fear of mine that I will put in your heart, that you will adhere and unite with me with perseverance. 3. I said there, I say it here: Do not be deceived, says the Apostle; No one laughs at God. Oh man! God is a witness not only to your words, but also to your thoughts. If you ask something from such a great Lord with sincerity and faith, believe that what you receive, you receive from the one from whom you ask; You do not want to honor Him outright and put yourself before Him in your heart, believing that the very thing you pretend to ask for is your own thing. Whoever says this, I no longer have to refute him with my reasons, but rather overwhelm him with the testimonies and affirmations of the saints. Is there any of these who does not continually ask God for perseverance, when when reciting the Sunday prayer one does nothing other than ask for said divine gift? 4. Read carefully and calmly the exposition of it in the book that the blessed Cyprian the Martyr composed on this subject, and whose title is De dominica oratione x, and you will see how many years before and what antidote he prepared against this future Pelagian poison. There are three main things, as you know, that the holy Catholic Church defends against them, namely: that the grace of God is not given according to our merits, since all, absolutely all the merits of the saints are gifts from God and are conferred by his pure grace; that no one lives in this corruptible body, however righteous, without some sins, 'and that every man is born subject to the sin of the first Adam and worthy of condemnation, unless the sin contracted by generation is forgiven by baptismal regeneration. In the aforementioned book of the glorious martyr the first two are discussed with such perspicuity that said heretics, new enemies of the grace of Christ, were defeated and confused long before they were born. Demonstrating that the merits of the saints, as well as perseverance, are free gifts from God, he affirms: We say Hallowed be your name not because we wish God that his name be sanctified by our prayers, but we ask him to be sanctified in us, because the source of all holiness, by whom will it be sanctified? But, since He said: Be holy, for I am the holy one, we ask and pray that we who were sanctified in baptism may persevere in that which we began to be.

And a little further on, dealing with the same subject and teaching us to ask the Lord for perseverance, which in no way would he say truthfully and sincerely if such perseverance were not a gift from God, he states: We beseech that this sanctification remain in us, and since the Lord and

Our Judge urges him who healed and quickened not to sin again, no, lest something worse happen to him, we continually, day and night, make this prayer and ask that the sanctification and quickening that we have received from his grace be preserved for us through his protection. Therefore, when, sanctified by baptism, we say: Hallowed be your name, this holy Doctor understands that we ask him for perseverance in holiness, that is, that we persevere in holiness. And to ask for what we have already received, what is it but to ask that we also be granted not to stop possessing it? Thus, when the saint begs the Lord to be holy, he certainly asks that he persevere in being holy; and the same is true for the chaste, who asks to be chaste; the continent, continent; the just, just; the pious, pious, and everything else that we defend against the Pelagians as gifts from God, there is no doubt that they ask for perseverance in those goods that they well know they have received. If you receive it, you certainly receive the same perseverance, which is the great gift of God. who preserves all his gifts. 5. Besides this, what do we ask of God when we say: Your kingdom come? Well, let what we are quite certain will come to all his saints come to us. Consequently, those who are already saints (or faithful) ask for perseverance in that holiness that has already been granted to them, since in no other way will the oar of God come to them, which only comes to those who persevere to the end.

6. The third request is: may your will be done in heaven and on earth, or as it is read in many codices, and it is what is most commonly said: on earth as it is in heaven, which many understand in this way: like the angels, so may we also do your will. The holy Doctor and martyr interprets our spirit and our flesh as heaven and earth, in such a way that, according to him, we ask that both in accordance fulfill the will of God. He saw, furthermore, in these words another meaning, completely in accordance with the purest faith, of which we have already spoken, namely: the faithful, who, as already clothed with the heavenly Adam, are deservedly called heaven, pray for the infidels, who are still earth, since they bear only the earthly Adam of the first nativity. With this he evidently indicates and affirms that the initium fidei is a gift from God, since the holy Church prays not only for the faithful, so that God may increase their faith or persevere in it, but also

good for the unbelievers, so that they begin to have that same faith that they did not have, and against which they had their hearts predisposed. But now we are not dealing with the beginning or principle of faith, with the initium fidei, of which we have spoken sufficiently in the previous book, but with the perseverance that must be had to the end, which is what the faithful who do the will of God ask for when they say: Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. If the will of God has already been done in them, why do they still ask for it to be done, except to persevere in what they began to be? It is true that it can be replied here that the saints do not ask that God's will be done in heaven, but that it be done on earth as it is done in heaven; that the earth imitates heaven, that is, man the angel, the unfaithful the faithful, and, consequently, the saints ask that what is not yet done be done, not that what is persevere, since whatever saint a man wants, he is still not equal to the angels of God and, consequently, the will of God is not done in them as in heaven. Hence, in that part in which we desire that unfaithful men become faithful, we do not ask for perseverance, but for initium fidei; But when we refer to men becoming equal to the angels in doing the will of God, when the saints pray with this intention, it is clearly seen that what they ask for is perseverance, since no one reaches that supreme happiness of the heavenly kingdom if he does not persevere to the end in the holiness he acquired on earth.

7. The fourth request is: Give us our daily bread today. The blessed Cyprian makes us see that here also what is asked is perseverance, because among other things he says: "We ask that this bread be given to us every day, lest those of us who are in Christ, those of us who are faithful to Christ and receive the Eucharist every day as the spiritual food of our lives, be separated from the body of Christ if, because of some serious crime, we find ourselves forced to abstain from taking communion this heavenly bread." These words of the glorious martyr clearly indicate that the saints ask God for perseverance when with this intention they pronounce the words Give us this day our daily bread, so that they may not be separated from the body.

8. Fifthly we say: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors. In this request it is the only one in which we do not ask for perseverance, since the sins that we ask to be forgiven are already past, they have already passed, and the perseverance that makes us saved forever is necessary in this life, not in the past time, but for the time that remains until the end of our earthly existence. Here it is very worthy to take into account how, expounding this petition, "1 blessed Saint Cyprian shot with the dart of unconquered truth at the heretics who were to exist a long time later, at these Pelagians, who dare to say that the just no longer commits any sin in this life and that in such men it is verified that the Church, already in this present time, has no spot or wrinkle, which is the only true wife of Christ, as if it were not a true wife. From Him is this Church that throughout the earth says and sings what it learned from Him, namely: Forgive us our debts. But notice how the most glorious martyr dismantles and dismantles these heretics in the aforementioned book: "How necessarily, how providentially and healthily we are warned that we are sinners when we are ordered to pray for our sins so that, when asking God's forgiveness, the soul searches its conscience! So that no one may flaunt his innocence and, becoming arrogant, fall deeper, he is taught that he sins every day, when he is ordered that all days ask for forgiveness. Finally the apostle Saint John, in his first Epistle, says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

10. But the brothers about whom you write to me say that "it should not be said of perseverance that it cannot be obtained by our prayers or lost by our bad and contumacious will." How little they pay attention to what they say! We are dealing with that perseverance with which one perseveres to the end; but if it was not persevered to the end, it is because it was not granted, which we have already discussed at length. It is not necessary to say that perseverance to the end has been given to someone as long as that end does not come and when it is seen that such a person perseveres to the end. Without a doubt, we call chaste what we now know as such, regardless of whether it will continue to be so or not; and the same if he has received any other virtue from God, which one can keep or lose, we say that he has them while he has them; but if he loses them, we say that he had them; But perseverance to the end, as no one has if he does not persevere to the end, many can have, but no one can lose it. And there is no need to fear that in those who persevere to the end an ill will will arise not to persevere to the end. Consequently, we can reach this gift of God with our supplications; But when it has been given to us, it cannot be lost, since by persevering to the end, neither this nor the other gifts of God can be lost, because, in fact, how could what makes it impossible to lose what can be lost be lost? 11. It will perhaps be said that, certainly, final perseverance cannot be lost when it has been received, that is, when one has persevered to the end; but that, in a certain way, it is lost when man's contumacy prevents him from reaching it, as we say that the man who does not persevere to the end loses the kingdom of God or eternal glory; not that he already possessed it, but that he would possess it if he had persevered. Let's stop talking about words. I grant that many things we do not have, but hope to have, we may lose; But who dares to tell me that God cannot grant what he commands us to ask? Thinking like this is not only irrational, but also foolish; It's not just someone who's crazy, but he's completely crazy. And who is going to deny this? But precisely we ask that He not let us fall into temptation so that this does not happen, and if we are heard, it certainly does not happen, because God does not allow it to happen, since nothing is done except what He does or allows to be done. God is powerful enough to bend the wills of evil to good and to convert those inclined to evil and direct them along paths of his pleasure, so it is not in vain that it is said: O God, you who convert, give life to us; Nor is one said to him in vain: Do not allow him to hesitate; nor that of Do not give me over to my sinful desire, and, finally, so as not to tire us, because many other quotes will occur to you, it is not in vain that it is said: Do not let us fall into temptation. For he who is not allowed to fall into temptation is certainly not allowed to fall into the temptation of his evil will, and if he is not allowed to fall into it, he will not be allowed to fall into any of them. As it is written: Each one is tempted, attracted and flattered by his own lust; but God tempts no one to evil with temptation; because there are useful temptations, which, far from seducing us, serve to test us, according to that: Oh my God, try me and tempt me. As for harmful temptations, of which the Apostle says: Lest the tempter tempt you and our work be useless, God, as I said, does not tempt anyone with them, that is, he induces no one to that temptation. For being tempted and not falling into temptation is not bad; On the contrary, it is a good; This is being tested. Therefore, when we say to God: Do not lead us into temptation, what else do we ask but that He not lead us into it? For this reason there are those who say and in many codices it is written, as the most blessed Cyprian puts it: Do not allow us to fall into temptation; However, in the Greek gospel I always saw do not lead us into temptation1.

It is much safer to attribute everything to God than to give a part to Him and another for ourselves, and this is stated by Saint Cyprian when exposing this part of the Sunday prayer: "When we pray to God that we do not come into temptation, we are made to see our weakness and helplessness, so that no one exalts himself or claims something to himself with pride and arrogance; and if he has had the glory of confessing Christ and even suffering for Him, the Spaniard, as we see, 110 translates: do not induce us, but: do not let us fall; and the same goes for the French: ne nous laissez pas succomber. CHAPTER VII 13. The consequence of all that has been said is that, even if we had no other authorities and supporting documents, this Sunday prayer would be enough for us in favor of the cause of grace, because it has left us nothing to boast about as our own, when it affirms that it is God alone who can give us the grace of not abandoning Him and asking Him for it. This in no way depends on the forces of human free will in the current state after the fall. If it was in the power of man before the first sin of Adam and how great was the presence and power of man's freedom in that primitive state, it can be seen in the good angels, that, when the devil and all his followers fell, they remained firm in the truth and deserved to reach the perpetual security of not falling, which we know with complete certainty that they now enjoy. But after the fall of man, God willed that man's return to Him and his not departing from Him should belong solely and exclusively to His grace. and, therefore, just as it depends on Him, just as it works in us to turn and draw closer to Him, so does not depart from Him. Therefore the prophet says to him: Manifest your power over your chosen one and over the son of man whom you confirmed for you, and we will never depart from you again. Certainly this chosen one is not the first Adam, in whom we deviate from God, but the second, on whom his power is manifested so that we do not deviate from the Lord; because Jesus Christ is a whole with his members with respect to the Church, which is his body and his fullness. When God, then, manifests his power so that we do not depart from Him, the influence of God reaches us, which is nothing more than the operation by which we remain united to God in Jesus Christ, since in Adam we

We had been separated from Him. In Christ we were called as by lot, having been predestined according to the decree of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. It depends on God's power, and not ours, that we do not depart from God, because this adhesion to the Lord is only in the hands of the one who said: I will put my fear in your heart so that you will not depart from me. 15. This is why God our Lord wanted us to ask Him not to lead us (do not let us fall), because if we are not led, exposed to temptation, we will in no way separate ourselves from Him. There is no doubt that He could give us this without asking Him, but He wanted our very prayer to reveal to us to whom we owed these benefits. From whom but from him to whom we were commanded to ask? Consequently, the Church does not have to make difficult inquiries in this matter and only attend to their prayers. The Church prays so that I03 unbelievers believe, and God converts them to faith; Pray for faithful believers to persevere, and God gives final perseverance. God foreknew (presupposed, if one may say so) from all eternity that this was to happen, and this foreknowledge constitutes the predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and immaculate in their obedience in charity, predestinating them to the adoption of sons to Himself through Jesus Christ according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace, with which He graced them in His beloved Son; in whom they have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he abundantly communicated to them with all wisdom and sense, notifying them of the arcanum of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in himself to dispense to him in the fulness of times, to recapitulate (establish) in Christ all things, those in heaven and those on earth, in Him. In whom we were also chosen by lot, as who had been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the determination of his will. Who of healthy and vigilant faith will admit any human cries against this very clear speaker of the truth?

16. But it is objected: "Why is not the grace of God given according to the merits of men?" I answer: Because God is merciful. "And why not everyone?" Because God is a just Judge; and for this reason precisely, precisely, he gives his grace freely and by God's just judgment it is manifested in others what it is that confers grace on those to whom it is granted. Therefore, let us not be ungrateful if, according to his good pleasure and for the glorious praise of his grace, the merciful God wants to free so many from well-deserved perdition, when, even if he did not free anyone, it would not be unjust, since by one they were all condemned, not because of unjustity, but because of a just and equitable sentence. Consequently, the pardoned person loves grace and is grateful for it; and he who is not pardoned, recognizes his debt and that he deservedly suffers the sentence. If goodness manifests itself by forgiving the debt, equity shines by demanding it; but no injustice can ever be seen in God our Lord. 17. But it is said: "Why, not only in toddlers, but also in two twins, is the same case resolved with such a different sentence?" This question becomes the same as this other: "Why the same sentence in different cases?" Let us remember the parable of those vineyard workers who worked all day and those who did so only for an hour; The work provided was very different, the salary, however, was exactly the same; And did the grumbling and murmuring hear anything from the father of the family other than "I want it that way, so what? If I feel like doing this, what about you?" He was the father of families in such a liberal manner towards some that he did not violate justice towards others in the least. In addition to this, it should be noted that there were rewards agreed upon by the Lord, but as regards justice and grace, the prisoner who is not pardoned can be told from the pardoned prisoner: Take what is yours and go; I want to give this other what is not owed to him; Am I not allowed to do whatever I want, or must your eye be evil because I am good? If he replied: "And why not me?", he would deservedly hear: O homo!, tu quies qui respondas Deo? (Man! Who are you to argue with God?) The objection is insisted upon and they say: "But, if it was appropriate for God, to show what should be done to all men, to condemn some so that his grace would appear more gracious in the vessels of mercy, why in the same case should he condemn me before the other, or pardon the other better than me?" Do you ask me why? I do not answer this, because I confess that I do not find what to answer, and if he still insists that why, in this specific case I tell you that just as his anger is just, as his mercy is great, so inscrutable are his judgments. 19. Suppose that he still insists: "And why does he not grant to some of his servants in good faith to persevere to the end?" Why do you think it is but because he is not lying who said: They came from among us, but they were not of us; Because if they were from us, would they have remained with us? But are there two natures of men? By no means. If there were two natures, there would be no grace, since no one would be freed free if he was given what was owed to him. Men believe that all who seem good and faithful should receive final perseverance; But God has judged it best to mix with his saints some who will not persevere, so that those for whom security in the temptations of this life do not want to believe themselves secure. Many are held back from this pernicious pride by what the Apostle says: Therefore, he who thinks he stands firm, take heed that he does not fall. By his own will he who falls falls and by the will of God he who remains firm remains firm, for God is able to sustain him; and, therefore, not he himself, but God, and so it is good not to be conceited, but rather to live in fear. The fall or stability of each one is always due to some thought, and the Apostle says, as he recalled in the previous book 1: We are not capable of ourselves to conceive any good thought as of ourselves, but our sufficiency or capacity comes from God; and following the same, the blessed Ambrose dares and says: Our hearts and our thoughts are not in our hands (they do not depend on us); what everyone who is humble and sincerely pious considers most certainly true. 20.

Chapter 1 says: "We often affirm that we must flee from the world, and I wish affection were as cautious and solicitous as speech is easy! But, unfortunately, the deceitful flattery of earthly desires sneaks into us and the obfuscation produced by vanities clouds our minds in such a way that you are turning over in your mind the very thing you wish to avoid. It is difficult for man to guard against this, Avoiding it at all is totally impossible; and that it is more a good wish than a true reality, the prophet attests by saying: Incline my heart to your prescriptions and not to greed. Neither our heart nor our thoughts are in our power, which suddenly cloud our spirit and drag it where you had not intended: to things that are vain, worldly, earthly, voluptuous, flattering and at the same time that we try to elevate our mind to the things of heaven; Assailed by a multitude of vain thoughts, we fall back, more often than not, into things of earth." Therefore, it is not in the hand of man that men have the power to be made children of God, but they receive it from him who inspires good thoughts, through which they attain faith, who works through charity; And to acquire such a great good, preserve it and progress perseveringly to the end, we are not capable of conceiving even a good thought as our own, but our sufficiency comes from God, who disposes of our hearts and our thoughts at his will.

21. Why, between two children, equally subject to original sin, is this one taken and abandoned to the other, and of two grown-up, impious adults, is this one called in such a way that he follows the caller, and the other is either not called or is not called like the first? Inscrutable are the judgments of God. Why, between two pious believers, is this one given final perseverance and not the other? Even more inscrutable are the judgments of God. But what the faithful must hold as certain with complete certainty is that the one is one of the predestined, and the other is not; because if he were one of us—says one of the predestinated ones who had drunk the secret in the very heart of Jesus—he would certainly have persevered with us. does this mean, I repeat? Were they not both created by God? Were they not both sons of Adam? Were they not both made of earth and had they not received from him who said: I have made every state, souls of exactly the same nature?; and, finally, were they not equally called and equally followed the divine call, and both justified, and both renewed by the baptism of regeneration? These questions would be answered by someone who undoubtedly knew very well what he was saying: "All these things are true, and, according to them, they were from among us; however, according to another certain difference, they were not from ours; because if they were from ours, both would persevere with us." And what, finally, is this difference? Let us open the holy books of God, let us not avert our gaze; the sacred Scripture cries, let us apply our ears: They were not of these, because they had not been chosen in Christ before the constitution and creation of the world; they had not achieved that luck in Him; They had not been predestined according to the purpose of Him who makes everything, for if they were all that, they would be of these and with them they would have persevered. 22. Without speaking of how easy it is for God to bring to his faith the withdrawn and even the adverse or contrary wills of men and to work in their hearts so that they resist and do not give in to any adversity and do not depart from Him, overcome by any temptation, since, as the Apostle says, He may not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength, without speaking of this omnipotence of the Lord, certainly, God knowing in His foreknowledge that they would fall, He could before this happened take them out of this life. Naturally, aren't we going to have to clarify again and show how absurd it is to affirm that the deceased are also judged for the sins that God in his foreknowledge knows they would commit if they lived? This is so contrary and horrendous to Christian and even human sentiment that even having to refute it causes shame. Why not also say that the preaching of the Gospel, which costs the saints so much work, sweat and pain, has been totally useless, since men could be judged even if they did not hear the Gospel, in accordance with the contumacy or obedience that God, through his foreknowledge, foreknowledged (presupposed) that the men who heard it would offer?

If I am asked why so many miracles were performed before those who, seeing them, would not believe and not before those who would believe if they saw them, what will I answer? Perhaps what was said in a certain book 1 in response to six questions from the pagans, without prejudice, of course, to considering other reasons that the prudent and learned can investigate? You know that when I was asked why Christ took so long to come, I said in that book: "Jesus Christ knew that in the times and places in which his Gospel was not preached, the times would be as they were for many of those who had the privilege of seeing him bodily, that even when he raised the dead they did not believe in him." In addition to this, in the same book, a little later, in answer to the same question, I say: "What is so special about it that Christ, knowing that the world in the early times would be full of unfaithful people, did not want his Gospel to be preached to those who would not believe in words or portents?" But, evidently, we cannot say this of Tire and Sidon, which, on the contrary, are an example of the hidden judgments of God in the secret causes of the predestination, to which at that time I did not want to refer. It is obvious to accuse the Jews of voluntary infidelity, who did not want to believe even in the face of the great miracles performed in their sight, and the Lord Himself harshly reproaches them saying: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were done in you had been performed in Tire and Sidon, they would have done penance long ago, covered in sackcloth and lying in ashes; But we cannot say that the Tyrians and Sidonians would not believe in the sight of the miracles and marvelous acts if they were performed before them, since Christ our Lord assures that they would do humble and sincere penance if all those portents had been performed in them. However, on the day of judgment, Tire and Sidon will be punished, although much less than those other cities that, despite and despite so many prodigies, remained steadfast in their disbelief, because Christ continues and says: Therefore, I tell you that Tire and Sidon will be less rigorously punished on the day of judgment than you.

Consequently, the Jews will be treated more severely, the Tyrians and Sidonians more benignly; but everyone will be punished. Now, if God is to judge men after they are dead for the sins they would commit if they had lived longer, then also, because they would have been faithful and good if the

Gospel with as many signs and wonders as the Jews, they will not be punished. However, they will be; Therefore, it is false of all falsehood that men are judged after death by what they would do if the Gospel had been announced to them. And if this is false, it is also false that children who die without baptism die as a punishment for what God foresees, that is, that even if they lived and the Gospel was preached to them, they would remain in their infidelity. All that remains is original sin, for which they are guilty and deserving of condemnation. We see in others that, having the same cause, only by the totally free grace of God are they forgiven with regeneration (or baptism), and by hidden, but just judgment of God (since in God there is no injustice), some who will perish living badly after baptism are preserved in life until they perish, who would not perish if death had been anticipated at their fall. In short: no one is judged by what he would do after death, good or bad, if he had not died; Otherwise, the Tyrians and Sidonians would not be suffering now for what they actually did, but rather for what they would have done, if the Gospel accompanied by signs and wonders had been announced to them, they would have achieved salvation through their great penitence and through their faith in Christ.

Of course, whoever says that those who had to apostatize and lose faith were given the great benefit of never having it, so that they would not be guilty of greater impiety, clearly shows that men are not judged of the sins that God foresaw that they would commit if, through a new benefit, he prevented them from committing them; as happened with that of who says in the sacred Scripture: He was raptured so that malice would not spoil his understanding. Over and over again we repeat without a hint of shame: Oh man, who are you to argue with God? His judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable...; and now we add this: Do not ask questions higher than yourself and do not scrutinize things that surpass you. 31. Do you see, then, dear ones, how absurd it is and how contrary to sound faith and sincere truth to say that infants who die before the use of reason will be judged according to what God foretold they would do if they lived? This opinion, which certainly causes horror to every human spirit endowed with a modicum of reason, and especially to every Christian spirit, has been forced to embrace all those who, out of horror at the Pelagian error, maintain that the grace of God through Jesus Christ, with which he only helps us after the fall of the first man, in whom we all fell, is given to us according to our merits. Pelagius himself condemned and rejected this opinion before the bishops of the East for fear of his own condemnation. Therefore, if it cannot be maintained that men will be judged by the good or bad works that they would have done if they had lived longer, since such works are nothing and in the same divine foreknowledge future non-existent; If this cannot be maintained without serious error, what remains but to clearly confess what the Catholic Church defends against the Pelagian heresy, namely: the grace of God is not given according to our merits, as is most evidently seen in infants? Because fate does not force God to help some and not others, the common cause being; Nor can it be believed that human affairs, as far as children are concerned, are not directed by divine Providence, but by blind destiny, perhaps the blind, when it comes to saving or condemning rational souls, when not a single bird falls to the earth without our heavenly Father's disposition. Did the People in faith and truth, who so often remember the doctrine of predestination, stop preaching the word of God? Because he said that God works in us to will and to act according to his good pleasure, did he perhaps stop exhorting us to want the things that please God and to practice them? Or because he said: He who began a good work in you will perfect and complete it until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, did he not immediately advise you to begin and persevere to the end? Our Lord Jesus Christ himself commanded us to believe, saying: Believe in God and believe in me, and for this reason those words are not false: No one comes to me, that is, no one believes in me, except my Father gives it. Nor is that precept vain because this statement is true. Why, then, should we judge the doctrine of predestination, which sacred Scripture so often reminds us of, as contrary and harmful to preaching, commands, exhortations, corrections, so frequent also in sacred Scripture? 35. Naturally, no one will dare to say that God did not previously know those to whom he was to give the grace to believe or to whom he was to give his Son so that none would be lost; and if he foresaw it (I presupposed it), he necessarily foresaw the benefits for which he deigns to free us. Therefore, the predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge of God and the preparation of his benefits, by which everyone who is saved is most certainly saved; Those who do not are abandoned by the just judgment of God in the mass of perdition, where those Tyrians and Sidonians remained, who would have believed if they had seen the wonderful works of Christ Jesus. But since they were not given that for which they would have believed, they were also denied belief. From this it follows that some receive from God the natural gift of intelligence, which would lead them to faith if they heard the appropriate word of God or saw the miracles on purpose, and yet, if by the highest judgments of God they are not separated, by the predestination of his grace, from the mass of perdition, they will neither hear the divine words nor see the facts by which they would come to faith if they heard or saw such things. The Jews who could not believe in the face of such great and clear wonders done in their presence have remained in that same mass of perdition.

And why they could not believe, the Gospel tells us: Even though Jesus had performed so many miracles before them, they did not believe in Him, so that the words that the prophet Isaiah said could be fulfilled: "O Lord! Who has believed what he heard from us?"

The teaching of the mystery of preaching does not prevent preaching and exhorting people to persevere in the faith and to make continuous progress in it, so that those who have been granted obedience may hear what is convenient for them, because how will they hear if there is no one to preach to them? In addition to this, preaching and exhorting it and persevering to the end does not go against the mystery of predestination, for thus, he who lives and obeys faithfully will not be proud of his obedience as if it were not a gift received, but whoever glories, glories in the Lord.

"We should not glory in anything, when nothing is ours," as Saint Cyprian taught most faithfully and with complete certainty, thus establishing in an uncontested manner the dogma of predestination, for if "we should glory in nothing, when nothing is ours," we certainly should not glory in our persevering obedience, because it is not ours, so that we have not received it. This obedience is a gift from God, which He foresaw to be given to every faithful Christian of those called with that vocation of which it is said: The gifts and vocation of God.

some things were said in such a way that they were milk for children and solid food for adults; as, v. gr., these words of Saint John: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was in God, and the Word was God. What Christian can remain silent about such a truth and who can understand it? What more sublime truth can be found in Christian doctrine? And yet, the same is taught to the great as to the little ones and the former do not hide it from the latter. But if there are circumstances in which the truth must be kept silent, there are also occasions in which it is necessary to proclaim it to all the winds. It would be too wordy to cite and list here all the causes that, at times, can compel us to keep silent about the truth. One of the main ones is not to make those who do not understand it worse, while we want to make the intelligent ones more learned, who by keeping quiet do not become more learned, but they do not become worse either. And what will we do when faced with the dilemma that, if we keep silent about the truth, those who can understand it are harmed, and if we tell it, those who do not understand it are made worse? Isn't it better to say it, and whoever can understand, let him understand, than to keep silent about it, so that no one understands it, but precisely the most intelligent becomes worse? All the more so that by hearing it and understanding it, one can teach it to many others, because the more one is able to understand something, the more suitable one is to teach it to others. The enemies of grace urge and urge in every possible way in order to make us believe that it is given to us according to our merits, and thus, grace is no longer grace. And are we going to remain silent about what sacred Scripture prescribes for us to say? Will we fear offending with the truth those who cannot understand it and will we not fear exposing those who can understand it to error and falsehood? 41. Therefore, either the doctrine of predestination is admitted and recognized as taught to us by the sacred Scriptures, that is, that in the predestined the gifts and vocation are immutable, or it must be admitted that grace is given to us according to merit, as the Pelagian heresy affirms. Although this sentence, as we have said many times, has been condemned by Pelagius himself, according to the acts of the eastern bishops.

But those for whom we write these pages are so far from the heresy of Pelagius, that, although they do not yet confess that the predestined are those who by the grace of God submit to faith and persevere in it to the end, they nevertheless admit that grace prevents the will of those to whom it is given; Therefore, in reality they do not truly believe that grace is given freely, as the eternal Truth affirms, but they con-

The gifts, then, that are given to the elect, called according to the plan of God, among which is beginning to believe and persevering in faith until the last moment of life, as we have proven with such a babble of reasons and authorities, these gifts, I say, are not foreseen (foreknown) by God if the doctrine of predestination that we defend is not true; but certainly, with complete certainty, they are foreknown, foreseen by "God (and this is predestination), therefore the doctrine we defend is true.

Sometimes predestination is designated by the name of foreknowledge; Thus says the Apostle: God did not reject his people, whom he knew in his foreknowledge. This word "praescivit", prior (presuppo), has no other meaning than predestinate, as seen from the context. It was about the relics of the Jews, who had been saved, leaving the rest to perish, since shortly before he had said what the prophet said to Israel: All day I had my hands extended to that unbelieving and rebellious people; and as if someone had answered: "Where then are the promises of God to Israel?", the Apostle adds to the point: And now I say: Has God perhaps rejected his people? Certainly not, for I myself am an Israelite, of the lineage of Abraham and of the tribe of Benjamin; as if he were saying: "I am from that same crowd"; and finally, he adds the phrase we are dealing with here: God did not reject his people, whom he knew in his foreknowledge. And to demonstrate that the salvation of that small number of Israelites was the grace of God and not the merit of his works, he adds: You do not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he directs his complaints against Israel, etc., etc. But what does the divine oracle answer? I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed their knee to Baal. Where it is noteworthy that it does not say: "They have reserved me" or "They reserved me", but He reserved me. Thus, at this time, by election of grace, by free election, that small residue number has been saved. But if by grace, that is, freely, then not by his Works; Otherwise, grace would not be graS. Inc. And as a conclusion to everything we have just mentioned: What then? He says in response to this question: That Israel has not found what it was looking for (justification), but the chosen ones have found it, all the others having been blinded. For these chosen ones and for this small number of Israelites saved by the election of his grace, Saint Paul designates the people, which he did not reject, because he foresaw it. This is that election by which he chose those whom he loved in Christ before the creation of the world to be holy and blameless in his presence, out of charity, having predestined them to be his adopted children. Therefore, no one who understands these things is allowed to doubt or deny that where the Apostle says: God did not reject his people, whom he knew in his foreknowledge, he meant predestination. He previously knew the small number of Israelites who by the choice of his grace were to be saved, that is, he predestined them. Without a doubt, He knew them previously (presupposed them) if He predestined them, since to predestinate is to know previously (foreknow) what He Himself wanted to do.

I would like someone to say to them: "Why are your exhortations and your corrections, if there is no good that comes from us, nor are our hearts or our thoughts in our power?" They did not fear this objection, although they knew very well that only a very few are granted to receive the doctrine of salvation directly from God himself or through the ministry of angels, while the vast majority must receive it through the ministry and preaching of men. However, in whatever way the word of God is announced to us, it is always the effect of his grace that we follow it in such a way as to submit to it. 49. Thus, then, said most excellent interpreters of the holy letters, teaching the doctrine of the true grace of God as it should be taught, that is, that to which; No human merit precedes, they did not cease to exhort the fulfillment of the divine precepts, so that those who received the gift of obedience would hear the commands that they had to obey. If some merit of ours precedes grace, certainly that merit will come from some deed, saying or thought, which implies some good will; but with all brevity and concision he who said: "There is no use in glorifying ourselves, because nothing is ours"; and whoever said that "Neither our heart nor our thoughts are in our hand," understood, without a doubt, what we can do or say, since all the actions and words of man proceed from the heart or thought. What more could the glorious martyr and very wise Doctor Saint Cyprian do than recommend to us in the exposition of the Sunday prayer to pray for the enemies of the Christian faith? And in the same place, we are born to see that the initium fidei is a gift from God, as well as, by showing us that the Church of Christ asks for final perseverance every day, it teaches us that God is only the one who gives it to those who persevere. St. Ambrose, expounding what St. Luke the Evangelist says: It seemed to me also, says: "This plan of St. Luke does not come from himself alone, because it was not formed by his sole will, but according to what pleased him who speaks of me, Christ, who makes what is good in himself, makes it seem good to us, since he calls the one on whom he has compassion, and, therefore, whoever follows Christ, when asked why he wanted to be a Christian, can answer: It seemed to me too."

And in saying this he does not deny that God is also the author of that plan: God prepares the will of men, and everything that the saints do to honor God is the effect of divine grace. The evangelist himself tells us why they did not receive him: Because his face was like that of someone walking to Jerusalem. The disciples wanted to enter Samarla; but God calls and sanctifies those whom he pleases. What more evident, what more precise can we ask of the interpreters of sacred Scripture, if we are pleased to hear what the sacred texts clearly tell us? These two illustrious testimonies are more than enough, but let us add the third. Saint Gregory clearly affirms that our faith in God and the confession of this faith is a divine gift when he says: "Confess the Trinity in one God, or, if it pleases you more, say that the three divine persons have the same nature, and we will ask God to grant you to profess by his Holy Spirit what you believe. "Without a doubt he will grant it to you, I am sure; for he who gave the main thing will give the secondary thing; He who gave to believe, will give to confess. 50. Therefore, so illustrious and holy doctors, who teach us that we have NOTHING to boast about as our own and that God has not given us; that not even our hearts and our thoughts are in our hand; who attribute everything, absolutely everything to God and who confess that from Him we receive conversion and perseverance, that we think it is good and that we want what is good, that we honor God, that we receive Christ so that from infidelity or indifference we pass to piety and devotion, that we believe in the blessed Trinity and confess it publicly - mind, they attribute all this to the grace of God, they recognize them as gifts from the Lord, they clearly attest that they come from Him, not of ourselves; And will there be any so daring that they dare to affirm that, thus recognizing the power of divine grace, they come to deny its prescience, when even the most ignorant and rude confess it and deny it?

Certainly, if they knew that God is the giver of these gifts, and that he foresaw that he would grant them, and that he could not help but know to whom he would give them, there is no doubt that they recognized predestination, which against the new heretics we so laboriously and diligently defend, and which was taught to us by the apostles themselves, to whom, preaching obedience to God our Lord and fervently exhorting the same, no one, however, could tell them: "If you do not want that obedience to which you so ardently exhort us to be warmed in our hearts, do not preach to us the grace of God saying that God gives the same thing that you exhort us to do."

51. Now, if the apostles and doctors of the Church who succeeded them have followed in their footsteps, teaching and preaching both things, namely: the gratuitousness of the gifts of God and his grace, which is not given according to our merits, and devout obedience to their savior precepts, why do these our brothers, despite and despite the force of the truth, which forces them to close their mouths, nevertheless dare to say that, even if what is said about predestination is true, it should not be preached to the people? Quite the opposite; It must be preached, and very loudly, so that he who has ears to hear, may hear. And who has them, if he has not received them from him who says: I will give you a heart to know and ears to hear? Whoever has not received them, let him reject it if he pleases; but he who understands it, let him take and drink; drink and live. Just as piety must be preached, so that he who has ears to hear may render to God the worship that is due to him, and purity must be preached to him, so that he does not commit sin against precious virtue, and charity must be preached to him, so that he may love God and his neighbor, so predestination must also be preached and taught, so that he who has ears to hear may glorify not in himself, but in our God. Sir. 52. Those brothers also say that there was no need to discuss something so uncertain, with which the hearts of the unintelligent have been troubled, and that this doctrine of predestination has not been necessary to defend with zeal and effectiveness for so many years the Catholic faith against heretics, especially against the Pelagians, in the books of so many Catholic writers and even in my previous ones. I am greatly amazed to hear such statements. You are lying, and I speak only of my works, in which they were written before Pelagius began to inoculate the poison of his heresy, and yet, not yet knowing the insidious Pelagian heresy, how true blows we strike when preaching and teaching that the grace, by which God frees us from our evils, errors and customs, is not given to us in view of our good merits, but according to his free mercy! And I realized this perfectly when at the beginning of my episcopate I wrote the treatise that I dedicated to Simplician, Bishop of Milan, of happy memory, when I also knew and affirmed and demonstrated that the initium fidei is a free gift of God.

DEI. DO S OF PERSEVERANCE

•53. Of all my books, the Confessions is the most popular and the one that has had the greatest acceptance; and although I wrote and published it long before the Pelagian heresy appeared, I said in them and often repeated to our God and Lord: "Give what you command and command what you want." On one occasion, a dear brother and co-episcope, speaking with Pelagius in Rome, recalled them, and the heretic became so furious and upset that he almost came to blows with that brother of ours. What does God command first and foremost but that we believe in Him? Therefore, He gives us that if we just say: "Give what you command." In addition to this, in books HI and IV, chapters 11, 12 and 13, respectively, where I narrate my conversion, the work of God, to this faith that I fought with miserable and furious talkativeness, do you not remember that when narrating it I stated very clearly that what prevented my perdition were the ardent supplications and the faithful and daily tears of my good mother? With which I preached and explained to the face of the world that God by his free grace not only converts the wills of men separated from healthy faith, but also those contrary and rebellious to it. You know well and can verify, if you wish, how and how much I pray to our Lord to grant me perseverance. Who will dare, not to say deny, but even to doubt, that God in his foreknowledge knew that he would give me these gifts, which I so desired and praised in my Confessions, and that, therefore, He did not know to whom he would give them? This is the very predestination of the saints, which later had to be defended with more diligence and point by point against the Pelagian heresy, because each new heresy raises particular questions in the Church, against which the authority of the sacred Scriptures must be defended with more care and scrupulosity. What else has forced us to explain more thoroughly and clearly the texts that speak of predestination other than the fact that the Pelagians affirm that God's grace is given according to our merits, which is to deny the gratuitousness of grace at all?

54. Consequently, to dismantle this doctrine that is most ungrateful to our God and enemy of the gratuitous benefits of the same, we clearly defend and affirm, in accordance with the holy Scriptures, of which we have adduced such abundant testimonies, that both the principle of faith, or initium fidei, and perseverance to the end are free gifts from God. i Defeated Manichaeans and Donatists, the Bishop of Hippo had to undertake the fierce fight against Pelagius, the most devious and subtle heresiarch of his time, and his heresy one of the most dangerous and radical of all time. The exaltation of human freedom, the poisonous larva of Greek stoicism, which had crept even into the austere monasteries of the Thebaid, had infected the doctrines of Theodore of Mompauostia, and through his disciple Rufinus the Syrian it penetrated into Rome, where Pelagius was to clothe it with the sophistry of heresy. The Breton monk, whose philosophical training had suffered the influence of Hellenic stoicism, easily adhered to the Syrian doctrines and became their coryphaeus. With skillful rhetoric and not without a certain prestige, he began to spread them in Rome in the early years of the 5th century. His eloquence initially won him illustrious friends, among whom was Saint Augustine himself, who wanted to meet him. Around the year 410, fleeing the invasion of Rome by Alaric, Pelagius arrived in Hippo, Augustine being absent, in Carthage, on the occasion of the conference with the Donatists. Only at the beginning of 411 did the holy Bishop have the opportunity to meet Pelagius in the capital of Africa, from where the Breton monk soon left, not finding a favorable environment there for the dissemination of his doctrines. At the end of the same year it seems that the date of the letter that Augustine wrote to Pelagius (Epist. 146) in response to the one he had addressed to the Bishop of Hippo must be fixed. The Saint's letter is very brief and perhaps only political. Pelagius had found in Rome a faithful satellite of his doctrines, Celestius, who, with less rhetoric and less dialectical skill, shamelessly divulged them. When Pelagius left Carthage for Palestine, Celestius remained for some time in the capital of Africa. But, denounced by the deacon Paulinus, the bishop of Carthage, Aurelius,

He called a council to judge the innovator. The council was held at the beginning of the year 412, presided over, on behalf of the emperor, by Flavius ​​Marcellinus, tribune of Carthage, a fervent Catholic and great friend of Augustine. But the Bishop of Hippo could not attend the council, which condemned the doctrines of Celestius; "Caelestius vero discipulus eius iam propter such assertiones apud Carthaginem, in episcopali iudicio, ubi non interfui, excommunicationem meruerat" (Retract., II, 33). But even after the council some supporters of Celestius did not stop pestering Marcellinus with leading questions regarding the condemned propositions. The illustrious tribune deemed it most convenient to refer them to Augustine so that he could refute them. All the Catholic clergy once again turned their gaze towards the debelator of the Manichaeans and Donatists. This gave rise to the three books De peccatorum mefitis et remissione: "Missis ergo mihi a Cartilágine quaestionibus eorum quas rescribing dissolverem, scripsi primum libros tres, quorum titulus est De peccatorum meritis et remissione" (ibid.). Bossuet notes (Déjense de la tradition et des Peres) that Saint Augustine had already laid the foundations of the Pelagian refutation in a sermon delivered in Carthage shortly before the council (Serm. 294). Indeed, in this sermon the holy Doctor already expounds the true doctrine on the baptism of infants, the title with which he also called his first work against Pelagius. But we have the irrefutable testimony of Saint Augustine himself: "Contra quam prius, cum opus erat, non scriptis, sed sermonibus et collocutionibus agebamus, ut quisque nostrum poterat aut debenbat" (Retract., II, 33). It is not appropriate for this place to present the Augustinian refutation of the doctrine of Celestius, which was none other than that of Pelagius. If we have given this brief news here it is because it is related to the origin of the treatise On the Spirit and the Letter.

to the treatise On the Spirit and the Letter, also dedicated to the illustrious tribune. Augustine begins his work by proposing to Marcellin, among the many alleged in the sacred Scriptures, several examples of possible things. God can make a camel go through the eye of a needle, even though it has never been done; He could make twelve thousand legions of angels fight for Christ, although this was not verified, and he could suddenly carry out the extermination of Israel's enemies, although this fact was carried out gradually. Likewise, although no man, except Jesus Christ, has achieved perfect justice, it is nevertheless possible with the help of God (c. 1, n. 1). The Bishop of Hippo meets possible objections. Thus it could be objected that the alleged examples refer to divine works; but justice, even when it is the most perfect human work, does not transcend the limits of man's activity. Therefore it should not be believed that no one has reached it (n. 2). Justice—Augustine answers—certainly falls within the limits of human activity, but it presupposes the help of God. It is a divine gift. Therefore it is also a divine work. Whoever denied it would have to demonstrate his assertion against the multiple testimonies of sacred Scripture. However, if someone believed that there has been or could be such a perfect man, assuming the grace of God, such an opinion would not be a very pernicious error, unless someone vainly believed himself to be perfect (n. 3). It would be, however, to believe that perfect justice can be achieved with human forces alone. Such an error—which was that of the Pelagians—must be vigorously combated. With all his dialectical acuity, Augustine prevents and refutes various Pelagian objections. Perhaps one could insist on objecting that justice is not achieved without divine help, since it is the work of human freedom, and this is already a gift received from God in creation. Furthermore, God teaches man the path of justice through the precepts with which he destroys his ignorance in the moral order (n. 4). Neither free will nor the teaching or instruction of the precepts are sufficient for justification—Augustine replies—; The help of the Holy Spirit is absolutely necessary, who infuses the soul with complacency and love for good. Because "we cannot embrace the good nor live justly if at the same time the good does not delight us and we do not love it." 5).

that one gave me death (Rom. 7, 11). When the Apostle writes: You shall not covet, he formulates the prohibitive law of all sin, since no sin is committed except for a certain unhealthy covetousness, and the prohibition urges the appetite to do evil, "for I do not know in what way that which is coveted becomes more pleasant when it is prohibited": "Nescio quo enim moda, hoc ipsum quod concupiscitur, fit iucundius dum vetatur" (n. 6), says the Saint with fine penetration of moral psychologist. Against this sinful greed, the Holy Spirit excites in the soul the healthy greed for good. Therefore, the law alone, without grace, kills, since it adds to covetousness the transgression of the law itself (n. 7), since the law was introduced so that sin would abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more. Which could be understood perversely by the perverse: "a perversis perverse posse accipi", who would try to sin more so that grace may abound more—"crede fortiter et pecca fortius", by Luther—, as if the Apostle had said that because of the abundance of grace sin was profitable. "For the more the healing virtue of medicine is praised, the more diseases are execrated and hated. In the same way, the praise and exaltation of grace is reproach and reprobation of crime" (n. 9). Human freedom is, therefore, insufficient by itself to achieve perfect justice. No one should claim ownership of divine gifts. God alone is the source of life and good works and the fountainhead of all light. Man separates himself from this source and this light through pride, wanting to become the autonomous reason for his life; "Haec cogitatio non effert in superbiam; quod vitium oritur, cum sibi quisque praefidit, seque sibi ad vivirdum caput facit" (n. 11). With the same reason as ancient Pelagianism, the proud autonomy of Kantian reason and all absolute rationalism could fall under this anathema of Saint Augustine. After demonstrating the insufficiency of freedom to do good by itself, Saint Augustine goes on to deal with the insufficiency of the law under the yoke of circumcision. The Jews boasted over other peoples that they were the possessors of the law, but they did not fulfill it.

For which reason the Apostle rightly reproaches them: That not the one who appears from the outside is the true Jew, nor the one who appears from the outside the true circumcision, but rather the Jew who is such in secret and the circumcision of the heart in spirit, not in letter. Circumcision of the heart the Apostle calls the pure will of all illicit concupiscence. Now, this will is not achieved by the letter, which instructs and commands, but by the spirit, which helps and gives healthy medicine:

"Quod non ñt littera teaching et minante, sed spiritu adiuvante et sanante" (n. 13). If the law without the Spirit kills, it is important to know the difference between the old law and the new law. Someone could believe that the Apostle understands the Jewish law by the law of works, and the Christian law by the law of faith. This distinction would be erroneous. The Apostle understands by law that which justifies no one. This is in itself good, although it is an occasion for sin and although it does not justify. "What shall we say then? Is the law a sin? Not so. The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, and just, and good (Rom. 7, 13). The law of works is the prohibitive law that prescribes: Thou shalt not covet. But does not the law of faith also prescribe this? For if it does not prescribe it (the Lutherans should have well noted this passage), what is the reason why, since we already live under its rule, we do not sin safely and with impunity?" "For this is what some of the Apostle himself judged to be saying, of whom he writes: And as some affirm that we say, 'Let us do evil that good may result,' of those who affirm that the condemnation is just (Rom. 3:8). Therefore, if the law of faith also prescribes: Thou shalt not covet, why is it not also called the law of works?" Therefore, the law is not enough to justify man—concludes the Doctor of Grace——; The faith of Jesus Christ, absolutely free grace, is necessary (c. 13). But by the law that justifies no one the Apostle does not mean—as it might seem—only circumcision and other figurative sacraments of the Old Testament, but the Decalogue itself. This is identical in the old and the new law, except for the sabbatical precept, which was the only figurative one. Saint Augustine notes various analogies between both laws. Both were written by the finger of God, who is the Holy Spirit. But there are essential differences between the two. That was written on stone tablets; this one, inside the hearts. That is a law of fear, enacted amidst threats and frightful terrors; this, law of love, for the justification of souls. "The law of God is charity." Which is enacted "when Charity itself is poured out in the hearts of believers" (n. 29).

Against the difference between both Testaments one could oppose that passage of the Apostle: For when the Gentiles, guided by nature, carry out the dictates of the law, they, without having the law, are law for themselves, as those who show that they have the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom. 2, 14-15). The objection is not of slight importance; because if the Gentiles naturally carry out the dictates of
OF THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER

the law, what would be the difference between Gentiles and Christians? Wouldn't the Gentiles thus be more privileged than the chosen people and the Christian people themselves, since they need grace to fulfill what the Gentiles naturally fulfill? (c. 25). Saint Augustine answers that the Apostle refers in this passage to the Gentiles already belonging to the New Testament, and that is why they naturally comply with the dictates of the law and carry the law written in their hearts. They are the Gentiles to whom Saint Paul himself refers by the name of the Greek when he writes that the Gospel is a force of God ordered to health for everyone who believes, both for the Jew, first, and for the Greek (Rom. 1, 16). Hence, both the Jew and the Greek, that is, anyone among the Gentiles, who believes, will equally achieve health through the Gospel. And "from where could he say that the Greek, that is, the Gentile, is justified, except by virtue of the grace of the Savior?" (no. 44). This power of nature comes from grace, from which the former is restored by the latter. The divine law was erased in hearts by sin; destroyed, the law is written again in hearts so that the dictates of the law act naturally (n. 47). But if those who naturally carry out the dictates of the law are not to be understood as Gentiles already belonging to the New Testament or having already been justified, "nevertheless, we have read, seen and heard about the Gentiles some actions which, according to the norms of right justice, not only are not blameworthy, but we consider them even worthy of praise" <n. 48). This arises from the fact that the image of God or the divine law was not completely erased in the soul by sin. Thus, the work of grace is to restore that image and perfectly engrave this law again in hearts: "lex Dei non ex omni parte deleta per iniustitiam, profecto scribitur renovata per gratiam." This is why that law written externally on tables of stone was not enough to carry out this new writing—justification—in the soul of the Jews, "in whom there still remained, as men, that native faculty by which the rational soul feels and acts some things according to the law." Grace, therefore, was necessary for Jews and Gentiles to be justified.

The holy Doctor recognizes, however, the capacity of free will, although violated by original sin, to execute some honest actions. Doctrine that was to serve as a foundation for the supreme pontiffs and councils in subsequent centuries to anathematize the errors of Protestants regarding the works of infidels. Is

It is true that such works, although honest, have no merit for eternal life without the grace of the Savior, except perhaps to mitigate a little the punishment of their impiety. "For, just as some venial sins, without which it is not possible to pass this life, do not prevent the righteous from deserving eternal life, so some good works are of no avail to the wicked for eternal life, without which the life of any evil man will hardly be found" (c. 28). Saint Augustine then poses the following question: "Is free will destroyed by grace? In no way," he answers, "but rather, it is strengthened by it. Just as the law is established by faith, so is free will by grace. The law is not annihilated, but established by faith, because faith achieves grace, and grace puts the law into practice; so also free will is not destroyed, but restored by grace, because grace heals the will for May justice be loved freely. Thus, the restoration of free will for the fulfillment of the law requires a complicated psychological process, which Saint Augustine ingeniously links in this kind of sorites: "The law is not made except by free will; but by the law the knowledge of sin is verified; by faith, the impetration of grace against sin; by grace, the healing of the soul from the wound of sin; by the healing of the soul, the freedom of will; by free will, the love of justice, and for the love of justice, the fulfillment of the law." Saint Augustine supports all these concepts with passages from Sacred Scripture, although they do not find this logical connection there (n. 52). This question is followed by another: "Is faith in our power?" Saint Augustine distinguishes between the power and the will of the will. Sometimes we want what we can't; Others, we can and we don't want to. He makes subtle reflections on the desire of the coerced will. To believe is to assent to the truth that is communicated to us. If we say no, we should fear the rebuke of the Apostle], who tells us: What do you have that you have not received?, being able to respond: "Behold, we have the will to believe without having received it."

Free will, he says, granted by the Creator to the rational soul, is that intermediate faculty that aspires to faith or that can incline to disbelief. Therefore it can no longer be said that the will with which man believes has not received it, since it arises from free will, that he received naturally when he was created. Do not forget that Saint Augustine considers the freedom violated by sin as a vestige of the perfect freedom, with which man was endowed in his creation. God therefore wants, adds the Saint, that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, but not in a way that violates their free will, of whose good or bad use they will be judged most justly. If we attribute to God the will to believe because it is born from free will, which we receive when we are created, the responsibility for sin must also be attributed to him, which is also the work of free will. It must be taken into account—answers the Saint—that the will to believe must not be attributed to God only because it comes from free will, which was given to us with creation—"quod nobis naturaliter." concreatum est"—but also because He works in us to will and believe through the suggestions of visible things, now extrinsically with evangelical exhortations, with the precepts of the law, when they persuade man of his weakness, making him seek the refuge of justifying grace, now also internally, where no one is the owner of having a single good thought, but only consent or dissent is proper to his will. By these various ways, by which God concurs with the rational soul, works in us to want to believe and in all things his mercy prevents us, since free will could believe nothing if some divine suggestion or vocation did not intervene to believe.

Saint Augustine ends his work fearing that he had become too wordy, reminding Marcellin of the cause that moved him to write it and reinforcing with new reasons and scriptural testimonies the possibility of achieving perfect justice with the grace of God and the cooperation of his free will. "Always," he concludes, "there is something mysterious and arcane at the bottom of divine judgments, so that they also

"let the mouth of the just close to their own praises and open only to the praises of God": "Aliquid ergo est in abdito et profound iudiciorum Dei, ut etiam iustorum omne os obstruatur in laude sua, et non aperiatur nisi in laudem Dei" (n. 66). Such is, in broad outline, the content of this second work of Saint Augustine against Pelagianism, which can be considered as a complement to De pcccatorum uteritis et remissione. It can be said that the Saint soon abandons the incidental question that motivated it and returns again to the capital points of the Pelagian heresy. In fact, the entire commentary on the Apostle's sentence: The letter kills, but the spirit gives life, is nothing other than a broad demonstration that the will and the law, without grace, are insufficient to justify. Thus, only faith is the principle of justification, and only charity, which excludes all fear of the law, can make it perfectly fulfilled. With admirable dialectic and subtle wit the holy Doctor refutes the objections that his adversaries might oppose him. He pursues them on all sides and closes all points of attack. The letter, together with the De peccatorum meritis et remissione, Saint Augustine laid down the unshakable foundations of his doctrine on grace, which was to earn him, over twenty years, the most glorious title of his theological wisdom: that of Doctor of Grace.

It remains for us to add a few words about the glorious death of Marcellinus, to whom these first works of Augustine on grace are dedicated. Perhaps no one contributed as much as he to the Bishop of Hippo going out to fight against the new heresy. The books that the Doctor of Grace dedicated to him are evident testimony of the Saint's close friendship. Prior to the preaching of Pelagius, the schism of the Donatists disturbed peace and endangered religious unity in Africa. But there came a time when both the more moderate Donatists and the Catholics wanted to reach a formula of harmony. Given these concerns and wishes of the schismatic and orthodox episcopate, the emperor Honorius issued on October 14, 410 an ordinance dated in Ravenna and addressed to the tribune of Carthage Flavius
OF THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER

Marcellin, naming him judge and supreme arbitrator of a great assembly of bishops from both sides. The conference, at which 278 Donatists and 286 Catholics were to be represented, took place in Carthage from June 1 to 8, 411. Augustine reduced the arguments and fallacies of the Donatists to dust. Marcellinus supported the Catholic cause with admirable fortitude and dignity and failed in the lawsuit against Donatus's supporters, who were forced to give up their seats. This fortitude was to cost the life of the zealous defender of Catholic interests in Africa. When Heraclius revolted in that province against Honorius, the Donatists, resentful of the tribune Marcellinus for his former efforts against the advances of the schism, accused him of complicity in the rebellion. The tribune was taken prisoner along with his brother Apringius, who had previously been proconsul of that same province. Count Marino, perhaps bought with the gold of the Donatists, instigated the persecution against the Catholics, and, fearful that those imprisoned could obtain freedom through the mediation of the bishops, he sentenced the two brothers to death and hastened the execution of the sentence. Thus the great tribune crowned the defense of the faith with the glorious palm of martyrdom, meriting that the Church included him in the catalog of its martyrs. Augustine visited his pious friend in the bitter hours of prison, bringing to his most noble soul the consolations of the religion, which he had defended with so much courage and zeal. In Epistle 151 the Bishop of Hippo has left us a reliable testimony of the great virtues of his illustrious friend. By then he had also dedicated the first three books of his magnum opus, The City of God, to him, in which he still had to invest many years. Thus, "the memory of Marcellin—writes Poujoulat—is presented to posterity under the guardianship of the genius and sanctity of the Bishop of Hippo" (Histoire du Saint Augustin, c. 33).

To guide this, the action of God is not necessary, but rather the capacity of man is sufficient; for if such perfection is possible in this life, there is no cause to believe that it does not exist without some example.
