Therefore, we cannot deny that such perfection is also possible in this life. Because all things are possible for God, both those that He accomplishes by His own will and those that He decreed that He could accomplish with the cooperation of the wills of His creatures. And for this reason, the one that is not realized among these possible things remains without example among the number of things realized; but in God and in his power is the reason why it could be realized, and in his wisdom, why it has not been realized; whose cause, if it remains hidden from man, he must not forget that he is a man, and thus he will not attribute insufficiency to God because he is not capable of fully understanding his wisdom. 8. law of God in all justice, when they were rather its transgressors. That is why the accumulation of sins committed by those who could not claim any ignorance was wracking them with the wrath of God. For even those who fulfilled what the law commanded did not do so out of love for justice nor aided by the Holy Spirit, but out of fear of punishment, and that is why before God there was no such thing in their will as to what seemed to men from outside in external works, but rather for that very reason they made themselves guilty before God, who knew what God would rather do, if it were possible, with impunity. For the Apostle calls circumcision of the heart the pure will of all illicit concupiscence; which is not achieved by the letter, which instructs and commands, but by the Holy Spirit, who helps and gives healthy medicine. And from those who do this is praise, which comes not from men, but from God, who through his grace grants them that they deserve to be praised. Therefore it is said of Him: In the Lord my soul will be exalted, just as it is also said to Him: My praise is before you; which is not done by those who only seek to pay God their praise insofar as they are men and themselves, on the other hand, in so far as they are just. 14. "But also," they argue, "we glorify God as the author of our justification, recognizing that He gave us the law, with the knowledge of which we learn how we should live." They do not pay attention to what they themselves read: That no man will be justified by the law in obedience to God. Because this justice can be simulated before men, but not before him who is the searcher of the heart itself and of the most secret will, in which He sees, although he who acts from fear of the law does something else, which, however, he would rather do, if it were lawful. And lest anyone should think that the Apostle meant here that no one is justified by that law, which in the ancient sacraments included many precepts in figure, among which was the circumcision of the flesh, which infants were to receive eight days after birth, he then adds to which law he was referring and says: For by the law the knowledge of sin. This, therefore, is that law of which he afterwards says: I did not know sin except by the law. For I would not know covetousness if the law did not precept: Thou shalt not covet. For what else does knowledge of sin mean by law?

This grace, which was hidden in the Old Testament, has been made manifest by the Gospel of Christ according to a very orderly economy of times with which the wisdom of God perfectly arranges all things. And perhaps it must refer to this concealment of grace that in the decalogue, given on Mount Sinai, only that which pertains to the Sabbath was veiled under a figurative precept. Well, Saturday is a day of sanctification. And it is not without cause that, among all the works that God performed in creation, sanctification is only spoken of for the first time at the moment in which he rested from all of them. But this is not the appropriate place to discuss this question. However—a warning that I consider sufficient in the matter at hand—the Jewish people were not unnecessarily commanded to abstain on that day from all servile work, by which sin is signified, because not sinning is the effect of sanctification, that is, of the gift of God through the Holy Spirit; and thus this precept alone, among all the others, was placed in the law, engraved on the tables of stone, as a figurative shadow under which the Jews observed the sanctification of the Sabbath, as signifying by this that that was the time in which the grace must remain hidden, which by the passion of Christ, as by the renting of the veil of the temple, was to be revealed. But what did the Apostle mean to infer from this when, repressing the boasting of the Jews, after saying: Not the hearers of the law, those are righteous before God, but the workers of the law, these will be justified, he next adds about them that, not having the law, they naturally fulfill the dictates of the law? Is this to be understood not of those who belong to the grace of the Mediator, but rather of those who, not worshiping the true God with true piety, nevertheless practice some good works in their impious lives? Or, perhaps, for this very reason he intended to demonstrate what he had already said before, that is, that there is no acceptance of persons for God, and what he affirmed shortly afterwards: that he is not only the God of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles? Or that those insignificant works of the law are not found impressed in those who did not receive the law but as relics of the image of God, which He does not reject when they believe in Him, for whom there is no acceptance of persons?

But whatever interpretation is accepted, it is clear that the grace of God was also promised by the prophet to the New Testament, and that this grace consists in the divine precepts being impressed on hearts.

52. Is free will destroyed by grace? No way; rather, we strengthen him with it. For as the law is established by faith, so free will is not annihilated, but strengthened by grace. Since not even the law itself can be fulfilled and it is not through free will, but through the law the knowledge of sin is verified; by grace, the healing of the soul from the wounds of sin; for the healing of the soul, the freedom of will; for free will, the love of justice, and, for the love of justice, the fulfillment of the law. Therefore, just as the law is not annihilated, but restored by faith, since faith achieves grace, by which the law is fulfilled, in the same way, free will is not annihilated, but rather strengthened by grace, since grace heals the will to ensure that justice is freely loved. All these concepts that I have linked in a concatenated way find their own expression in the Holy Scriptures. The law says: You shall not covet. Faith says: Heal, Lord, my soul, because I have sinned against you. Grace says: Behold, you have been healed; Do not want to sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you. Health says: Lord, my God, I cried to you and you healed me. Free will says: I will offer a voluntary sacrifice to you. The love of justice says: Sinners told me their pleasures, but not according to your law, O Lord! Why, then, do miserable men boldly pride themselves, now on their free will, now on their own strength, after they have already been liberated? They do not stop lying that the very name of free will means, without a doubt, freedom. Because where the spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. But if they are slaves to sin, why do they boast about free will? For whoever is defeated by another, for the same reason, remains a slave to the one who defeated him. And if they have already been set free, why do they boast about their works as if they were their own and boast as if they had received nothing? Are they so free that they do not want to have as their Lord the one who tells them: Without me you can do nothing; and also: If the Son gives you freedom, then will you be truly free?

53. Perhaps someone will ask if faith, which seems to be the principle of justification, as well as of the other graces that I have listed in sequence, is in our power. We will understand this more easily if, first of all, we examine with due diligence what the power of our will consists of. Willing and power are two very different things, so that he who wants cannot always, nor does he who can always want; and so, in the same way that sometimes we want what we cannot, so other times we can what we do not want. But by the very sound and evolution of the words it is sufficiently indicated that the name of will (voluntas) is derived from willing (velle), as well as the name of power or power (-potestas) is derived from power (posse). Therefore, just as he who wills has the faculty of willing or will, so also he who can has the faculty of power or potency. But for power to do something, the will must intervene. For it is not usually said that he who executes something acts voluntarily if he acts under duress. Although, if we examine this with all subtlety, we will notice that, even if someone is coerced to do something, if he does it, he still does it voluntarily; but because he would rather do something else, that is why it is said that he acts by force, that is, not wanting to act! For being coerced to act for some bad thing, which he would like to avoid or reject from himself, insofar as he does it as long as he is forced. Because if the will is so powerful that it wants more not to execute this action than to suffer that violence, then it undoubtedly resists whoever coerces it and does not execute that action. And therefore, if he acts, he certainly does not act with full and free will, although it is true, however, that he does not act without the faculty of willing, since since the will is followed by action, it cannot be said that the one who acts lacks power. But if, yielding to coercion, he wanted to act and could not, we would not say that the will was missing, although violated, but rather the power. On the contrary, if he did not act insofar as he did not want to, then without a doubt there was power, but it was lacking.

I am referring to that faith that we give when we give credit to something, not to that which we give when we make some promise. Because this is also called faith. But in a way we say: "He had no faith in me"; and from another very different: "He did not keep faith in me." Well, that means: "He didn't believe what I told him"; this other: "He didn't do what he told me." According to the faith with which we believe, we are faithful to God: according to the faith with which what is promised is fulfilled, God is also faithful to us. This is what the Apostle testifies to us: God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond your ability. What we ask, then, is: whether it is in our power to achieve the faith with which we believe in God or. with which we believe in God. Consider now whether there will be anyone who can believe, if he will not, or not believe, if he will. If this is absurd—because what is believing but assenting to what we are told is true? And assent, certainly, is an act of the will—then, without a doubt, faith is in our power. But—as the Apostle says—there is no power except from God. Why, then, should we not also be told of this, of faith: What do you have that you have not received? Because God also granted us what we can believe. However, we never read in the holy Scriptures: "There is no will except that of God." And precisely this is not written, because this is not true.

Well, otherwise, if there is no will that does not come from Him, God would also be—what is inadmissible—the author of sin; because bad will by itself is already a sin, even if the effect is not followed, that is, even if it cannot effect what it wants.

57. It remains, therefore, to investigate somewhat whether the will with which we believe is also itself a gift from God or whether it is applied naturally as an act of our innate free will. Now if we say that it is not a gift from God, we must fear, lest we judge that we have found some conclusion contrary to the doctrine of the Apostle when he rebukes and says: What have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? as if we could answer him: "Behold, we have the will to believe and we have not received it." "Behold, we boast of a thing which we have not received." But if we say that this will is also a gift from God, we must still fear that the unfaithful and impious themselves will rightly try to excuse themselves, as if their excuse of not having believed was just, because God did not want to grant them this will. For what has been said: That it is God who works in us both to will and to act according to his good pleasure, is already an effect of grace, which faith achieves, so that the works of man can be good, which work the same faith animated by charity, which is spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. If we believe that we can achieve this grace, and we certainly believe by an act of the will, we must inquire into the origin of this wanting in us. If it comes from nature, why not in everyone, since the same God is the Creator of all? And if it is a gift from God, why is it not also granted to everyone, since God wants all men to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth? 58. Let us examine the first and see if this question is satisfactorily answered by affirming that free will, naturally granted by the Creator to the rational soul, is a kind of intermediate faculty that can be directed either towards faith or towards disbelief; Well, if this is so, it can no longer be said that man has the will with which he believes God as if he had not received it, since when he is called by God, that will of free will is born in him that he naturally received when he was created. This is how God's will is never defeated. It would be, certainly, if He did not find a way to act towards those who despise Him or if they could somehow avoid what He has determined about them. Well, what does it mean, for example, when it is said: "I want all my servants to work in my vineyard and after work to eat restfully, in such a way that whoever does not want to do so is always grinding in the bakery"? In truth, whoever disregards such a command would act against the will of his master: but only then will he be able to overcome it, when by disregarding it, he manages to escape from the bakery, which is in no way possible under the power of God. Therefore it is written: The Lord spoke once, that is, without change; although this could also be understood from the Only Begotten Word. And adding next what God spoke unchangeably, he says: These two things I heard: that the power is in God, and in you, O Lord, the mercy, because you reward each one according to his works. Therefore, whoever, in order to accept faith, despises his mercy, will become guilty of condemnation under the power of God. But whoever believes and takes refuge in Him to be absolved of all his sins, cured of all his vices, enlightened and inflamed with his light and his heat, will exercise himself with his grace in good works, by which he will be freed even in his body from the corruption of the flesh and will be crowned and filled with goods that are not temporal, but eternal, much greater beyond comparison than what we can ask for or even understand. 59. The book that we present here to the readers of the B.. A. C. is one of the first that Saint Augustine published against Pelagius and was composed around the year 415. In an epistle written at the end of the same year, he says: "I have also written a voluminous book against the heresy of Pelagius at the request of some brothers to whom he had inoculated his most pernicious doctrine against the grace of Christ" *. In this, as in the other anti-Pelagian books, Saint Augustine is the champion of true humanism. Like Pelagius, he admires and celebrates the excellence of nature, as the work of a sovereign craftsman. But while his enemies were inflatores et praecipitatores of man, he follows a middle path between pessimism and optimism: "Let us worthily exalt the nature of man, but let his praise be directed to the glory of the Creator. For in such a way we must be grateful for the natural gifts, that we will not be ungrateful nor reject the medicine of our healing."

Christian and Augustinian humanism avoids the two pitfalls in which anthropological thought can founder: that of the Manichaeans, who admitted a substantial and incurable corruption of man, and that of the Pelagians, who deny all disease and all hereditary sin and the evil of concupiscence. Even fallen nature deserves great praise, for-

which is a figure and reverberation of the wonders and glory of God; but let us not take it as something entirely healthy and perfect, but rather sick and weak and in need of heavenly help. True humanism does not consist of singing songs about the greatness and self-sufficient power of the human spirit, much less separating it from the sources of the Savior. It needs more humble confession than fallacious defenses, says the author of De natura et gratia. God and man are better defended by confessing the Creator and Savior than when the magnitude of nature is inflated and the need for salvation is denied. God manifests a greater greatness and mercy in Catholic soteriology than in Pelagianism, which nullifies the great riches of God's being, especially in its most attractive aspect: his mercy and the mystery of his humility, just as the greatest depths and riches of Christ are revealed not in his doctrine, but in his redemption. In reality, Pelagius defended nature against the grace of God, and although the dialogue De natura has a metaphysical title, however, its author is above all a moralist and ascetic who considers the human being in his moral possibilities, praising his vigor against the indolent, who want to live as they please and not according to the difficult norms of virtue, alleging the impossibility of fulfilling them. The Pelagian man enjoys a perfect moral balance, and the change, introduced by sin, does not affect his nature, but his merit. When he sins, he becomes guilty of his bad action; once it is forgiven, he returns to his perfect state, without any morbid inclination towards evil or weakening of the forces of free will. That is why the Breton monk was demanding with those who followed his spiritual direction. Pelagian ethics carries within itself the germ of a rigid and dry moral idealism, which would have ended up in the abstract formalism of Kantian ethics, devoid of all sublime and creative energy of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Saint Augustine was not only more metaphysical, but also more psychologist than Pelagius, that is, he was endowed with a wealth of experience and a deeper knowledge of the human underworld and the despotism of the passions and the automatism of concupiscence. Man is sick because the image of God is tarnished by the sin of Adam and personal sin and he is unable by himself to resolve the great conflict within.

between the flesh and the spirit and to illuminate the darkness of existential problems. Thus the anthropology of Pelagius and that of Saint Augustine radically differ, as do their ethics and doctrine of salvation. Pelagianism professes an ethic of pure law and a theory of salvation without a Savior, to which the Doctor of the Church opposes the ethic of redemption and grace and interior freedom, with which Christ has freed us. In reality, with this doctrine he does not go against nature, but rather in its best defense. Pelagius had written his book to defend the splendid endowment of man's natural conditions; Saint Augustine responds in this book to defend grace, which does not go against nature, but saves and directs it: Librum ergo quo huic responded defendens gratiam, non contra naturam, sed per quam natura Uberatur et regiture. The Pelagians considered grace to be incompatible with free will; For Saint Augustine, it perfects, ennobles, heals and sanctifies man. Medicine does not go against nature, but against disease; grace does not go against nature, but against its vices and defects. The entire book De natura et gratia lays the foundations of the theological adage: Gratia non tollit, sed perficit naturam. Nature and grace are not forces that destroy each other, but rather they join forces and help each other. Thus, Saint Augustine has contributed with this book to clarify the relationships between the two, affirming the distinction and intimate union that they maintain between themselves.

11. And the author proposes to himself, as if through the mouth of an interlocutor, the following objection: "But you will say: That man can certainly be just, but by the grace of God." To which he responds: "Thank you for your benevolence, because not only have you not been content with not combating my assertion, which you have little combated, but you adduce proof in its favor. Because to say: "It certainly can, but by this or that means," is not only to admit the possibility, but also to show how or in what way it can be so. No one, then, admits the possibility of a thing better than one who formulates the conditions for it, since the qualities require a real object as support." Having made the previous statement, the objection is raised again: "But in this passage you seem to deny the grace of God, since you do not mention it." To which he responds: "Am I perhaps the one who rejects grace when, in confessing a thing, I necessarily admit the means of achieving it, or is it you, who, by denying the thing, also annul the means by which it is achieved, whatever they may be?" The author has already forgotten that he responds to one who does not deny the thing, whose objection he had proposed shortly before by saying: "Man can certainly be without sin, but by the grace of God." How can he deny the possibility, for whose defense he strives so hard, who says to him: "Is it possible, but with the grace of God?" But if, leaving this man who already confesses the thing, he messes with those who deny the possibility of finding a man without sin, what does it matter to us? Let him mess with whoever he pleases, as long as he confesses what he denies with execrable impiety, namely, that without the grace of God he cannot live. Therefore, James has not said nor declared with those words that it was easier to control the language than the wild beasts; On the contrary, he wanted to show how great an evil language is in man, so that no one can subdue it, even though men tame even wild beasts. That is not the wisdom that comes from above, but earthly, animal, demonic wisdom. Because where there is envy and quarrels, there is no shortage of turbulence and all kinds of evils. Such is the wisdom that dominates the tongue, the wisdom that has a celestial origin and does not come from the human heart. Who will dare, then, to snatch it from the grace of God and proudly place it in the natural power of the future? If he can have it from his own harvest, why does he implore himself to receive it? Or perhaps you don't want to ask for the honor of free will, which is sufficient for itself with its own resources to fulfill all the precepts of justice? Well, the same apostle James also contradicts himself when he warns us and says: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives it to all generously and without reproach, and it will be granted to him; but ask for it with faith, without hesitating in the least. For because of the tongue, which no man can restrain, but wisdom, which comes from above, we all lack in many things. Rather, it is a deprivation of substance, because the delicacy is the substance. And to what he objects by saying that "the Lord could die although he was free from sin," we answer that for Him also being born was a voluntary work of mercy, not a condition of nature; He also died because he wanted to, making himself our price to redeem us from death. And this is precisely what the Pelagians want to nullify with their disputes by defending human nature with such determination that the price of the death of Christ is not necessary for free will so that it can pass from the power of darkness and the prince of death to the kingdom of Christ the Lord. And yet, when the Lord walked to the passion, he said: Behold, the prince of this world will come and find nothing in me; That is, he will not find any sin that gives him the right to kill me. But so that everyone may know, he added, that I do my Father's will, get up, let's go here. It means: I do not die because of the force of sin, but because I want to obey. 27. He also maintains that "no evil is the cause of any good!" As if it were a good thing, and yet it has been a cause of conversion for many. There are, then, evils that take advantage of the ineffable mercy of God. Was the Psalmist speaking of a good thing when he said: You withdrew your face from me and I was troubled? Certainly not; and yet this disturbance was in some way a salutary remedy for his pride, for he had said in his prosperity: In this state I will always remain, attributing to himself what was a favor from God. Well, what did I have that I hadn't received? It was appropriate to tell him the source of his assets so that he could humbly recover what he had lost through pride. And may He lead us to the promises, where His path leads us, for it is also said to Him: Because there your hand will take me and your right hand will hold me. And He will feed those who rest with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, as it is written: And he will seat them at his table, and going from one to another, he will serve them. By remembering these truths we do not destroy free will, but rather we preach divine grace. 38. Of course, I greatly applaud the response to the objectors who say: "What you maintain seems reasonable, but it is arrogant to say that men can live without sin." He answers that if that is the truth, there is no pride in saying it. And he adds with great acuity and truth: "Where should humility be placed? Without a doubt, none of it should go with falsehood, if pride is on the side of truth." Therefore he concludes, and rightly so, that humility must be associated with the truth and not with lies. Hence it follows that the words of Saint John: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not on our side, are a true expression of the truth, nor should it be believed that under the pretext of humility he invented such a lie. And that is why he added: and the truth is not with us, when it would have been enough to say: "we deceive ourselves", looking at some who might think that this last expression was said because he who boasts of true goods also becomes arrogant. Adding then: The truth is not with us, clearly shows—and our author follows him very well on this point—that this is not absolutely true, saying that we are without sin, lest humility, going hand in hand with lies, lose the reward of truth. 39. Pelagius, by exaggerating the forces of nature, prides himself on taking the cause of God by force, nor does he notice that, by maintaining the perfect health of man, he rejects the mercy of the Physician. In affection, oneself are the Creator and Savior of nature. We must not, therefore, praise the Creator in such a way that we are forced and persuaded to add that the Savior is superfluous. Let us exalt human nature with worthy praises and toast with them to the glory of the Creator; and let us be so grateful for the goods of creation that we do not disgrace God for the grace with which he has redeemed us. Let us attribute the vices from which He heals us, not to the work of God, but to the will of man and the just punishment deserved for our sins; But if we confess that in the beginning we were able to remain exempt from such vices, let us agree that later their cure is the work of mercy.

He also writes: "If in the sacred Scriptures there appear examples of some who sinned—if one reflects carefully—they were not written to plunge us into the despair of not sinning or to give us in a certain way the security of sinning," but so that we would learn either humility in penitence or also to encourage our hope in similar falls. 43. They may object, he continues: "Could sacred Scripture enumerate the sins of everyone?" Those who say to him will respond well: "The author has not responded in a coherent way to our objection, although I see that he did not want to remain silent." Consider, I pray you, his words: "This may well be said of those of whom the Scripture does not mention either good or bad works; but in the case of the righteous, whose holy works it remembers, it would undoubtedly have also mentioned the bad ones if it had believed that they sinned." In that case, say that the lively faith of those who with great concurrence preceded and followed with praise to the donkey on which the Lord was sitting and among the fury of the enemies, rabid against this manifestation, cheered him saying: Glory to the Son of David; blessing to him who comes in the name of the Lord. Dare to say, if you can, that in such a gathering of people there was not a single man guilty of any sin. And if this is a most absurd assumption, why did the divine Scripture not mention any sin when it so carefully exalted the great faith of those protesters? 44. The force of this objection was surely felt by Pelagius, and that is why he added: "Moreover supposing that in other times, because of the multitude of men, the enumeration of sins was suppressed, but sticking to the origins of the human race, when there were only four people, why did he not want to inform us of all their crimes? Because of the crowd? There was none. Or does he only remember the sins of the guilty, being unable to mention those of the innocent, who had committed none? And he develops this opinion with greater clarity of reasons: "We know that then there were only four men: Adam and Eve, from whom Cain and Abel were born; Eve sinned, as the Scripture declared; Adam also sinned, according to the testimony of the same Scripture; and let's say the same of Cain, whose sin was recorded in the holy books. The seriousness of these sins is indicated there even. Therefore, if Abel had sinned, he would be saved.

45. When writing these words, the author forgot what he had said shortly before, that is, that "when the human race multiplied, sacred Scripture was able to avoid the enumeration of all sins because of the very numerous mass of men." If I had reflected on this enough, I would have found even in a single man a mass and multitude of light sins that either could not be recorded or, even if they could, should not be recorded. Because in what he left us written we had to keep a limit and with few examples sufficiently instruct the reader for many necessary things. In fact, Holy Scripture did not want to leave us a detailed account of even the hoiribres of that time, although they were few; how many or who they were, that is, how many sons and daughters Adam and Eve fathered, and the names they gave them. For this reason, many, not noticing the gaps that exist in the sacred Scripture, thought that Cain had carnal intercourse with his mother to obtain the offspring that is mentioned, believing that they were not brothers of those sons of Adam, because the Scripture had then left them silent, who later, completing what was omitted, mentions when it says: Adam begat sons and daughters, without indicating either the time of birth or the number or names. According to this, there was no reason to describe whether Abel, although rightly called righteous, ever lacked temperance in laughter, or indulged in dissipation, or committed any sin of desire, or was carried away by excessive greed in gathering the fruits of the earth, or lacked moderation in eating, or had distractions in prayer, and how many times he had these and other similar slips. Are these not sins, and does not the Apostle advise us to guard against them and avoid them when he says: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as not to obey its desires? We must maintain a daily and perpetual struggle to not consent to these illicit or inconvenient movements. Because of this vicious inclination, the eyes wander and pour out after what is not convenient; and if it gains strength and prevails, it leads to bodily adultery, which

46. With a notable sentence the author closed this place, saying: "Let us believe, then, what we read and consider it a crime to believe what is not written." On the contrary, I oppose, we must not believe everything we read, as the Apostle admonishes us: Read all things, but retain what is good. Likewise, I say that it is no crime to admit what we do not read. Indeed, we can in good faith, as witnesses, admit what we know from experience, even without having read it anywhere. Here the author will surely reply: "When I spoke in that way, I was referring to the holy books." I wish to God that I didn't admit what I don't read, but anything contrary to what they teach. For with submissive fidelity I would accept what is written there: Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it was transmitted to all men, in whom all sinned. Admitting this, I would not eclipse the grace of such an excellent Physician by not wanting to confess that man's nature is flawed. I wish I could read with the eyes of a Christian that apart from Jesus Christ there is no other name under heaven in whom it is appropriate for us to be saved. I would not defend the forces of nature until I came to say that man through free will, even without the virtue of that Name, can be saved.

51. What, then, should we stop further? Let's come to the core of the cause, which is the only or almost the only one we have with these Pelagians. As Pelagius says that "for the question that interests you it does not concern you to find out whether there have been or are some innocent men in this life, but whether it is possible that there were or that there are", so I, even granting him that there were or are now, maintain that in no way could or can there be righteous without the justifying grace of God through Jesus Christ, our Lord, and him crucified. The same faith saved the ancient righteous and saves us, namely, that of the Mediator between God and men, the Man Jesus Christ; faith in his blood, faith in his cross, faith in his death and resurrection. Therefore, having the same spirit of faith, we also believe, and for this reason we also speak. 52.' Let us see, then, how Pelagius responds to the question proposed, with a solution inadmissible for Christians. Because he says: "But, apparently, it impresses many that man is granted the possibility of living without any sin without counting on the grace of God." Certainly, that is what impresses us, that is what we reproach him for. Here comes the heart of the matter. This is what we can't stand. The love we have for others and for ourselves does not allow us to tolerate disputes among Christians about these things. Let us see, then, how it is disentangled from this objection. "Oh blindness of ignorance! he cries; oh apathy of the unlearned soul, which believes that it can defend itself without the grace of God what should be attributed to God alone!" If we did not look at what follows, sticking to these words, it would be believed that we have formed a false current of opinion against the Pelagians by letting ourselves be carried away by what is rumored by fame and the testimony and assertions of some brothers. And he illustrates his proposition with examples: "I can speak, to give an example; this faculty of speaking does not come from me, it is not my thing; on the other hand, what I speak belongs to me, that is, it depends on my own will; and since what I speak is the work of my free will, I can do both, speak or not speak; but as for the faculty of speaking itself, since it does not depend on me and is not a matter of my will and will, I necessarily always possess it, and, if I want, I can not speak, but I cannot help but possess the faculty of speaking, unless I cut off my tongue, which is the organ of speech." Much could be said about the possibility of preventing speech if a man wants, even without amputating the limb that serves that function. 65. I ask, then, where nature lost this freedom for which it sighs when it says: Who will set me free? He does not accuse the substance of the flesh, when he asks to be delivered from this body of death, since both the nature of the body and that of the soul are to be attributed to God, as Cause; The Apostle refers to the vicious inclinations of the body. For bodily death separates from the body; but contracted through the body, we carry inherent vices, to which the just punishment that the rich man received in hell is due. From this last punishment, could he not be freed who cries: Who will free me from this body of death? But wherever he has lost this freedom, he possesses as an inadmissible endowment that possibility of nature and the power to act with the help of natural help and the will of free will. Why, then, does he seek the sacrament of baptism? Perhaps to obtain forgiveness for past sins, the commission of which cannot be annulled? Leave it; do not drown out that cry of man. For he not only desires indulgence and remission of past sins, but also the strength and vigor not to commit them in the future. THE REMISSION OF SINS ACCORDING TO THE PELAGIANS (XVIII, 20).

The Pelagians did not dare to openly combat the article of the Symbol: I believe in the remission of sins. But they considered sin above all in its legal aspect and connection with punishment. Without a doubt, it imprints a deformity, which cannot be annulled by the action of any creature and requires the power of the Creator. In the Augustinian conception, the sinner violates the rights of God and is entitled to punishment, but also in a profound oncological sense he corrupts and deforms and disfigures the image of God. And grace not only lifts the punishment or frees us from the wrath of God, but also restores the divine beauty, lost through guilt. The effects of divine forgiveness are much deeper in the Augustinian doctrine than in the Pelagian one; and, for the same reason, the desire for forgiveness is more urgent and painful, because the entire human being has become degraded and diminished in strength and health. Pelagian grace is the simple return to divine forgiveness with which sin disappears, because it is no longer worthy of God's punishment: Augustinian grace is all that; but together with an intimate renewal of the being, which is once again clothed in the ontological similarity with its eternal exemplar. 9.
SIN IS NOT SUBSTANCE (XX, 22).—In the discourses

This chapter shows the lack of metaphysics of the enemies of grace. They, without a doubt, wanted to interpret the Catholic doctrine of original sin as an echo of the Manichean doctrine, as they blame Saint Augustine Julian. But the great Doctor had thoroughly eliminated the Manichean system. He had professed a substantialist metaphysics of evil which was one of the greatest obstacles to his conversion. The Manichean solution to the problem of evil was based on dualism, that is, on the sovereignty of two absolute and contrary principles that mutually war and contradict each other. They are two eternal substances, from which good and bad come. But with the method of Platonic philosophy he glimpsed the true nature of evil, and found that it was not a substance, but the perversity of the will, which departs from the supreme substance, which is God, to throw itself into the exterior, squandering its own treasure: Kt quaesivi quid esset iniquitas, et non inveni substantiam; sed a summa substantia, te Deo, detortae in Ínfima voluntatis perversitatem, proiicientis intima sua, et lumescentis foras (Conf., V I I, ió: P L 32, 744). The Doctor of Grace had meditated a lot on these problems of the essence of sin, when Pelagius, with apparent acuity, described as impossible the moral violation and havoc of human nature. THE LIGHT AND THE MYSTERY OF GRACE (XXVI, 29).—St. Augustine uses here one of the great metaphors of his metaphysics to clarify the mystery of grace. Thus his thinking regarding the natural and supernatural order acquires a certain connection with the link of this common analogy. The two statements of Saint John: Deus lux est and Deus caritas est, gave rise to Augustinian thought in the resolution of the most arduous problems related to God and man. The metaphor of light illuminates the double elevating and healing aspect of grace, which gives the human spirit a new visual power to glimpse higher realities; creates what he calls the Holy oculus fidei, the organ of faith, whose object is the invisible world. The spirit acquires a type of perception superior to that of reason. The Pelagians attributed to the Apostle an angelic perfection, maintaining that the infelix homo of the aforementioned epistle, whose psychology he describes, is not the same; Rather, he personifies panting humanity struggling with its lusts. «Hoc enim quod tu de Apostólo intelligere cupis, omnes ecclesiastici viri iu peccatoris et sub lege adhuc positi asseruut eum dixisse persona, qui nimia vitiorum consuetudine velut quadam teneretur necessitate peccandi, et quamvis bonum appeteret volúntate, usu tamen praecipitaretur in malum» (De grat. Christi, 1, 39, 43: P L 44, 379-380). That's what Pelagius called him. •He alludes to this objection in sermon 154, 3, 4 (PL 38, 834): "There are those who say that in these places the Apostle transfigures in himself I don't know what other fighter who looks faint, defeated, captive." But the Holy Doctor, based on various testimonies, does not believe that certain struggles of the flesh against the spirit, which served as a protection for his humility and were the occasion for great victories and merits, are incompatible with the relative perfection of justice, typical of this world. This is how he interprets the passage in the sermon cited: Ne magnitudeine revelationum mearum extollar, datus est mihi stimulus carnis tneae, angelus satanás qui me collaphizet. According to the Doctor of Grace, there are three categories of men; It is convenient to know: the totu-s carnalis, the partim carnalis et partim spiritualis and the totus spiritualis. The first is a plaything of his lust, which drags him wherever he wants. The second, assisted by the grace of God, resists evil desires and overcomes them, living according to the law of God. Although according to his flesh he is carnal, according to his mind he is spiritual: mente spiritualis, carne carnalis. The third is perfectly spiritual, with the complete extinction of his passions: he no longer feels the sting of the flesh, because he is

A SENTENCE ATTRIBUTED TO POPE SIXTH II

Lagio cited in his favor some words from Pope Saint Sixtus I, under whose name a collection of moral sentences written in Greek, of Pythagorean origin and attributed to the philosopher Sextus, ran in the 4th century. In the 111th or 11th century this collection was retouched and Christianized by an unknown author, and Rufinus of Aquileya disseminated in the West a Latin version made by him: Sextum in latinum veril, quein Sextum ipsum esse iradunt, qiii apud vos, id cst in Urbe Roma Xystus voealur, Episcopi et Martyris gloria decóralas. From the words of Saint Augustine it is inferred that the collection was well known, and to the sentence with a Pelagian flavor, used by his adversary, he gives my orthodox meaning. Later, knowing the error, disclosed above all by Rufino, he issued this retraction: In quo verba quaedam quae velwt (Relract., IT, 42: PIL 3'2, 647). Without a doubt, Saint Jerome helped him out of his error. Cf. Epist. ad Cthesiphontem, 133, 1030 (PL 22, 1152). Still in the Roman Breviary (August 6) the ancient opinion that was formed about the Roman Pope by the apocryphal collection of his sentences is reflected: Xystus secundas atheniensis, ex pliilosopho Christi diseipulus. 20.
HEALING AND PRESERVATION (LX'VII, SO).—God has, according to Saint

Augustine, a double providence for human illnesses: sometimes he cures and staunches them, other times he prevents and avoids them. We already know that the Pelagians regarded prevenient grace with particular aversion. Both modes of healing recall the double liberative and preservative redemption. This distinction has its importance in the doctrine of grace and in the spiritual life for self-knowledge and divine benefits, which we often miss. Saint Therese of the Child Jesus says very well on this subject: "I imagine that the son of a great doctor, upon tripping over a rock! walking, falls and breaks a limb. His father comes quickly, lifts him up with love, and heals all his wounds, using all his skill and experience in the profession. Completely healthy, the daughter wants to express her gratitude without delay. This son has the imperative duty to love his father. But here is another case. Suppose that the father, having realized that stone is so dangerous for his son, goes ahead and pushes him away, without being seen by anyone. Surely, his son.

For one who had such loving providence, ignoring the misfortune from which his father's hand has delivered him, he will not give thanks and will love him less than if he had saved him from a mortal wound. But if you could understand everything, wouldn't you feel obliged to love him more? (History of my soul, I V, 27). Saint Augustine, regarding the preservative benefits, says in his Confessions: I am indebted to your grace and mercy that you have melted my sins like ice. And I am also indebted for the sins that I have not committed or could not commit, because you were my guide: «Gratiae tuae deputo et misericordiae tuae, quod peecata me a tanquam glaciem solvisti. Gratiae tuae deputo, et quaecumque non fecit mala... Et omnia mihi dimissa esse íateor, et quae mea sponte feci mala, et quae te duce non feci» (Conf., I I, 7).
